content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l241-l332","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THIS VOLUME IS ENDOWED IN PART BY CHARLES S. PETERSON OF CHICAGO / ACKNOWLEDGEMENT / GENERAL INTRODUCTION / WHAT IS THE POETIC EDDA?; lines 241-332","start":"241","end":"332","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory discussion of the Poetic Edda’s uncertain origins, its relationship to Snorri Sturluson’s Prose Edda, early modern scholarly debates over attribution (including Sæmundr the Wise), the 1643 discovery of the Codex Regius manuscript and later additions from other manuscripts, and competing proposals for the meaning of the word “Edda.”","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that the poems called the Edda have a “mysterious” history and that it is not known who composed them, when/where they were composed, who collected them, or what the word “Edda” definitively means.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A prose work preserved in 13th–early 14th century manuscripts is described as a poet’s handbook containing mythological stories, explanation of figures/tropes of Norse poetic diction, and a treatise on metrics; it is commonly known as Snorri Sturluson’s Edda (the Prose/Younger Edda).","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage reports an Icelandic tradition that persisted in ascribing an Edda (or similar work) to Sæmundr the Wise, and describes how Arngrímur Jónsson argued in the early 17th century that Snorri must be responsible for the work in question.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage states that in 1643 Bishop Brynjólfur Sveinsson discovered a manuscript (written as early as 1300) containing 29 poems, some sharing lines/stanzas used by Snorri, and that this find was labeled as Sæmundr’s Edda and became known as the Elder/Poetic Edda.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage identifies the Codex Regius (R2365) in the Royal Library in Copenhagen as the basis for published editions, and notes other manuscripts and later additions, giving totals such as 34 poems in many editions and describing specific supplementary manuscripts/poems.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage presents multiple scholarly guesses about the meaning of “Edda,” including an early idea linking it to “Poetics,” and Jacob Grimm’s proposal connecting it to a word in Rigsthula meaning (conjecturally) “great-grandmother,” with the comment that “Tales of a Grandmother” is inappropriate.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Unnamed composers/collectors of the Eddic poems (unknown)","description":"The passage emphasizes that the composers and collectors of the poems are not known.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Snorri Sturluson","description":"Named as the composer of the Prose/Younger Edda; death given as 1241; his work quotes poems used as sources.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Arthur G.     "quote": "",
    "summary": "An overview of Old Norse literary history (c. 850–1300): Scandinavian migrations and battles; Iceland’s settlement and cultural development; Christianity’s introduction and its effects on learning; a major era of oral literature followed by the writing-down of traditions by saga writers; a later decline after political subjugation and disasters; and a rough division of the surviving literature into sagas, skaldic poetry, Eddic poems, and didactic/religious/legal works.",

    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Old Norse literature is described as covering approximately 850–1300, with major Scandinavian wanderings early in that period.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Harald the Fair-Haired is said to have won the sea-fight of Hafrsfjord (872), breaking independent nobles and becoming overlord of nearly all Norway; some defeated nobles fled overseas.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "The passage mentions Northmen inroads in France, including Hrolf Gangr (Rollo) laying siege to Paris in 885.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Norwegians are described as going to Ireland; Dublin is mentioned as built by their compatriots; their control is said to have lasted until Brian Boru’s victory at Clontarf (1014).",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Migrations to Iceland are presented as especially important; Iceland is characterized by independence and remoteness from Norway’s wars, while maintaining contact with southern culture through a roving life.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Christianity is said to have been introduced throughout the Norse world about the year 1000, bringing stability of learning; Icelanders are described as makers, students, and recorders of history.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "The years 875–1100 are described as a spontaneous period of oral literature, with leaders also being poets; narrative prose is said to have flourished due to a passion for storytelling and story-hearing.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "After 1100, saga writers (“sagamen”) are said to have collected oral material and given it permanent written form; much of Old Norse literature is said to have originated orally and been finalized by scholars (mostly Icelanders) in the century after 1150.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "After 1250, a rapid decline is described: Iceland loses independence (becoming a Norwegian province); later Norway falls under alien rule; pestilence, famine, and volcanic disturbances are mentioned; literary production is said to shift toward translations of French romances, with poorer native poetry and prose.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "The collected/written literature (largely 1150–1250) is divided into four groups: sagas (mostly prose narratives), skaldic poetry (complex figurative praise and other songs), Eddic poems (more impersonal; contrasted with skaldic style), and didactic works (religious/legal treatises, etc.).",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    }
  ],

    "translation": "The Poetic Edda",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."

  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "An introductory note summarizes the structure and themes of the poem Völuspá: Othin seeks knowledge from a völva; she recounts creation and early events, then prophesies the gods' destruction in a final battle involving overwhelming fire and flood, followed by a renewed world and Baldr's return. The note discusses possible Christian and Celtic influence. The passage then opens the poem with stanzas in which the seer addresses Valfather, recalls giants, nine worlds in a tree, the primordial age of Ymir and a yawning gap, the making of Miðgarðr by Búri's sons, the early unassigned courses of sun/moon/stars, and the gods' council that names parts of the day and counts years.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "The introductory note describes a narrative framework in which Othin calls on a völva (wise-woman), who recounts the past (creation, origins) and then prophesies the final destruction of the gods, followed by a new world arising and Baldr returning.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The introductory note states that in the final battle, fire and flood overwhelm heaven and earth as gods fight their enemies.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "The introductory note discusses scholarly views about the poem’s date and character, asserting the poet was heathen while also claiming there are striking evidences of Christian influence and likely contact with converted Celtic peoples.",
      "category": "other",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "In stanza 1, the speaker asks to be heard by the 'holy races' and 'Heimdall's sons,' and addresses 'Valfather' with a promise to relate old tales remembered from long ago.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "In stanza 2, the speaker remembers 'giants of yore' who gave her bread, and says she knew nine worlds, the nine in a tree with mighty roots beneath the mold.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "In stanza 3, a primordial time is described when Ymir lived; there was no sea, cool waves, sand, earth, or heaven above, but a yawning gap and no grass.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "In stanza 4, Búr's sons lift the land and make Miðgarðr; the sun from the south warms the stones of earth, and the ground becomes green with growing leeks.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "In stanza 5, the sun (called sister of the moon), the moon, and the stars lack knowledge of their homes, might, or stations.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "In stanza 6, the gods seek assembly-seats, hold council, and give names to noon, twilight, morning, the waning moon, night, evening, and thus number the years.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    }

lines 805-954","start":"805","end":"954","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes early divine activity (building and craftsmanship), the arrival of giant-maids, the creation and listing of dwarfs, the finding and ensouling of the first humans (Ask and Embla), the world-tree Yggdrasil and the three wise maidens who allot fate, the burning and repeated rebirth of Gollveig/Heith and the beginning of war, divine councils and broken oaths, sacred objects hidden under the tree and in Mimir’s well (Heimdall’s horn; Odin’s eye), a gathering of Valkyries, foretelling of Baldr’s fate involving mistletoe and vengeance, and a figure bound in wet woods with Sigyn beside him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The gods meet at Ithavoll, build shrines and temples, establish forges, and craft tools; they live in peace and play at tables, lacking no gold.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Three giant-maids, huge of might, come from Jotunheim to the gods’ place.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The gods hold council to decide who should raise/create the race of dwarfs out of Brimir’s blood and the legs of Blain; the list is said to be known for all time.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Three come forth from the home of the gods and find Ask and Embla on land, described as without fate and empty of might; Odin gives soul, Hnir gives sense, and Lothur gives heat/motion and goodly hue.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Yggdrasil is named as a great ash tree, wet with white water; dews fall into dales from it; it grows green by Urth’s well.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Three maidens mighty in wisdom come from a dwelling beneath the tree (Urth, Verthandi, Skuld); they score on wood, make laws, allot life, and set fates for the sons of men.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A first war in the world is remembered: the gods spear Gollveig and burn her in a hall; she is burned three times and born three times, and yet lives; she is named Heith, a wide-seeing witch who works magic and bewitches minds.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Odin hurls a spear over a host and war first comes; the wall around the gods is broken and the field is trodden by the warlike Wanes; the gods hold councils about tribute/worship and about who filled the air with venom or gave Oth’s bride to giants; Thor rises in rage and oaths/pledges are broken.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Heimdall’s horn is hidden under a high-reaching holy tree; a mighty stream pours from Valfather’s pledge; Odin’s eye is said to be hidden deep in Mimir’s well, and Mimir drinks mead from Odin’s pledge each morning.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Valkyries are seen assembling, ready to ride to the ranks of the gods; lines 1219-1311","start":"1219","end":"1311","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes summarizing mythic episodes referenced in Völuspá: Loki’s theft of Andvari’s treasure and its curse; creation of the first man and woman (Ask and Embla) by three gods, possibly from trees; Yggdrasil tended with healing water from Urðr’s well; the three Norns and fate-runes cut on wood; the war between the gods and the Vanir and a treaty involving hostage exchange; Gollveig/Heiðr and the power of gold; and a tale of rebuilding Ásgarðr by a giant builder demanding the sun, moon, and Freyja, foiled by Loki and slain by Thor, with later enmity due to broken oaths.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A dwarf named Andvari is said to have been treacherously robbed of his wealth by Loki; Andvari placed a curse on the treasure, and the curse is said to have brought about multiple deaths (including Sigurðr, Gunnarr, and Atli).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes state that three gods (Óðinn, Hœnir, and Lóðurr) go forth to create a man and a woman, Ask and Embla, and that Snorri says this pair was made out of trees.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Hœnir is described as surviving the destruction and, in the new age, assuming the gift of prophecy; he was given as a hostage to the Vanir after their war in exchange for Njǫrðr.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Lóðurr is described as apparently an older name for Loki; Loki is characterized as treacherous but ingenious, and is associated with giving heat to the newly created pair, possibly reflecting an origin as a fire-god.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Yggdrasil (the world-ash) is said to be kept green by being sprinkled with marvelous healing water from Urðr’s well.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Three maidens identified as the Norns—Urðr, Verðandi, and Skuld (Past, Present, and Future)—are discussed; the notes say that magic signs (runes) controlling human destinies were cut on pieces of wood.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A first war is described as occurring between the gods and the Vanir; it ended with a treaty and exchange of hostages, and the Vanir are said to have been originally water-deities; Gollveig’s ill-treatment is described as the immediate cause of the war.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Heiðr is described as a name often applied to wise-women and prophetesses; the stanza’s reference is suggested to involve the magic and destructive power of gold, though its application is said to be unclear.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After a battle and victory of the Vanir, the gods are said to have taken council, debating whether to pay tribute or to admit the victors to equal rights of worship.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A rebuilding of Ásgarðr is described: the gods hire a giant builder who demands the sun, the moon, and Freyja as reward; Loki delays the giant by a trick so the work is not finished in time; the giant threatens the gods and Thor slays him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The notes state that the gods, by violating oaths made to the giant builder, aroused the undying hatred of the giants’ race, making them enemies in the final battle.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Andvari","description":"A dwarf robbed of his wealth by Loki; he laid a curse on his treasure.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Loki (also linked with Lóðurr)","description":"A treacherous but ingenious god; said to have robbed Andvari; linked with Lóðurr; associated with giving heat; forced to delay a giant builder by a trick.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Sigurðr","description":"Named among those whose deaths were brought about by the curse on Andvari’s treasure.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Gunnarr","description":"Named among those whose deaths were brought about by the curse on Andvari’s treasure.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"Named among those whose deaths were brought about by the curse on Andvari’s treasure.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Óðinn (Hár / ‘the High One’ / Hor)","description":"One of three gods said to go forth to create man and woman; identified with ‘the High One’.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Hœnir","description":"One of three gods involved in creating man and woman; later a hostage exchanged after the war with the Vanir; survives destruction and gains prophecy in the new age.","role_refs":["role:7","role:8","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Lóðurr","description":"Named with Óðinn and Hœnir as going forth to create man and woman; THE WISE-WOMANS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 1415-1514","start":"1415","end":"1514","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes describing places and beings in Völuspá stanzas 37–49: dwarfs’ dwellings; Nastrond as a realm of the dead with punishments; Níðhǫggr beneath Yggdrasil; Fenrir’s parentage and binding; signs and awakenings for the final struggle (wolves chasing sun and moon; storms; cocks crowing; Gjallarhorn); guardians of Hel’s realm; and the myth of Mímir’s preserved, speaking head as a source of wisdom.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Niðavellir/Niðafjǫll is described as a home of dwarfs; Sindri is a dwarf gold-worker; Okolnir may be a volcano; Brimir is presented as a leader of dwarfs and possibly linked to Ymir and the dwarfs’ origin from blood in an earlier stanza.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Nástrǫnd is identified as a land of the dead ruled by Hel where the wicked undergo tortures; a 'smoke-vent' is explained by reference to an Icelandic house roof opening.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A stanza is said to depict torments for oath-breakers and murderers; Níðhǫggr is described as a dragon beneath the ash Yggdrasil gnawing at its roots, symbolizing destructive elements.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Fenrir is described as a wolf child of Loki and the giantess Angrbotha; he is chained by the gods with the chain Gleipnir, made by a dwarf from six things; the binding costs the god Týr his right hand.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A giantess connected with Ironwood is noted; her children with Fenrir are the wolves Skǫll and Hati, who take the sun and moon; this has been interpreted by some scholars as an eclipse-myth.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The final struggle account includes signs such as the sun growing dark and mighty storms; beings and groups are awakened or summoned: Eggþér as a giant watchman; Fjalar and Gollinkambi as cocks waking giants and gods/heroes; an unnamed rust-red bird waking Hel’s people; Heimdall blowing Gjallarhorn; and the world-tree Yggdrasil trembling.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Garm is described as a dog guarding the gates of Hel’s kingdom; Gnipahellir is a cliff-cave entrance to the world of the dead.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Mímir’s head is described as cut off by the Vanir and returned; Óðinn embalms it and by magic gives it speech so its wisdom remains available.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Surt is described as a giant ruling the fire-world Muspellsheim; Fenrir is said to slay Óðinn in the final struggle; Jǫtunheim is identified as the land of the giants.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Dwarfs","description":"A people associated with Niðavellir/Niðafjǫll; Sindri is a notable gold-worker among them; Gleipnir is fashioned by a dwarf.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sindri","description":"A great worker in gold among the dwarfs.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Brimir","description":"A giant possibly identified with Ymir; also explained as a leader of dwarfs in this context.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Hel","description":"Goddess ruling Nástrǫnd / Hel’s domain, associated with the world of the dead and punishments for the wicked.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Níðhǫggr","description":"A dragon beneath the ash Yggdrasil that gnaws at its roots, symbolizing destructive elements.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Yggdrasil","description":"An ash tree whose roots are gnawed by Níðhǫggr; the tree trembles during end-time events.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Fenrir","description":"A wolf, child of Loki and Angrbotha; chained by the gods with Gleipnir; in the final struggle he slays Óðinn.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Loki","description":"Named as Fenrir’s father; with Angrbotha he also fathers Miðgarðsormr and Hel.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Angrbotha","description":"A giantess named as Fenrir’s mother; mother of Miðgarðsormr and Hel as well.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Miðgarðsormr (Midgard Serpent)","description":"Named as one of Loki and Angrbotha’s children.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Týr","description":"A god who loses his right hand in the course of Fenrir’s chaining.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Skǫll","description":"A wolf, child of Fenrir and a giantess associated with Ironwood; steals the sun.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Hati","description":"A wolf, child of Fenrir and a giantess associated with Ironwood; steals the Gjallarhorn.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Gjallarhorn","description":"The 'Shrieking Horn' used by Heimdall to call the gods to the last battle.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Fjalar","description":"A cock whose crowing wakes the giants for the final struggle.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Gollinkambi (Gold-Comb)","description":"A cock who wakes the gods and heroes.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:19","name_or_label":"Rust-red bird (unnamed)","description":"A bird that wakes the people of Hel’s kingdom.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:21","name_or_label":"Gnipahellir","description":"The cliff-cave entrance to the world of the noted here).","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:24","name_or_label":"Vanir (Wanes)","description":"Described as cutting off Mímir’s head and returning it to the gods in a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l1516-l1627","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VOLUSPO / THE WISE-WOMANS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 1516-1627","start":"1516","end":"1627","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes identifying figures and objects in the Ragnarök/destruction section and the subsequent renewal/new-world section of Völuspá: giants and monsters (Hrym, Fenrir, the Midgard Serpent), Loki steering a ship, Surt as fire-world ruler, gods (Othin, Thor, Vithar, Baldr, Hoth, Freyr), the ship Naglfar, Bifrost, runes, golden tables, and the blissful hall Gimle. The notes also mention scholarly debate about possible Christian influence/interpolation in a stanza describing an unnamed new ruler.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hrym is identified as the leader of the giants and as helmsman of the ship Naglfar.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The serpent is identified as Mithgarthsorm (Midgard Serpent), a child of Loki and Angrbotha; it is cast into the sea and encircles the land.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The eagle is identified as the giant Hrsvelg, who sits at the edge of heaven in eagle form and makes winds with his wings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Naglfar is described as a ship made from dead men's nails to carry giants to battle.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes distinguish 'people of Hel' from 'people of Muspell': Muspell's people cross the bridge Bifrost, while Hel's people come in a ship steered by Loki.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The wolf is identified as Fenrir; Loki is identified as the brother of Byleist.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Surt is identified as ruler of the fire-world; 'scourge of branches' is glossed as fire.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hlin is glossed as another name for Frigg; after losing Baldr, she is fated to see Othin slain by Fenrir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Vithar (Othin's son) is described as a silent god with a great shield and great strength, and he survives the destruction.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Thor (identified as the warder of earth/son of Fjorgyn) slays the serpent and then dies from its venomous breath.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After the account of destruction, the notes describe the beginning of a new world rising from the wreck of the old one.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Runes are described as magic signs carved on wood and also as sung or spoken charms.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The notes mention the gods finding 'golden tables amid the grass' (variant reading) and discuss 'golden tables' as a motif in the poem's earlier stanzas.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Baldr and his brother Hoth return together; their union is said to symbolize a new age of peace.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"In the new age, Hnir is said to have the gift of foretelling the future; Vindheim is glossed as heaven.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Gimle is presented as a place associated with a hall on a mountain, home of the happy, contrasted with another hall for the dead described by Snorri from elsewhere in Völuspá.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A stanza describing an unnamed new ruler is noted as absent from Regius and possibly spurious; the notes state that a suggestion of Christianity is 'unavoidable' but uncertain and possibly an interpolation.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Hrym","description":"Leader of the giants; helmsman of the ship Naglfar.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Giants","description":"A group carried to battle by the ship Naglfar; associated with Hrym.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Mithgarthsorm (Midgard Serpent)","description":"Child of Loki and Angrbotha; cast into the sea; encircles the land; later slain by Thor.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Loki","description":"Father of the serpent; steers the ship bringing the people of Hel; identified as brother of Byleist.","role_refs":["role:5","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Angrbotha","description":"Named as mother (with Loki) of the serpent.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Hrsvelg (in eagle form)","description":"A giant at the edge of heaven in the form of an eagle who makes winds with his wings.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Fenrir","description":"Identified as the wolf; slays Othin; fought by Vithar.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Surt","description":"Ruler of the fire-world.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Frigg (Hlin)","description":"Othin's wife; after losing Baldr she is fated to see Othin slain by Fenrir.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"Called the Ruler of Gods; fated to be slain by Fenrir; associated with Valhall as battle-hall (via Hropt).","role_refs":["role:12","role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Vithar","description":"Othin's son; silent god with great shield and strength; survives the destruction; goes to fight the wolf.","role_refs":["role:14","role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Thor","description":"Othin's son; warder of earth/son of Fjorgyn; slays the serpent; dies from its venomous breath.","role_refs":["role:16","role:17"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Freyr","description":"Called Belis slayer; killed the giant Beli with his fist; belongs to the Wanes and is brother of Freyja.","role_refs":["role:18"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Baldr","description":"Frigg's son; returns in the new age with his brother Hoth.","role_refs":["role:19"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Hoth","description":"Baldr's brother; unwittingly slew Baldr at Loki's instigation; returns together with Baldr.","role_refs":["role:20"],"evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Hnir","description":"In the new age has the gift of foretelling the future.","role_refs":["role:21"],"evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Unnamed new ruler (stanza 65)","description":"A new ruler whose name is nowhere given; stanza is noted as possibly spurious and suggestive of Christianity.","role_refs":["role:22"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"leader of giants","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Hrym is glossed as 'the leader of the giants'.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"helmsman of Naglfar","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Hrym 'comes as the helmsman of the ship Naglfar'.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"army carried to battle by ship","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"Naglfar is 'to carry the giants to battle'.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"world-encircling sea serpent","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"The serpent is cast into the sea and 'completely encircles the land'.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"ship-steerer for the people of Hel","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"The people of Hel 'came in a ship steered by Loki'.","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"parent of monster","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"The serpent is identified as one of the children of Loki and Angrbotha.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"parent of monster","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"The serpent is identified as one of the children of Loki and Angrbotha.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"wind-maker at edge of heaven","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"Hrsvelg 'sits at the edge of heaven' and 'makes the winds with his wings'.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"wolf adversary / slayer of a god","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"Fenrir is identified as the wolf; Frigg is fated to see Othin slain by Fenrir; Vithar goes to fight the wolf.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:10","label":"ruler of the fire-world","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"Surt is glossed as 'the ruler of the fire-world'.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:11","label":"mourning mother figure","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"Frigg (Hlin) is said to have lost her son Baldr.","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"role:12","label":"chief god fated to be slain","assigned_to":["fig:10"],"basis":"Othin is called 'Ruler of Gods' and is fated to be slain by Fenrir.","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:11"]},{"id":"role:13","label":"lord of battle-hall","assigned_to":["fig:10"],"basis":"Hropt is named as another name for Othin; 'His battle-hall is Valhall'.","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"role:14","label":"avenger / combatant against the wolf","assigned_to":["fig:11"],"basis":"Snorri quotation gloss: 'Othins son ... to fight with the wolf' is identified here as Vithar.","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"role:15","label":"survivor of the destruction","assigned_to":["fig:11"],"basis":"Vithar 'survives the destruction'.","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"role:16","label":"warder of earth","assigned_to":["fig:12"],"basis":"Thor is glossed as 'the warder of earth'.","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"role:17","label":"serpent-slayer who dies from venom","assigned_to":["fig:12"],"basis":"Thor 'after slaying the serpent, is overcome by his venomous breath, and dies'.","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"role:18","label":"giant-slayer","assigned_to":["fig:13

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l1949-l2115","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HOVAMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE HIGH ONE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 1949-2115","start":"1949","end":"2115","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A series of gnomic stanzas offering practical and moral counsel: the value of clothing and social standing, the loneliness of the unloved, the short-lived heat of false friendship, modest gifts and hospitality, moderation in wisdom and foreknowledge, speech as a marker of character, diligence and early rising, preparedness for needs, shame and poverty, isolation in a crowd, caution in sharing thoughts, prudence among the brave, the fickleness of wealth, the certainty of death, the enduring value of reputation and fame, runes and the safety of silence, and when praise is appropriate.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker says he once gave his garments in a field to a pair of carved poles; with clothes they seemed like heroes, but a naked man is nought.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A fir-tree on a drear hillside dies; it is compared to a man whom no one loves.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Friendship between false friends is said to burn hotter than fire for five days, cooling on the sixth day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker says little gifts can purchase praise, and he made a fast friend with half a loaf and a half-filled cup.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The stanzas state each man should have a measure of wisdom, but not too much; too-great wisdom makes the wise man's heart seldom happy; one should not see fate beforehand to be freer from sorrow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A brand is kindled from a brand, and fire is begotten from fire; a man is known by his speech, and the stupid by stillness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A man who would get another's goods must go early; the idle wolf wins little meat, and the sleeping man little success.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A man with few workers must go early and seek work; much remains undone for the morning-sleeper; swiftness wins half of wealth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"One should know how much thatching and wood is needed for a month or half-year.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"One should go to council washed and fed, and not care too much for clothes; none should be ashamed of shoes, hose, or the poor horse he rides.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"When the eagle comes to the ancient sea, it snaps and hangs its head; this is likened to a man in a throng who finds few to speak for him.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Those who wish to be known as wise must be ready to question and answer; one may tell thoughts to one but beware of two, since what three know becomes widely known.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A prudent man uses his might in measured fashion and finds among the brave that he may not be the boldest.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The stanzas include a broken/omitted section, followed by a statement that often one gets an evil gift for words spoken to others.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The speaker says he came too early to many meetings and sought some too late; the beer was either all drunk or not yet brewed; the loathed man finds little.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The speaker says men would bid him to homes if at meal-time he needed no meat, or if he would hang two hams in a true friend's house where only one had been eaten.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Fire is called the fairest gift for men, along with power to see the sun; health and a life not stained with sin are also valued.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"It is said no man is wholly wretched even if sick; some have joy from sons, some from kinsmen, some from wealth, some from worthy works.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"It is better to live than to lie a corpse; the speaker saw flames rise for a rich man's pyre while he lay dead before his door.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The lame can ride, the handless can be herdsman, the deaf can be bold in battle; the blind is better than one burned, and no good comes of a corpse.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"A son is better though late-born after his father has died; memory-stones seldom stand by the road unless a kinsman honors his kin.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The tongue is said to slay the head; the speaker looks for a fist in each furry coat.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"He welcomes the night whose fare is enough; a parenthetical note says the yards of a ship are short; autumn nights are uneasy and weather changes often.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Gold is said to beget apes; one man is wealthy and another poor, yet none should scorn him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Among Fitjung's sons the speaker saw well-stocked folds, but now they bear the beggar's staff; wealth is swift as a winking eye and is the falsest of friends.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Cattle die, kinsmen die, and one dies oneself; but a noble name will never die if good renown is gained, and the fame of a dead man's deeds never dies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Something sought from runes is said to have been made by the gods and painted by the Master-Poet; the stanza concludes that silence is safest and best.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"An unwise man who wins a maiden's love or wealth grows proud, but not wiser, and fares in conceit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"Praises are to be given at their proper time: the day at evening, a woman on her pyre, a tried weapon, a maid at wedlock, ice when crossed, and ale when drunk.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:22"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Speaker (first-person narrator)","description":"A first-person voice offering observations and advice, recounting personal experiences (e.g., giving garments; coming too early/late).","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Man (generic)","description":"A generic human subject used in maxims about wisdom, work, shame, speech, and death.","role_refs":["role:2","role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7","ev:8","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"False friends","description":"Friends whose friendship burns briefly and then cools.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Eagle","description":"An eagle that comes to the ancient sea and snaps and hangs its head.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Wolf (idle wolf)","description":"A wolf that lies idle and wins little meat.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Rich man (dead, with pyre)","description":"A rich man lies dead before his door while flames rise for his pyre.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Sons / kinsmen","description":"Relatives who can be sources of joy; kinsmen who honor kin with memory-stones.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:12","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Fitjung's sons","description":"A group formerly having well-stocked folds, later bearing the beggar's staff.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"The gods","description":"The gods are said to have made something that is sought from runes.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Master-Poet","description":"A figure said to have painted what is sought from runes.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Maid / woman (pyre; wedlock)","description":"A maiden whose love may be won; a maid at wedlock; a woman on her pyre is mentioned in advice about when to give praise.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:21","ev:22"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Advisor / moral instructor","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The speaker delivers a sequence of maxims and counsels drawn from experience.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7","ev:10"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Wise person (ideal)","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"Those wishing to be known as wise must be ready to question and answer; wisdom should be measured.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:9"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Prudent person (measured strength)","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"A prudent man makes measured use of his might among the brave.","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"Unwise person (proud, conceited)","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"An unwise man who wins love or wealth grows proud without gaining wisdom.","evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"Unreliable friend","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"False friends' friendship is described as briefly burning and then cooling.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Fire / brand","literal_form":"Fire; a brand kindled from a brand; flames rising for a pyre; fire as a gift.","associated_figures":["fig:6"],"taxonomy_refs":["fire"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:11","ev:13"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"Fir-tree","literal_form":"A fir-tree dying on a drear hillside.","associated_figures":[],"taxonomy_refs":["tree"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"Runes","literal_form":"Runes from which something is sought; made by the gods and painted by the Master-Poet.","associated_figures":["fig:9","fig:10"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"sym:4","label":"Memory-stones","literal_form":"Memory-stones standing by the road to honor kin.","associated_figures":["fig:7"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"sym:5","label":"Wealth tokens","literal_form":"Gold; well-stocked folds; the beggar's staff; wealth as a 'falsest' friend.","associated_figures":["fig:8"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:17","ev:18"]},{"id":"sym:6","label":"Hospitality food and drink","literal_form":"Half a loaf and a half-filled cup; beer brewed or drunk; hams in a friend's house; ale that is drunk.","associated_figures":["fig:1"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:10","ev:22"]},{"id":"sym:7","label":"Ice (crossing)","literal_form":"Ice that is crossed (praise is given after crossing).","associated_figures":[],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:22"]},{"id":"sym:8","label":"Ship (short yards)","literal_form":"A remark that the yards of a ship are short.","associated_figures":[],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"sym:9","label":"Clothing on carved poles","literal_form":"Garments given to a pair of carved poles so they seem like heroes.","associated_figures":["fig:1"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]}],"scenes":[{"id":"scene:1","label":"Giving garments to carved poles","summary":"The speaker recounts giving garments to carved poles in a field, making them

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l2117-l2278","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HOVAMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE HIGH ONE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 2117-2278","start":"2117","end":"2278","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A series of counsel-stanzas warns about prudence, unreliable things and people, and the pitfalls of desire. The speaker then narrates personal episodes: longing for an unattainable woman, a failed attempt to meet Billing’s daughter that ends in deception, and an account in Suttung’s hall where the speaker passes through stone, receives the marvelous mead from Gunnloth, brings it up to humans, and leaves Gunnloth grieving; later frost-giants inquire about Bolverk, and an oath on a ring is described as untrustworthy.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage offers practical counsel linking conditions to actions (e.g., hew wood in a gale, seek water in fair winds) and seeks benefits from specific things (ship for swiftness, shield for protection, sword for cuts, maiden for kisses).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage advises specific practices: drink ale by the fire, skate over ice, buy a lean steed and a tarnished sword, and then fatten the horse at home and keep the hound in the dwelling.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage warns against trusting a maid’s oath or a woman’s word, describing hearts as fashioned on a whirling wheel and breasts as fickle.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A long list of unstable or dangerous things is given as examples of what not to trust (e.g., breaking bow, burning flame, ravening wolf, croaking raven, broken-root tree, seas, bubbling kettle, flying arrow, falling waters, new ice, serpent folds, broken sword, sick calf, stubborn thrall, flattering witch, foe newly slain, brother’s slayer, half-burned house, swift horse with a hurt leg).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage cautions against overconfidence in early harvest and against trusting too soon in one’s son, noting that fields need weather and sons need wisdom, and either may be denied.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage compares the fickleness of women’s love to hazardous activities such as starting over ice with an unshod steed, steering a rudderless ship in a storm, and hunting reindeer while lame on slippery rocks.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker states that men too can be false to women, and that fair speech can hide false intent and deceit working against wisdom.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage describes wooing tactics: speaking soft words, offering wealth, praising a maiden’s beauty, and that the best wooing wins.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The speaker describes desire and love as powerful enough to fetter the wise and make wise men into fools, and says the head alone knows what is near the heart; lack of longed-for joy is described as a severe sickness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker recounts sitting in reeds awaiting love, loving a wise maiden as his life, yet never having her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The speaker says he found Billing’s daughter asleep on her bed, and later is advised to return in the evening if he would win her; he returns at night when warriors are awake with burning lights and brands, and later returns in the morning to find a dog bound on the bed in the maiden’s place.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The speaker concludes from the episode that many maids may be false, that he sought to gain the maiden with wiles, received foul scorn from a crafty maid, and won nothing from her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The passage advises that even when glad at home with guests, a man should be wary and wise; one seeking wisdom must keep speech fair; a fool is one who can say nothing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The speaker says he found an old giant and spoke many words in Suttung’s hall to get his will, gaining little from silence.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The mouth of Rati made room by gnawing space in stone for the speaker’s passage, with giants’ paths above and below, and the speaker says he risked his head.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Gunnloth gave a drink of marvelous mead on a golden stool; the speaker says he gave her a harsh reward for her heroic heart and troubled her spirit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The speaker says Othrrir has been brought up to the midst of the men of earth, and that he would hardly have come home and left the giants’ land if Gunnloth had not helped him and held him in her arms.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The day after, frost-giants came to win some word of Hor and asked of Bolverk whether he was back among the gods or had been slain by Suttung.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The speaker says Othin swore an oath on his ring and questions who can trust his troth; it states that he sought Suttung’s betrayal with drink and left Gunnloth in grief.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Othin (the speaker / High One)","description":"The speaker names Othin and recounts his own actions and counsel.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"A man (generalized)","description":"A generalized man is advised about conduct, trust, speech, and love.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Women / maidens (generalized)","description":"Women and maidens are discussed as objects of love/wooing and as potentially unreliable; men are also said to be false to women.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Billing’s daughter","description":"A specific maiden found asleep on her bed; later replaced by a dog bound on the bed.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Gunnloth","description":"A maiden who gives the speaker a drink of marvelous mead on a golden stool, helps him leave the giants’ land, and is left grieving.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Suttung","description":"Associated with Suttung’s hall; later mentioned in connection with whether he slew Bolverk; the speaker seeks Suttung’s betrayal with drink.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Old giant (unnamed)","description":"An old giant is found by the speaker before he speaks in Suttung’s hall.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Rati","description":"Rati’s mouth gnaws space in stone to make room for the speaker’s passage.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Frost-giants","description":"They come the next day and ask about Bolverk and Suttung.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Hor","description":"Mentioned as someone from whom frost-giants came to win some word; also referenced as a hall.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Bolverk","description":"A figure asked about by the frost-giants: whether he is back among the gods or slain by Suttung.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Dog (bound on the bed)","description":"Found bound on the bed in the maiden’s place.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"counsel-giver / speaker of maxims","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The speaker delivers multiple advisory stanzas and announces he will speak clearly.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"wooer / seeker of a woman’s love","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The speaker narrates attempts to win a maiden and describes wooing and desire in first person.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"desired maiden","assigned_to":["fig:4","fig:5"],"basis":"Billing’s daughter is the target of the speaker’s visit; Gunnloth is embraced and involved in the mead episode.","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"giver of marvelous mead","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"Gunnloth gives the speaker a drink of the marvelous mead on a golden stool.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"giant/giants’ domain holder (hall/land context)","assigned_to":["fig:6","fig:7"],"basis":"The speaker speaks in Suttung’s hall and references leaving the giants’ land; an old giant appears in this context.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"questioners / inquirers","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"Frost-giants come and ask about Bolverk and whether Suttung slew troth.","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"one left grieving (after assistance given)","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"The speaker says he left Gunnloth to grief after seeking betrayal with drink.","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"fire (ale by the fire; burning lights/brands)","literal_form":"fire; burning lights; waving starting over ice","associated_figures":["fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":["water"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"water / sea (seeking water; billowy seas; falling waters)","literal_form":"water; billowy seas; falling waters","associated_figures":["fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":["water"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"sym:4","label":"ship (swiftness; lines 2879-2950","start":"2879","end":"2950","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editor’s notes on Hávamál stanzas 144–165: identifies named beings (including Othin under multiple names), mentions Dain and Dvalin and their association with Yggdrasil in other poems, describes a religious formula involving runes, prayers, and sacrifices, introduces the Ljódhátal as a list of charms with stated applications, notes a lethal practice of sending a runic-inscribed root, describes night-riding witches (“house-riders”), notes a pre-Christian custom of sprinkling a child with water, gives a brief divine genealogy (Delling and Night’s son Day), and comments on interpolations/obscurities in certain stanzas.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Dain and Dvalin are identified as dwarfs (with a note that Dain may here be an elf), and the names occur together elsewhere applied to harts that nibble the top twigs of Yggdrasil.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Alsvith is stated to appear nowhere else as a giant’s name.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"“Myself” is glossed as Othin, and the notes state there is no further information about a list of those who wrote the runes for various races.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A stanza is described as a regular religious formula focused on prayers asked and sacrifices offered/sent, rather than on writing and tinting runes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Thund is identified as another name for Othin; a phrase about coming home is linked (presumably) to Othin’s earlier obtaining of the runes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Ljothatal is described as a list of charms where the magic songs are not given but each charm’s application is explained, including use against sickness, pain, and sorrow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Sending a root with runes written on it is described as a way of causing death; Grettir the Strong is said to have died in this way.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"“House-riders” are described as witches who ride by night on the roofs of houses, generally in the form of wild beasts.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Sprinkling a child with water is described as an established custom long before Christianity’s conception of baptism.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Delling is described as a god who married Not (Night), and their son was Dag (Day); Hroptatyr is glossed as Othin; Thjothrrir is noted as not mentioned elsewhere.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A stanza reference to Loddfafnir is described as likely an interpolation introduced after combining poem sections.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Dain","description":"Named as a dwarf (with possibility noted that he may here be an elf); elsewhere paired with Dvalin as a name applied to a hart nibbling Yggdrasil’s top twigs.","role_refs":["role:5","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Dvalin","description":"Named as a dwarf; elsewhere paired with Dain as a name applied to a hart nibbling Yggdrasil’s top twigs.","role_refs":["role:5","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Alsvith","description":"Said to appear nowhere else as a giant’s name.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Othin (Odin)","description":"Glossed as “Myself”; also identified by the names Thund and Hroptatyr in these notes.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Harts (four, in Grimnismol context)","description":"In another poem, Dain and Dvalin are names applied to two of the four harts that nibble at Yggdrasil’s topmost twigs.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Yggdrasil","description":"A tree whose topmost twigs are nibbled by harts (as referenced via another poem).","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Unspecified rune-writers (for various races)","description":"A list of those who wrote the runes for various races is mentioned, but the notes say there is no further information about it.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Grettir the Strong","description":"An Icelandic hero said to have died as a result of a runic-inscribed root being sent to cause death.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"House-riders (witches)","description":"Witches who ride by night on the roofs of houses, generally in the form of wild beasts.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Delling","description":"A god who married Not (Night); father of Dag (Day).","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Not (Night)","description":"Married Delling; mother of Dag (Day).","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Dag (Day)","description":"Son of Delling and Not (Night).","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Loddfafnir","description":"Referenced at this point in the poem according to the notes, but the stanza is described as likely an interpolation.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Thjothrrir","description":"Named as not mentioned elsewhere (per the notes).","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"bearer of multiple names (Othin/Thund/Hroptatyr)","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"The notes gloss “Myself” as Othin and identify Thund and Hroptatyr as names for Othin.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"rune-writer list (unspecified individuals)","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"A list of those who wrote runes for various races is referenced, with no further information given.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"night roof-rider (witch)","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"House-riders are defined as witches riding by night on rooftops, often as wild beasts.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"victim of runic killing (example)","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"Grettir the Strong is cited as dying from the sending of a runic-inscribed root.","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"dwarf (with possible elf identification for Dain)","assigned_to":["fig:1","fig:2"],"basis":"Dain and Dvalin are called dwarfs; Dain may here be an elf rather than the dwarf of that name.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"name applied to a hart nibbling Yggdrasil (in another poem)","assigned_to":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:5"],"basis":"The names Dain and Dvalin are said to be applied to two of the four harts that nibble Yggdrasil’s topmost twigs (in Grimnismol).","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"giant name (rare/unique attestation)","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Alsvith is noted as appearing nowhere else as a giant’s name.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"world-tree (named tree)","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"Yggdrasil is referenced as the tree whose top twigs are nibbled by harts.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"parents of Dag (Day)","assigned_to":["fig:10","fig:11"],"basis":"Delling marries Not (Night) and they have a son, Dag (Day).","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"role:10","label":"child of Delling and Not","assigned_to":["fig:12"],"basis":"Dag (Day) is identified as the son of Delling and Not (Night).","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"role:11","label":"named addressee/figure referenced in an interpolated stanza","assigned_to":["fig:13"],"basis":"The notes state stanza 164 is likely an interpolation and includes a reference to Loddfafnir.","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"role:12","label":"rare/otherwise unattested named figure","assigned_to":["fig:14"],"basis":"Thjothrrir is stated to be not mentioned elsewhere.","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Runes (written/tinted; {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l3494-l3625","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VAFTHRUTHNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF VAFTHRUTHNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 3494-3625","start":"3494","end":"3625","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes summarizing mythic background for Vafthruthnismol: identifications of figures (Othin/Odin, Frigg, Vafthruthnir), creation-material about Ymir and Ginnunga-gap, cosmic geography (rivers, fire-world, nine worlds), Ragnarok-related details (Surt, Vigrith, mighty winter), Valhalla’s daily battling heroes, and post-cataclysm human survivors (Lif and Lifthrasir) sheltered in Hoddmimir’s wood (linked to Yggdrasil/Mimir).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Othin (Heerfather, Ygg) is identified as Odin; Frigg is identified as Odin’s wife; Vafthruthnir is a giant known only from what is told in the poem.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Othin is described as traveling under assumed names (e.g., Gagnrath).","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Surt is described as ruler of the fire-world (Muspellsheim) who comes to attack the gods in the last battle; Vigrith is described as the field of battle.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The river Ifing is described as never freezing, preventing giants from crossing it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ymir is described as a giant from whose body the gods made the world.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When the gods slew Ymir, so much blood flowed that all frost-giants drowned except Bergelmir and his wife, who escaped in a boat.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Elivagar is described as ‘stormy waves’; venom in its waters froze into ice-banks over Ginnunga-gap, and then dripped down to make the giant Ymir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ymir’s son and daughter are described as being born under his left arm; his feet together created a son; one offspring is described as six-headed (with a note that giants may have many heads).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hrsvelg is described as a giant in eagle form.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Njorth is described as associated with the Wanes and as given as a hostage to the gods at the end of a war.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Heroes brought to Valhall by Valkyries are described as fighting each day; after fighting they are healed of wounds and feast together.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"‘Nine worlds’ and Niflhel (Dark-Hell) are noted; before the final destruction three winters follow one another with no intervening summers.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Hoddmimir’s wood is identified as probably the ash-tree Yggdrasil, sometimes referred to as Mimir’s Tree (watered from Mimir’s well); Lif and Lifthrasir are described as a pair from whom a new race of men will spring.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Mundilferi is identified as father of Mani (Moon) and Sol (Sun); Snorri’s account is summarized in which the gods take them to drive the moon and sun.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Delling is described as husband of Not (Night) and father of Dag (Day); Nor/Narfi is described (per Snorri) as Night’s father among the giants.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Othin (Odin; Heerfather; Ygg; Gagnrath)","description":"Identified as Odin, called Heerfather and Ygg, and described as traveling under assumed names such as Gagnrath.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Frigg","description":"Identified as Odin’s wife.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Vafthruthnir","description":"A giant; nothing is known beyond what is told in the poem.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Ymir","description":"A giant from whose body the gods made the world; his slaying produces a flood of blood; he is also described as formed from dripping matter after ice-banks formed over Ginnunga-gap.","role_refs":["role:5","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"The gods (as a group)","description":"Described as slaying Ymir and making the world from his body; described as being attacked in the last battle.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Frost-giants / giants (as a group)","description":"Described as drowning in Ymir’s blood-flood except for Bergelmir and his wife; also described as unable to cross the never-freezing river Ifing.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Bergelmir","description":"Survives the drowning of frost-giants by escaping in a boat with his wife.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Bergelmir’s wife","description":"Survives the drowning of frost-giants by escaping in a boat with Bergelmir.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Surt","description":"Ruler of the fire-world (Muspellsheim) who comes to attack the gods in the last battle.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Hrsvelg","description":"A giant in eagle form.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Njorth","description":"Associated with the Wanes; given as a hostage to the gods at the end of a war.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Wanes (Vanir; as a group)","description":"Described in connection with Njorth and a hostage exchange ending a war.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Valkyries (as a group)","description":"Bring heroes to Valhall.","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Heroes in Valhall (einherjar; as a group)","description":"Fight each day; are healed after fighting; then feast together.","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Lif","description":"One of a pair (with Lifthrasir) from whom a new race of men is to spring; connected with Hoddmimir’s wood (linked to Yggdrasil).","role_refs":["role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Lifthrasir","description":"One of a pair (with Lif) from whom a new race of men is to spring; connected with Hoddmimir’s wood (linked to Yggdrasil).","role_refs":["role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Hoddmimir / Mimir","description":"Hoddmimir is presumed another name for Mimir; Mimir is associated with a well and with the tree (Yggdrasil) being watered from his well.","role_refs":["role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Mundilferi","description":"Father of Mani (Moon) and Sol (Sun); Snorri’s account is noted in which the gods take them to drive moon and sun.","role_refs":["role:17"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:19","name_or_label":"Mani (Moon)","description":"Child of Mundilferi; described as the boy; linked to driving the moon in Snorri’s account.","role_refs":["role:18"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:20","name_or_label":"Sol (Sun)","description":"Child of Mundilferi; described as the girl; linked to driving the sun in Snorri’s account.","role_refs":["role:19"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:21","name_or_label":"Delling","description":"Husband of Not (Night) and father of Dag (Day).","role_refs":["role:20"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:22","name_or_label":"Not (Night)","description":"Wife of Delling and mother of Dag (Day); her father is given (per Snorri) as Norvi/Narfi among the giants.","role_refs":["role:21"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:23","name_or_label":"Dag (Day)","description":"Son of Delling and Not (Night).","role_refs":["role:22"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:24","name_or_label":"Nor / Norvi / Narfi","description":"Given (per Snorri) as the father of Night (Not) and placed among the giants.","role_refs":["role:23"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"disguised traveler (name-assumer)","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Othin is said to travel under a name
