content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l3660-l3765","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / GRIMNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF GRIMNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 3660-3765","start":"3660","end":"3765","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note explains the manuscript context and narrative structure of Grimnismol, including that Othin (as Grimnir) is tortured by King Geirrth between two fires and later reveals his name, leading to Geirrth’s death. The prose frame then narrates: King Hrauthung’s sons Agnar and Geirrth are driven to shore; they winter with a poor peasant couple who separately care for them, with the peasant teaching Geirrth wisdom. Geirrth returns home and becomes king after pushing Agnar’s boat back to sea. Othin and Frigg observe the worlds from Hlithskjolf and wager about Geirrth’s hospitality. Frigg sends Fulla to warn Geirrth of a magician; Geirrth seizes the man the dogs will not attack (Grimnir in a dark-blue mantle) and tortures him between two fires for eight nights. Geirrth’s young son Agnar gives Grimnir a drink and criticizes the king; the fire burns Grimnir’s mantle and he begins to speak.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The note states that the Grimnismol appears after the Vafthruthnismol in the Codex Regius and is also complete in the Arnamagnan Codex; Snorri quotes many of its stanzas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The note describes an underlying dramatic narrative: Othin, disguised as Grimnir, is tortured by King Geirrth, bound between two fires, displays wisdom to the king’s young son Agnar, then reveals his names; Geirrth falls on his sword and is killed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note claims the poem is preceded by a long prose narrative and concluded by a brief prose statement about Geirrth’s death; the prose notes are dated linguistically to the 12th–13th century.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Two brothers, Agnar (ten winters) and Geirrth (eight), row out fishing; wind drives them out to sea; in night darkness they are wrecked on shore and go up to a poor peasant’s house for the winter.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"During the winter the housewife cares for Agnar, and the peasant cares for Geirrth and teaches him wisdom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In spring the peasant gives Geirrth a boat; on return Geirrth leaps to land first, pushes the boat out, and tells the other to go where evil may have him; the boat drifts out to sea.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Geirrth goes to the house, is well received, his father is dead, and Geirrth is made king and becomes renowned.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Othin and Frigg sit in Hlithskjolf and look over all the worlds; Othin contrasts Agnar (with a giantess in a cave) with Geirrth (a ruling king).","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Frigg says Geirrth is miserly and tortures guests if too many come; Othin calls this a lie; they make a wager.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Frigg sends her maid Fulla to warn Geirrth about a magician and gives a sign: no dog is so fierce as to leap at him; the king tortures him to make him speak, placing him between two fires for eight nights.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Geirrth has a son named Agnar (ten winters old), who gives Grimnir a full horn to drink from and says the king does ill to torment him without cause.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Grimnir drinks; lines 3934-4067","start":"3934","end":"4067","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes beings associated with the world-tree Yggdrasil (a squirrel messenger, an eagle above, Nithhogg below, harts and serpents that gnaw the tree), names valkyries who bring drink to warriors, gives cosmological details about the sun’s course and its dangers, recounts the creation of the world from Ymir’s body, mentions notable divine possessions (including the ship Skithblathnir), and presents Odin (speaking as Grimnir) listing many names and declaring judgment on King Geirrth; Geirrth then accidentally falls on his sword and dies, after which Odin vanishes and Agnar rules as king.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ratatosk, a squirrel, runs on the ash-tree Yggdrasil carrying words from an eagle above to Nithhogg beneath.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Four harts (Dain, Dvalin, Duneyr, Dyrathror) nibble the highest twigs of the tree.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Many serpents are said to be beneath the ash; several are named, and they gnaw at the twigs of the tree.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Yggdrasil is described as suffering evil: a hart bites its top, its trunk is rotting, and Nithhogg gnaws beneath.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Named female figures (including Hrist, Mist, Skeggjold, Skogul and others) bring beer to the warriors at the speaker’s will.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Arvak and Alsvith drag the weight of the sun; an “iron cool” has been set under their yokes by the gods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Svalin stands as a shield in front of the sun; if it fell away, mountains and sea would be set in flames.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Skoll follows the glittering god toward Ironwood, and Hati awaits the “burning bride of heaven.”","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The earth, ocean, hills, trees, and heavens are fashioned from Ymir’s flesh, blood, bones, hair, and skull; the gods make Mithgarth from his eyebrows and clouds from his brain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Ivaldi’s sons fashioned Skithblathnir, described as the best of ships, for Freyr, the son of Njorth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The speaker lists superlatives (e.g., Yggdrasil best of trees; Skithblathnir best of boats; Othin greatest of gods; Sleipnir best of steeds; Bilrost best of bridges).","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The speaker says he has raised his face to the gods’ race and awakened wished-for aid, and that a message has gone to all the gods who sit and drink in certain seats/doors.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The speaker lists many names for himself and says he has never had a single name since he first fared among men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The speaker identifies himself as Grimnir in Geirrth’s hall and recounts other names and deeds, including deceiving the giant Sokkmimir.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The speaker addresses Geirrth, calls him drunk, and says Geirrth has lost help from the speaker and his heroes; the speaker foresees a blood-wet sword and declares Geirrth’s life ended, urging him to behold Othin.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The speaker declares “Now am I Othin,” gives additional names, and states that the listed names are names for none but him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"In prose, King Geirrth rises to take Othin from the fire; the sword slips, falls hilt-down, and the king stumbles forward onto it, being pierced and slain; Othin vanishes; Agnar rules as king afterward.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ratatosk","description":"A squirrel that runs on the ash-tree Yggdrasil bearing words between the eagle above and Nithhogg beneath.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Yggdrasil","description":"An ash-tree associated with multiple creatures; it suffers harm from biting/gnawing above and below, and is called the best of trees.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Eagle (unnamed)","description":"An eagle located above on/near Yggdrasil whose words are carried by Ratatosk.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Nithhogg","description":"A being beneath Yggdrasil; Ratatosk tells it words, and it gnaws beneath the tree.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Four harts (Dain, Dvalin, Duneyr, Dyrathror)","description":"Four harts that nibble the highest twigs of the tree.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Serpents beneath the ash (Goin, Moin, Grabak, Grafvolluth, Ofnir, Svafnir, etc.)","description":"Multiple serpents beneath the ash that gnaw at the twigs of the tree.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Valkyries (Hrist, Mist, Skeggjold, Skogul, Hild, Thruth, Hlokk, Herfjotur, Gol, Geironul, Randgrith, Rathgrith, Reginleif)","description":"Named maids who bring beer to the warriors at the speaker’s will.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Arvak and Alsvith","description":"Two beings who drag the weight of the sun under yokes with an “iron cool” set under them.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Svalin","description":"A shield that stands in front of the sun as protection; if it fell away, mountains and sea would burn.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Skoll","description":"A wolf that follows the glittering god toward Ironwood.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Hati (son of Hrothvitnir)","description":"A wolf who awaits the “burning bride of heaven.”","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Ymir","description":"A primordial being from whose body parts the world is fashioned (earth, ocean, hills, trees, heavens, clouds).","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"The gods (collective)","description":"They fashion the world from Ymir, make Mithgarth for humans, and are addressed by the speaker; lines 4070-4189","start":"4070","end":"4189","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Translator/editor notes explaining names, places, and mythic details in Grimnismol, including Odin’s watch-tower, multiple divine halls/dwellings, a Skathi–Njorth residence-compromise between mountain and sea, Valhall’s feasting/cooking details (kettle, cook, ever-renewed boar), Odin’s wolves and ravens, Forseti as a judge, Vidar’s vengeance on Fenrir, and references to Valhall’s gate and surrounding river as well as an attack by the people of Hel.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hlithskjolf is described as Odin’s watch-tower in heaven from which he can overlook all nine worlds.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Agnar is said to receive a gift identified as Odin’s mythological lore.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Thrymheim is described as a mountain home built by the giant Thjazi; Skathi (Thjazi’s daughter) and Njorth disagree about living in the mountains versus by the sea and attempt a compromise schedule, which they cannot endure.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Breithablik is described as a house in heaven free from anything unclean where Baldr lived.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Himinbjorg is described as Heimdall’s dwelling at the end of the bridge Bifrost, where he keeps watch against the giants.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Folkvang is described as the location of Freyja’s hall Sessrymnir, and Freyja is associated with receiving half of the dead.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Glitnir is described as Forseti’s home; Forseti is said to settle hard cases so that those who come to him go away satisfied, and he is called the best judge among gods and men.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Noatun is described as Njorth’s home, and Njorth is said to calm the waves.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Valhall is described as a hall where slain heroes are brought by Valkyries and also as a favored home of Odin; Valgrind is described as the outer gate of Valhall; a river (Thund) is described as surrounding Valhall.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In Valhall there is a great kettle (Eldhrimnir); a cook (Andhrimnir) daily cooks the flesh of a boar (Shrimnir); the boar’s flesh is sufficient for all the heroes, and each evening the boar becomes whole again to be cooked the next morning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Freki and Geri are described as two wolves who sit by Odin at the feast; Odin gives them the food set before him and is said to take wine as his food and drink.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Hugin and Munin are described as two ravens on Odin’s shoulders who fly forth daily to bring him news of the world; Midgard is glossed as the earth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Vidar is said to avenge his father Odin by slaying the wolf Fenrir.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A note states that stanzas 18–20 appear also in Snorri’s Edda and may be an interpolation in this location.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A note interprets the last two lines (of the referenced stanza) as referring to an attack on Valhall by the people of Hel, and also explains a kenning about ‘Thjothvitnir’s fish’ as presumably the sun caught by the wolf Skoll.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Odin (Othin; Heerfather; Veratyr)","description":"A god associated here with a heavenly watch-tower (Hlithskjolf), receiving news via ravens, and feasting with wolves; also associated with Valhall as a favored home.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7","role:8","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:9","ev:13","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Frigg","description":"Identified as Odin’s wife; the notes state she and Odin nearly always disagreed in such a way as outlined in the story.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Agnar","description":"A figure said to receive Odin’s mythological lore as a gift.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Thor","description":"A god whose hall Bilskirnir is located in Thruthheim (as glossed).","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Ull","description":"A god described as an archer whose home is Ydalir.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Thjazi","description":"A giant who built his home on the mountain Thrymheim.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Skathi","description":"Thjazi’s daughter; wishes to live in her father’s mountain hall and is involved in a residence compromise with Njorth.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Njorth","description":"A divine figure who marries Skathi, prefers Noatun by the sea, and is said to calm the waves.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Baldr","description":"A god described as living in Breithablik, a house in heaven free from anything unclean.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Heimdall","description":"A god who dwells at Himinbjorg at the end of Bifrost and keeps watch against giants.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Freyja","description":"A goddess whose hall Sessrymnir is in Folkvang; associated here with receiving half of the dead.","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Forseti","description":"A god associated with Glitnir; described as the best judge among gods and men, satisfying those who bring hard cases.","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Andhrimnir","description":"Described as the daily cook in Valhall who cooks the boar’s flesh in the kettle Eldhrimnir.","role_refs":["role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Shrimnir (the boar)","description":"A boar whose flesh is cooked daily in Valhall and who becomes whole again each evening.","role_refs":["role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Freki and Geri (Odin’s wolves)","description":"Two wolves who sit by Odin at the feast and receive his food.","role_refs":["role:17"],"evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Hugin and Munin (Odin’s ravens)","description":"Two ravens on Odin’s shoulders who fly daily to bring news.","role_refs":["role:18"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Vidar (Vithar)","description":"Said to avenge Odin by slaying the wolf Fenrir.","role_refs":["role:19"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Fenrir","description":"A wolf slain by Vidar in vengeance for Odin.","role_refs":["role:20"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:19","name_or_label":"Skoll","description":"A wolf said (in the note’s explanation of a kenning) to have caught the sun.","role_refs":["role:21"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:20","name_or_label":"People of Hel","description":"Mentioned in a note as attackers of Valhall (as an interpretive reference).","role_refs":["role:22"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"watcher from a heavenly watch-tower","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Hlithskjolf is Odin

lines 4291-4389","start":"4291","end":"4389","translation":"The Poetic Edda (Bellows, Project Gutenberg)","notes":"Passage consists of Bellows' explanatory notes on multiple stanzas (esp. 34–45), including cross-references to Snorri and other Eddic poems."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes discuss: a stanza listing serpents (linked to a prior note and later Odin-names); a list of Valkyries; cosmological details about the sun’s horses and a myth of Mundilfari’s children (Máni and Sól) set in the sky; the cooling shield Svalin; wolves Sköll and Hati that devour sun and moon; creation/cosmology details tied to Ymir’s body and the building of Midgard’s wall; Odin’s immediate predicament between two fires and a kettle under a smoke-vent; interpolated stanzas on Ivaldi and dwarven craftsmanship (ship Skíðblaðnir, spear Gungnir, Sif’s hair); Sleipnir’s origin via Loki’s shapeshifting into a mare; and brief notes on Bifröst/Bilröst, Bragi and Iðunn, Garm, and Ægir.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that little is known about the serpents listed in the referenced stanza, that meanings of many names are conjectural, and that Snorri quotes the stanza; the note also remarks that the names Ofnir and Svafnir are later used by Odin as self-names elsewhere in the poem.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes report that Snorri quotes a stanza that concludes a passage describing Yggdrasil, and that some stanzas in that section may be later interpolations.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A list of Valkyrie names is provided, and the notes state Snorri quotes this list; the notes also point to a different list in Völuspá.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes describe Arvak and Alsvith as the horses of the sun and summarize Snorri’s story in which the gods take Mundilfari’s children (Máni and Sól) and place them in heaven; Sól drives the sun’s car drawn by the horses, and the gods set bellows under the horses’ yokes to cool them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Svalin is described as a shield associated with cooling, with a note that it is otherwise referenced only in Sigrdrífumál.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Sköll and Hati are identified as wolves that devour the sun and moon respectively; Hati is described as the son of Hróðvitnir (Fenrir), and the notes reference ‘Ironwood’ in connection with this tradition.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A cosmological account is summarized: stones are made from Ymir’s teeth and broken bones, and Midgard is a mountain-wall made from Ymir’s eyebrows set around the earth because of enmity from giants.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes state that Odin returns to his immediate situation, bound between two fires; he calls down a blessing on the man who will reach into the fire and pull aside a great kettle hanging under a smoke-vent, preventing someone above from looking down into the house interior; Ull is mentioned as an archer-god.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Ivaldi is identified as the father of craftsmen-dwarfs who made the ship Skíðblaðnir, Odin’s spear Gungnir, and golden hair for Sif after Loki cut off her hair; Freyr is also mentioned in connection with this note.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Skíðblaðnir is described as a ship that always has a fair wind when the sail is set and can be folded up and put in a pocket.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Sleipnir is described as Odin’s eight-legged horse, born from Loki after Loki shapeshifted into a mare to lure away the stallion Svathilfari; this delayed a giant builder’s work on a fortress for the gods, preventing him from winning a promised reward (Freyja and the sun and moon).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Bilröst is noted as probably another form of Bifröst; Bragi is described as a god of poetry and his wife as Iðunn, goddess of youth; Hobrok is noted as otherwise unknown; Garm is cross-referenced to Völuspá; and Ægir is identified as a sea-god.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Snorri (Sturluson)","description":"Cited as quoting or closely paraphrasing multiple stanzas or lists discussed in the notes.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Odin (Othin)","description":"Mentioned as using the names Ofnir and Svafnir; later described as bound between two fires and calling down a blessing; associated with spear Gungnir and horse Sleipnir in notes.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:8","ev:9","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Valkyries (named list)","description":"A list of Valkyrie names is given and described as quoted by Snorri; another list is said to appear in Völuspá.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Mundilfari","description":"In Snorri’s account summarized here, a man whose children were named Máni and Sól; the gods take the children and set them in heaven.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Máni","description":"In Snorri’s account summarized here, Mundilfari’s son set in heaven by the gods.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Sól","description":"In Snorri’s account summarized here, Mundilfari’s daughter set in heaven; she drives the car of the sun drawn by Arvak and Alsvith.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Arvak and Alsvith","description":"Identified as the horses of the sun; the gods set bellows under their yokes to cool them.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Sköll and Hati","description":"Identified as wolves that devour the sun and moon respectively; Hati is said to be the son of Hróðvitnir (Fenrir).","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Ymir","description":"In Snorri’s elaboration summarized here, stones and Midgard’s wall are made from Ymir’s bodily parts (teeth, bones, eyebrows).","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Giants","description":"Midgard’s wall is said to be set around the earth because of the enmity of the giants.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Ull","description":"Identified as an archer-god; mentioned in connection with Odin’s blessing speech in the notes.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Ivaldi","description":"Identified as father of craftsmen-dwarfs responsible for notable divine artifacts.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Craftsmen-dwarfs (sons of Ivaldi)","description":"Said to have made Skíðblaðnir, Odin’s spear Gungnir, and golden hair for Sif.","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Loki","description":"Said to have cut off Sif’s hair; elsewhere in these notes, he shapeshifts into a mare to lure away Svathilfari, producing Sleipnir.","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Sif","description":"Thor’s wife; said to have received golden hair made by dwarfs after Loki cut off her hair.","role_refs":["role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Thor","description":"Mentioned as Sif’s husband (Thor’s wife, Sif).","role_refs":["role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Freyr","description":"Mentioned in connection with the note on Skíðblaðnir and cross-references to other poems.","role_refs":["role:17"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Sleipnir","description":"Identified as Odin’s eight-legged horse; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l4391-l4441","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GRIMNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF GRIMNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 4391-4441","start":"4391","end":"4441","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes discuss the unstable oral-transmission condition of certain stanzas and provide glosses for many of Othin’s/Odin’s by-names, emphasizing that he often appeared in disguise and therefore had many names. The notes mention Snorri’s tripartite question-and-answer framing (Har, Jafnhar, Thrithi) and suggest possible early Christian influence on this form.   "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Editorial notes summarize characters and objects in Skírnismál: Njörðr’s family (Freyr and Freyja) and their attributes; identifications of places (Hlíðskjálf) and beings (Gymir, Hrimnir, Heimdall, Hræsvelgr); and explanations of key items and plot elements (Freyr’s sword given away, apples of youth/fruitfulness, the ring Draupnir, a coercive curse using a magic staff, an ‘eagles’ hill’ overlooking hell, and mention of multi-headed giants).",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Njörðr is said (per Snorri) to have two children in Nóatún: Freyr and Freyja; Freyr rules rain, sunshine, and the fruitfulness of the earth, and is invoked for plenty and welfare; Freyja takes half the slain, travels in a cart drawn by two cats, and is invoked in love-matters.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Hlíðskjálf is identified as Óðinn’s watch-tower.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Gymir is identified as a mountain-giant, husband of Aurbotha, and father of Gerðr.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Freyr gives his sword to Skírnir; later Freyr kills Beli bare-handed and is later slain by the fire-demon Surtr when weaponless.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "The apple is described as a symbol of fruitfulness and of eternal youth; Íðunn is said (per Snorri) to keep apples the gods eat when they grow old.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "The ring Draupnir is described as dwarf-made for Óðinn; Óðinn lays it on Baldr’s pyre; Baldr sends the ring back from hell; Andvari’s ring is described as having a similar power of creating gold.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "After bribes and threats fail, Skírnir begins a curse that is to fall on Gerðr if she refuses Freyr, and the curse is said to work by the power of Skírnir’s magic staff.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "‘Eagles’ hill’ is described as a hill at the end of heaven overlooking hell; the giant Hræsvelgr sits in an eagle guise and makes winds with his wings.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Hrimnir is identified as a frost-giant; the ‘watchman of the gods’ is identified as Heimdall.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "Giants with numerous heads (including ‘three-headed giants’) are noted as a topic of comparison to other poems.",
      "category": "other",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    }
  ],

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l4986-l5183","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HARBARTHSLJOTH / THE POEM OF HARBARTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 4986-5183","start":"4986","end":"5183","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note describes the poem Harbarthsljoth as a loosely metered, chaotic “contest of abuse” between Thor and Othin, with Othin appearing disguised as the ferryman Harbarth. The poem’s opening scene is summarized and then presented in dialogue: Thor, returning from the East, reaches a sound and calls to a ferryman across the water to take him over, offering food in payment. The ferryman answers with insults and ominous remarks (including that Thor’s mother is dead) and questions Thor’s worthiness and identity. Thor names himself and boasts of his lineage and strength; the ferryman names himself Harbarth. Thor threatens to wade across and repay the mockery; the exchange turns to boasting about past exploits, including Thor’s fight with the giant Hrungnir and Harbarth’s account of living with Fjolvar on an island for five winters, fighting, killing, seeking, and mastering women.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states that the poem is preserved in the Codex Regius (complete) and in the Arnamagnan Codex (from part of stanza 19 to the end).","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The introductory note characterizes the poem as unusually formless and metricaly mixed, with speech-like verse and some parts that appear to be prose.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The introductory note describes the poem as a contest of abuse between Thor and Othin, with Othin appearing disguised as the ferryman Harbarth.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Thor is said to be on his way back from a journey in the East when he comes to a sound; a ferryman with a boat is on the other side.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Thor calls to the ferryman and asks to be ferried over; he offers to feed the ferryman in the morning and says he has a basket with herrings and porridge.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The ferryman replies with insults (calling Thor a peasant), says Thor does not know the future, and claims Thor’s mother is dead; the ferryman also mocks Thor’s poor clothing and lack of hose.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The ferryman says the boat was entrusted to him by Hildolf, whose home is at Rathsey’s sound, and that he is not to ferry robbers or horse-stealers but only worthy men he knows; he asks Thor’s name if Thor wants to cross.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Thor identifies himself by lineage and relations (Othin’s son, Meili’s brother, Magni’s father) and calls himself strong among the gods; he asks the ferryman’s name.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The ferryman gives his name as Harbarth and says he seldom hides his name; he also says he would guard his life even if he had a quarrel with someone like Thor unless doomed to die.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Thor threatens to wade the waters across and repay Harbarth’s mocking words if he gets across; Harbarth says he will stand and await Thor and claims Thor has found no fiercer man since Hrungnir died.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Thor recounts fighting the giant Hrungnir (whose head was of stone) and says he felled and stretched him; he asks what Harbarth did meanwhile.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Harbarth says he was with Fjolvar for five winters and lived on an island called Algrn; he says they could fight and fell the slain, seek much, and master maids.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Thor","description":"A god returning from the East who calls across a sound for passage, offers food as payment, is insulted by the ferryman, threatens to wade across, and boasts of killing the giant Hrungnir.","role_refs":["role:1","role:3","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Harbarth (the ferryman)","description":"A ferryman across the sound who insults Thor, questions his worthiness, states rules for ferrying, gives his name as Harbarth, and boasts of past deeds with Fjolvar.","role_refs":["role:2","role:4","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"Named in the introductory note as one of the two opposing figures, appearing in disguise as the ferryman Harbarth.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Thor's mother (unnamed)","description":"Said by the ferryman to be dead; Thor calls this the mightiest grief.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Hildolf","description":"Named by the ferryman as the one who bade him keep the boat and set rules about whom to ferry; Hildolf’s home is said to be at Rathsey’s sound.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Meili","description":"Named by Thor as his brother.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Magni","description":"Named by Thor as his son (Thor calls himself Magni’s father).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Hrungnir","description":"A giant described as haughty with a head made of stone; multiple related mythic episodes involving Thor and other gods and giants (e.g., Thor’s eastward journey and the Midgard Serpent disguise, Magni’s rescue of Thor, Thor’s duel with Hrungnir, and the abduction and recovery of Ithun).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker refers to toil and trouble while the sun still shines.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Thor says the conversation will be brief because Harbarth speaks only in mockery, and Thor says he will repay Harbarth later if they meet.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Harbarth tells Thor to go away, invoking that every evil thing will have him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes identify Harbarth (Gray-Beard) as Othin and characterize Thor as the thunder-god who journeys frequently.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes describe Thor’s eastward journey (as related by Snorri) including encounters with the giant Skrymir and in Utgartha-Loki’s house lifting a cat that turns out to be Mithgarthsorm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes describe Magni (son of Thor and the giantess Jarnsaxa) lifting a dead giant’s foot from Thor’s neck when no other god could, and state that Magni and Mothi inherit Thor’s hammer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The notes recount Thor’s duel with the giant Hrungnir, including a stone head/heart and a grindstone weapon, the hammer Mjollnir shattering Hrungnir’s head, and Thor being knocked down and pinned by the giant’s foot until freed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes recount that the giant Thjazi tricked to take possession of the goddess Ithun and her apples; Loki, using Freyja’s hawks-dress, turns Ithun into a nut and flies with her; Thjazi pursues in eagle form; the gods kindle a fire that burns the eagle’s wings and then kill him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The notes mention \"riders by night\" described as witches who ride on wolves in the dark.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The notes state a proverb about \"The oak\" (found elsewhere) with a sense comparable to \"to the victor belong the spoils.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The notes compare Thor to Robin Hood in British ballads in that Thor is often temporarily worsted but ultimately comes out ahead.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Thor","description":"A speaking figure in the poem; described in notes as the thunder-god who undertakes many journeys and fights giants.","role_refs":["role:1","role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Harbarth (Gray-Beard)","description":"A speaking figure who mocks Thor and tells him to go away; identified in notes as Othin.","role_refs":["role:2","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"Named in the notes as the identity of Harbarth.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Skrymir (giant)","description":"A giant encountered by Thor on his journey in the East (per Snorri, as summarized in notes).","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Utgartha-Loki","description":"Host/figure associated with the house where Thor lifted a cat (per Snorri, as summarized in notes).","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Mithgarthsorm (Midgard Serpent)","description":"Identified as what the cat turned out to be in the Utgartha-Loki episode (per notes).","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Magni","description":"Son of Thor and the giantess Jarnsaxa; as a brother.","role_refs":["role:8","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Mothi","description":"Named as Magni’s brother who inherits Thor’s hammer.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Jarnsaxa (giantess)","description":"Named as Magni’s mother.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Hrungnir (giant)","description":"A giant who duels Thor; described with a stone heart and head and a direction of attack and kills the dummy giant.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Dummy giant (helper made for Hrungnir)","description":"A giant-shaped Thjalfi.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Loki","description":"In the Ithun episode, goes after Ithun using Freyja’s hawks-dress, turns Ithun into a fire.","role_refs":["role:5","role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Freyja","description":"Mentioned as the owner of the hawks-dress used by thunder-god.\"","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"disguised identity (Harbarth = Othin)","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:3"],"basis":"The notes state: \"Harbarth (Gray-Beard): Othin.\"","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"giant","assigned_to":["fig:4","fig:10","fig:15"],"basis":"Skrymir, Hrungnir, and Thjazi are each described as giants in the of Utgartha-Loki\" during the lifting of the cat episode.","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"serpent (Midgard Serpent)","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"The notes identify the cat as having \"turned out to be Mithgarthsorm.\"","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"rescuer (frees Thor from giant’s foot)","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"The notes say Magni was the only one strong enough to lift the dead giant’s foot from Thor’s neck.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"heir of Thor’s hammer","assigned_to":["fig:7","fig:8"],"basis":"The notes state Magni and his brother Mothi inherit Thor’s hammer.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:10","label":"giantess; mother of Magni","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"The notes identify Magni as son of Thor and \"the giantess Jarnsaxa.\"","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:11","label":"servant of Thor","assigned_to":["fig:11"],"basis":"The notes identify Thjalfi as \"Thors The narrative then begins: Thor wakes to find his hammer stolen; Loki borrows Freyja’s feather-dress to travel to the giants, where Thrym admits hiding the hammer deep in the earth and demands Freyja as his bride in exchange. Freyja refuses angrily, the gods hold counsel, and Heimdall proposes disguising Thor as a bride with veil, Brising necklace, and women’s dress; Loki accompanies him as a maid as they set off toward Jotunheim for the wedding ruse.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states the poem survives only in the Codex Regius and that the story does not occur in the Prose Edda.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The note characterizes the poem as famous and artistically strong, and suggests it assumed its present form around 900; it also notes the poem is preserved without serious gaps and lacks prose narrative links.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note reports suggestions of stylistic similarity and possible common authorship connections among Thrymskvitha, Skirnismol, Lokasenna, and possibly Baldrs Draumar.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Thor wakes, discovers his mighty hammer is missing, and searches for it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Thor tells Loki that the hammer is stolen and that this is not known to humans on earth or in heaven.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Loki goes with Thor to Freyja’s dwelling and asks to borrow her feather-dress in order to seek the hammer; lines 8074-8141","start":"8074","end":"8141","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes on Baldrs Draumar: identifies figures (Baldr, Othin, Frigg, Loki, Hel, etc.), provides genealogical and cosmological glosses (Niflhel, Hel’s realm), explains Odin’s disguise as Vegtam when questioning a wise-woman, recounts traditional details of Baldr’s death (Hoth, mistletoe, Loki’s instigation) and vengeance (Vali born to avenge), and includes cross-references/parallels to other Eddic poems (e.g., Voluspo, Thrymskvitha).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Baldr is described as the best and noblest of the gods, the son of Othin and Frigg, and as one who comes again among the survivors after the final battle.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Baldr is said to be almost never mentioned except in connection with the story of his death; Snorri is noted as having a short passage praising his virtue and beauty.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sleipnir is identified as Othin’s eight-legged horse, the son of Loki and the stallion Svathilfari.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Niflhel is described as the murky dwelling of Hel, goddess of the dead.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A hound (identified as Garm) is mentioned and cross-referenced to Voluspo.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Othin is described as appearing constantly as the god of magic.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hel is described as the offspring of Loki and the giantess Angrbotha; Fenrir and Mithgarthsorm are named as siblings.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hel is said to rule the world of the unhappy dead, described either as those who led evil lives or (in another tradition) those who had not died in battle.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Vegtam (“The Wanderer”) is identified as Othin in disguise; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l8144-l8258","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / RIGSTHULA / THE SONG OF RIG / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 8144-8258","start":"8144","end":"8258","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note discusses the Rigsthula’s manuscript situation, likely date and place of composition, possible praise of a specific king, and Celtic influence; it also notes an annotator’s identification of Rig with Heimdall and suggests the poet may have meant Othin. A short prose preface says the god Heimdall traveled along a seashore, reached a dwelling, and called himself Rig. The poem then begins: Rig travels, enters a house where a fire burns and the old couple Ai and Edda sit; he sits between them, speaks wise words, is served bread and broth, and then lies down to sleep in the bed between them.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The poem (Rigsthula) survives in the Codex Wormanius manuscript associated with Snorri’s Prose Edda, and the end of the poem is missing due to incompleteness of the last sheet.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The introductory note describes the poem as a cultural poem that explains, on a mythological basis, the origin of early social castes (thralls, peasants, warriors) and culminates in the emergence of a future king, presenting the poem as praise of the royal estate.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note argues the poem was likely composed on the Continent (especially Denmark) and discusses possible royal dedicatees (e.g., Gorm the Old or Harald Blue-Tooth), with an approximate composition date in the first half of the tenth century.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The note states that the name “Rig” is likely of Celtic origin, and that the poet picked up bits of Celtic speech and something of the Celtic literary spirit, while also emphasizing extensive Norse-Celt contact as a context for influence.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A later medieval annotator identifies Rig with Heimdall, while the note states there is little in the poem itself to warrant this and suggests the poet likely had Othin in mind to trace royal origin to the chief of the gods.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In the prose preface, Heimdall travels along a seashore to a dwelling and calls himself Rig.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the opening stanzas, Rig travels “by ways so green” and then goes “on the midmost way” to a dwelling.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rig enters the dwelling; a fire is on the floor, and two hoary ones sit by the hearth, named Ai and Edda.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Rig sits in the middle of the room with Ai and Edda on either side, and Rig is described as knowing wise words to speak.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Edda brings a heavy, thick loaf of bread and sets it on the table; there is broth in a bowl, and boiled calf’s flesh is mentioned as the best dainty.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Rig rises to sleep and lies in the bed with Ai and Edda on either side.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Rig (a god; identified in prose as Heimdall)","description":"A god who travels to a dwelling, calls The notes also comment on manuscript gaps and stanza arrangement, explain names and name-meanings (e.g., Ai/Edda, Thrll), mention a pre-Christian custom of sprinkling water on children, note an association of dark hair with foreignness and slavery, and point to Celtic linguistic influence in certain words (e.g., Rig from Old Irish for “king,” and a term for “cart”).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The prose annotator identifies Rig as Heimdall but provides little information beyond what is in the poem; the annotator is suggested to have written around 1300 or later and is not credited with considerable mythological knowledge.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes state there is little support for identifying Rig with Heimdall beyond vague passages in other poems, while elements in Rigsthula (e.g., “aged and wise” and references to runes) are said to fit Othin well; the notes conclude Rig is probably Othin rather than Heimdall.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes explain “Rig” is almost certainly based on the Old Irish word for king (ri/rig).","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Editors are said to assume gaps/lacunae and rearrangements in the manuscript; multiple specific stanza-line issues and conjectural reconstructions are described.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A custom of sprinkling water on children is noted as pre-Christian and referenced as antedating Christianity.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Dark hair (“Black”) is described as a mark of a foreigner among blond Scandinavians, hence of a slave, in the note’s explanation of Thrll (Thrall/Slave).","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A term glossed as “cart” (kartr) is described as a clear sign of Celtic influence.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Prose annotator (of the introductory note)","description":"A later annotator (c. 1300 or later) who content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l8706-l8848","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HYNDLULJOTH / THE POEM OF HYNDLA / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 8706-8848","start":"8706","end":"8848","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note describes the Hyndluljoth’s late manuscript preservation (in Flateyjarbok), its apparent composite nature, and an inserted fragment identified as the “short Voluspo,” characterized as an inferior imitation. The poem then begins: Freyja wakes the wise-woman Hyndla in a cave and urges a ride toward Valhall; Freyja speaks of divine gifts and honors Thor. Freyja and Hyndla travel with a boar and a wolf; Hyndla suggests Freyja’s lover Ottar rides with them, while Freyja points to the golden-bristled boar Hildisvini made by dwarfs. Freyja explains a wager involving Ottar and asks Hyndla to recite genealogies; she also mentions Ottar built a stone shrine and made blood offerings. Hyndla begins tracing Ottar’s ancestry and related heroic lineages.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states the Hyndluljoth is preserved in Flateyjarbok (c. 1400) rather than the two major Poetic Edda manuscripts, and that the surviving text is in poor shape and appears to be two poems (or parts) clumsily combined.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The note says a 51-line fragment is inserted into Hyndluljoth and is identified via Snorri as the “short Voluspo,” described as a late and inferior imitation of the great Voluspo.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Freyja addresses Hyndla, calling her “sister,” and tells her to wake in her hollow cave; Freyja says they must ride to Valhall to seek the sacred hall as darkness approaches.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Freyja says they seek the favor of “Heerfather,” who gives gold to his followers and previously gave Hermoth helm and mail-coat and Sigmund a sword.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Freyja lists different gifts granted to different people: triumph, treasure, wisdom and skill in words, fair winds for sailors, art for singers, and a manly heart for heroes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Freyja says she will honor Thor and ask that Hyndla may ever find Thor’s true favor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Freyja asks Hyndla to lead forth one of Hyndla’s wolves to run with Freyja’s boar, because the boar goes slowly on the road of the gods and Freyja does not wish to weary her steed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hyndla tells Freyja she asks falsely and claims that Freyja’s lover travels with her on the “way of the slain,” naming him as Ottar the young, son of Instein.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Freyja rejects Hyndla’s claim and points to a boar with bristles of gold named Hildisvini, made by the dwarfs Dain and Nabbi.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Freyja proposes they leap down from their The notes also reference Odin and related figures, including Sigmund drawing a sword from a tree after a stranger (identified as Odin) thrusts it there, and provide genealogical lore about Halfdan the Old and descendants of Odin used in heroic/royal ancestries. Additional comments include the \"road to Valhöll\" and material details such as altar fires vitrifying stone.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ottar is said to have wagered his entire inheritance with Angantyr concerning which of them has loftier ancestry.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ottar is said to have induced Freyja to help establish his genealogy by making rich offerings; the note implies Hyndla hints at less commendable methods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Freyja is said to have turned Ottar into a boar as a disguise and to have called on the giantess Hyndla to aid her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Hyndla is said to detect Ottar and accuse Freyja of having her lover with her; the phrase \"the way of the slain\" is glossed as the road to Valhöll.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"There is a note that Freyja’s \"worthy steed\" is a boar, identified as Ottar in boar form.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Sigmund is said to have been the only one able to draw a sword from a tree after a mysterious stranger (identified as Odin) thrust it into the tree.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Skjold is described as a mythical king, said to be Odin’s son and the ancestor of Danish kings.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Halfdan the Old is described as a mythical king about whom a prophecy foretold that for three hundred years no one in his line would lack great repute; after slaying Sigtrygg he marries Almveig/Alvig and has eighteen sons, nine born at one time, with differing fates for the groups of sons.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Altar fires are described as constant enough to fuse stone into glass.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A boar with golden bristles is mentioned in connection with Freyja/Freyr; dwarfs Dain and Nabbi are named in that context.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Freyja","description":"A goddess who assists Ottar with genealogy, disguises him as a boar, and seeks help from Hyndla.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ottar","description":"A man who wagers his inheritance on ancestry, makes offerings to gain Freyja’s help, and is disguised as a boar.","role_refs":["role:2","role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Angantyr","description":"The person with whom Ottar wagers his inheritance regarding the loftiness of ancestry.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Hyndla (\"She-Dog\")","description":"A giantess called on by Freyja; GROUGALDR / GROAS SPELL / II. FJOLSVINNSMOL / THE LAY OF FJOLSVITH; lines 9748-9913","start":"9748","end":"9913","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In a question-and-answer exchange, Svipdag asks Fjolsvith about a hall surrounded by magic flames, its name and makers, a mountain where Mengloth lies, and maidens at her knees who aid those who give offerings. Fjolsvith says only Svipdag may sleep in Mengloth’s arms because she is destined to be his bride. Svipdag demands the gates be opened; Fjolsvith announces him. Mengloth threatens punishment if Fjolsvith lies, then asks Svipdag’s origin and name; Svipdag identifies himself, and Mengloth welcomes him, stating she has waited on Lyfjaberg and that they will live together to the end.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Svipdag asks what the hall is called, describing it as encompassed with flickering magic flames.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Fjolsvith says the hall is called Lyr and that it shall long tremble on the tip of a spear-point; mankind has heard of it but known little more.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Fjolsvith lists multiple beings as makers/builders of the hall: Uni, Iri, Bari, Jari, Var, Vegdrasil, Dori, Ori, Delling, and Loki.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Svipdag asks the name of the mountain on which the maid lies; Fjolsvith says it is Lyfjaberg and that it brings joy/healing to the sick and sore; women who climb it do well though they have long been sick.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Fjolsvith names the maidens sitting at Mengloth’s knees: Hlif, Hlifthrasa, Thjothvara, Bjort, Bleik, Blith, Frith, Eir, and Aurbotha.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Fjolsvith says these maidens soon bring aid to all who give offerings on holy high altars and guard the sons of men from ill when they see danger.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Fjolsvith states no man may seek to sleep in Mengloth’s arms except Svipdag alone, because the sun-bright maid is destined to be his bride.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Svipdag commands the gates be flung back and the gateway made wide, and asks that Mengloth’s gladness toward him be found out.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Fjolsvith tells Mengloth a man has come; he describes hounds fawning and the house bursting open, and thinks Svipdag is there.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Mengloth threatens that hungry ravens on a high gallows will pluck out Fjolsvith’s eyes if he lies about the hero’s coming; she asks the newcomer’s origin, how he came, and the name his kinsmen call him as a sign she is destined to be his bride.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Svipdag identifies himself as Svipdag, Solbjart’s son; he says he came by wind-cold ways and adds that no man should war with the words of Urth, though her gifts be unearned.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Mengloth welcomes Svipdag, offers a kiss, says she has waited long and sat on Lyfjaberg awaiting him day by day, and says they yearned alike and will live together to the end.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Svipdag","description":"Questioner who seeks entry, identifies himself as Solbjart’s son, and is said to be the only one destined to sleep in Mengloth’s arms.","role_refs":["role:1","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Fjolsvith","description":"Respondent who answers Svipdag’s questions about the hall, mountain, maidens, and who may sleep in Mengloth’s arms; he announces Svipdag’s arrival to Mengloth.","role_refs":["role:2","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Mengloth","description":"A maid who has sat on Lyfjaberg awaiting Svipdag; she tests the claim of his arrival, asks for his identity, then welcomes him and affirms their destined union.","role_refs":["role:3","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Maidens at Mengloth’s knees (Hlif, Hlifthrasa, Thjothvara, Bjort, Bleik, Blith, Frith, Eir, ill.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Urth","description":"Named figure whose 'words' are said not to be warred against; her gifts may be given unearned.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Ravens (hungry)","description":"Hungry ravens associated with a high gallows, said to pluck out eyes as content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l10069-l10184","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LAYS OF THE HEROES / VLUNDARKVITHA / THE LAY OF VLUND / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 10069-10184","start":"10069","end":"10184","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An editorial introductory note discusses the manuscript state and probable transmission of the Weland/Vlund tradition (including links to Anglo-Saxon and German materials). A prose narrative then introduces King Nithuth of Sweden and three brothers (Slagfith, Egil, Vlund) who meet three women with swan-garments (Valkyries), take them home, and live with them for seven winters until the women fly away; the men attempt pursuit, and Vlund remains behind. The note ends by stating that King Nithuth has Vlund seized by force; the poem opens with a stanza about maids from the south flying through Myrkwood and spinning flax on the shore.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states that the Vlundarkvitha stands between Thrymskvitha and Alvissmol in the Codex Regius, and that the Regius text is in very bad shape; another manuscript (Arnamagnan Codex fragment) preserves only a few opening lines of prose.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The note discusses the Weland/Vlund tradition and explicitly mentions relations between the Vlundarkvitha and the Weland passage in Deor's Lament; it further states that the story came to the North from Saxon regions and was not a native product of Scandinavia.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note says the main story involves the laming of the smith by King Nithuth and Weland's revenge, and that an introductory swan-maiden story has been added, in which the swan-maiden is also said to be a Valkyrie.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A prose narrative says there was a king in Sweden named Nithuth with two sons and one daughter named Bothvild.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The prose narrative says three brothers, sons of a king of the Finns (Slagfith, Egil, Vlund), hunted on snowshoes, came to Ulfdalir, built a house, and there was a lake called Ulfsjar.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The brothers found three women on the lake shore spinning flax; near them were swan-garments, and they were Valkyries; they are named and given parentage (two daughters of King Hlothver; the third daughter of Kjar from Valland).","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The prose narrative reports pairings: Egil took Olrun, Slagfith took Hlathguth Swan-White, and Vlund took Hervor All-Wise; they dwelt seven winters; then the women flew away to find battles and did not return.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The prose narrative says Egil and Slagfith set out on snowshoes to follow their departed partners, while Vlund stayed in Ulfdalir and is described as a most skillful man known from old tales; it then states King Nithuth had him taken by force.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The opening stanza describes 'maids from the south' flying through Myrkwood, resting on the shore of the sea, and spinning flax.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"King Nithuth (of Sweden)","description":"A king in Sweden; father of two sons and a daughter named Bothvild; later has Vlund taken by force.","role_refs":["role:1","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Bothvild","description":"Daughter of King Nithuth.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Nithuth's two sons","description":"Two sons of King Nithuth (not named here).","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Slagfith","description":"One of three brothers, sons of a king of the Finns; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l10186-l10346","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LAYS OF THE HEROES / VLUNDARKVITHA / THE LAY OF VLUND / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 10186-10346","start":"10186","end":"10346","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Three women associated with swan-feathers live with three men for several years, then leave for the woods. Vlund remains alone, makes rings, and is raided by King Nithuth’s men, who take a ring. Vlund is later captured, chained, and—at the queen’s urging—has the sinews in his knee-joints cut and is set on the island Svarstath to smith for the king. Vlund lures Nithuth’s two sons to his workshop, kills them, hides their bodies, and fashions objects from their skulls, eyes, and teeth, sending these to Nithuth, the queen, and Nithuth’s daughter Bothvild. Bothvild later speaks of having broken a ring.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hlathguth and Hervor are named as Hlothver’s children, and Olrun the Wise as Kjar’s daughter.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Egil takes one woman in his arms and to his bosom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A second sister is described as “Swan-White” and wearing swan-feathers.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A third sister throws her arms around Vlund’s neck.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The women sit with the men for seven winters; later they yearn for the murky wood and depart to follow their fate.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Vlund returns from hunting with Egil and Slagfith and finds the hall empty; they search everywhere.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Egil goes east after Olrun, Slagfith goes south to seek Swan-White, and Vlund lies alone in Ulfdalir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Vlund fashions red gold with gems and strings rings on ropes of bast while waiting for his wife to return.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Nithuth learns Vlund is alone in Ulfdalir; by night his men enter the hall and see rings on bast ropes, described as seven hundred.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The raiders take the rings but leave all except one, which they carry away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Vlund returns from hunting, roasts bear flesh with fire, rests on a bearskin, counts the rings, and finds one missing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Vlund falls asleep and wakes to see heavy chains on his hands and fetters binding his feet.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Vlund asks who has bound him with bast ropes; Nithuth questions how Vlund obtained treasures in Ulfdalir.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Vlund says the gold was not on “Grani’s way,” and that their realm is far from the hills of the Rhine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Nithuth’s wife says Vlund does not look kind who comes from the wood; she says the glow of his eyes is like gleaming snakes and he gnashes his teeth if the sword or Bothvild’s ring is shown.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The queen urges that Vlund’s sinews of strength be cut and that he be set in Svarstath; the sinews in his knee-joints are cut and he is set on an island called Svarstath.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"In Svarstath, Vlund smithies precious things for the king; no one dares go to him except the king.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Vlund states that a sword he made gleams at Nithuth’s girdle and that Bothvild has a golden ring once belonging to Vlund’s bride.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Two boys, Nithuth’s sons, come to Vlund’s door to gaze; they ask for keys to a chest and see gems, gold, and precious stones.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Vlund tells the boys to come alone the next day for gold and to tell no one they sought him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The next day the boys return; Vlund smites off their heads and hides their feet under the sooty straps of the bellows.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Vlund sets the boys’ skulls in silver and sends them to Nithuth; he fashions gems from their eyes and gives them to Nithuth’s wife; he makes a brooch from their teeth and sends it to Bothvild.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Bothvild boasts of her ring and says she has broken it, and says she dares not tell it except to Vlund.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Vlund (also called ‘greatest of elves’, ‘master of elves’)","description":"A hunter and skilled smith who makes rings and later is captured, hamstrung, and set on Svarstath to work; he kills Nithuth’s sons and crafts items from their remains.","role_refs":["role:3","role:6","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7","ev:9","ev:10","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Egil","description":"One of the men associated with the women; he takes a woman in his arms and later goes east after Olrun.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Slagfith","description":"One of the men; he searches for the women and goes south to seek Swan-White.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Hlathguth","description":"Named with Hervor as Hlothver’s children; one of the women in the group of three sisters.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Hervor","description":"Named with Hlathguth as Hlothver’s children; one of the women in the group of three sisters.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Olrun the Wise","description":"Kjar’s daughter; associated with Egil, whom she is pursued by when the women depart.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Swan-White (unnamed sister)","description":"Described as wearing swan-feathers; sought by Slagfith after the women depart.","role_refs":["role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Nithuth, lord of the Njars","description":"Learns Vlund is alone, sends men to raid, and later keeps Vlund on Svarstath; wears Vlund’s sword and gives a ring to his daughter Bothvild.","role_refs":["role:8","role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Nithuth’s men (raiders)","description":"Enter Vlund’s hall at night and take a ring from the bast rope.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Nithuth’s wife (the queen)","description":"Speaks about Vlund’s appearance and urges cutting his knee-joint sinews and setting him in Svarstath; receives gems made from the boys’ eyes.","role_refs":["role:11","role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Bothvild (Nithuth’s daughter)","description":"Receives a gold ring taken from Vlund’s house and later receives a brooch made from the boys’ teeth; says she broke a ring and confides to Vlund.","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:10","ev:12","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:
