content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l11252-l11299","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HELGAKVITHA HJORVARTHSSONAR / THE LAY OF HELGI THE SON OF HJORVARTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / OF HJORVARTH AND SIGRLIN; lines 11252-11299","start":"11252","end":"11299","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In a sequence of speeches, Helgi (son of Hjorvarth) is reported to have fallen at Frekastein. Mortally wounded, Helgi bids farewell to Svava and asks her not to weep and to prepare to share a bed and love with the younger hero Hethin. Svava replies that she vowed she would not embrace an unfamed man if Helgi died. Hethin asks Svava for a kiss and declares he will not return to certain places until he has taken vengeance for Helgi. A closing note states that Helgi and Svava were born again.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker asks what happened to Helgi, Hjorvarth's son, and says harm has come; if the sea struck him or a sword cut him, the speaker will bring ill to all his foes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Sigar states that Helgi fell in the morning at Frekastein; he calls him the noblest king beneath the sun, and says Alf has the joy of victory.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Helgi greets Svava, says this is their last meeting in life, reports his wounds bleeding, and says the sword has come close to his heart.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Helgi tells Svava not to weep, to prepare the bed for Hethin, and to yield her love to the young hero.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Svava says she had a vow at home: when Helgi sought her with rings, she would not, of her will, fold in her arms an unfamed man if the warrior died.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hethin asks Svava to kiss him and says he will not come back to Rogheim or Rothulsfjoll until he has vengeance for the son of Hjorvarth, the noblest king beneath the sun.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A concluding statement says that Helgi and Svava were born The poem’s opening stanzas narrate Helgi’s birth amid cosmic imagery; Norns come at night to shape his life and weave a web of fate with golden threads fixed in the moon’s hall, and they cast a chain to be firm. Ravens speak from a treetop about the newborn son of Sigmund, described as standing in a mail-coat a half-day old, with sharp flashing eyes and as a friend of wolves. Helgi is named and given multiple place-names and a “blood-snake bedecked.” He grows strong and generous with gold. At fifteen he kills Hunding; Hunding’s sons seek compensation, which he refuses, predicting a storm of lances and Odin’s grimness. Warriors go to battle at Logafjoll, breaking “Frothi’s peace,” and “Vithrir’s hounds” go hungrily through the     "quote": "",
    "summary": "Editorial notes summarize manuscript superscriptions, identify figures (Helgi, Sigmund, Hunding, etc.), and explain elements such as portents at a hero's birth, the Norns shaping destiny, a king bestowing lands and a symbolic object on his son, and Valkyries associated with lightning/clouds; the notes also provide cross-references to other Eddic poems and saga material.",

      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "The notes state that screaming eagles and water pouring from heaven were portents of the birth of a hero.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The notes state that the Norns preside over Helgi's early destiny in this lay (rather than a Valkyrie).",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "The notes say the Norns give Helgi fame in the East, West, and North, with his renown particularly enduring in the North.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Sigmund is described as a link between the Helgi and Sigurth stories, with multiple children by different wives and an incestuous connection producing Sinfjotli.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]

      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "A king (identified as Sigmund) gives his son a symbol of the lands he bestows on him; the notes mention a leek in connection with this symbol.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "The notes gloss 'Blood-snake' as meaning a sword.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "The notes gloss 'Vithrir's hounds' as wolves, identifying Vithrir as Othin and naming the wolves Freki and Geri.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]

      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "The notes state that lightning accompanies the Valkyries and suggest this supports identifying them with clouds.",

The notes identify Hogni as Sigrun’s father, explain Helgi and Sinfjotli as Volsungs (sons of Sigmund), and discuss traditions/confusions about descent from Yngvi (possibly associated by some with Freyr) versus the Volsungs’ claimed descent from Othin. A stanza mentioning Hringstathir may be an interpolation or contain a mistake about whether Helgi received it from his father or conquered it from Granmar’s sons.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that “Fire-beasts” (dragons) refers to ships, and that Norse warships were often Reginthing (The Great Council) as an apparent national council-place distinct from a local council, and give names for horses (Melnir/Mylnir/Sporvitnir).","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes gloss Myrkwood as a dark forest name and Sparinsheith as a heath about which nothing more is known.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes gloss “Flame of wounds” as sword.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes state that “Wound-givers” probably means Valkyries (with doubt about the original word), and explain that the wolf (said to be giantesses’ customary steed) eats corpses (food of birds of Hming (a son of Hunding) is at home at that time.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In a stanza, Helgi instructs someone to tell Hming that Helgi knows whom the heroes have hidden in armor, describing a gray wolf within their hall, which Hunding’s man Hamal thought was something else.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"King Hunding sends men to Hagal to seek Helgi; Helgi evades them by putting on the clothes of a bond-woman and working at the mill; the searchers do not find him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Blind (described as evil-minded) remarks that Hagal’s bond-woman has bright eyes and that the millwork is so violent that millstones break and boards are shattered.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A stanza states that the hero has a hard fate, needing to grind barley, and that his hand would better fit a sword-hilt than millstones.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hagal replies that it is no wonder boards are splintered because the mill is turned by a monarch’s daughter who once rode through clouds and fought battles; he adds that Helgi held her captive and names her as sister of Sigar and Hogni, explaining the bright eyes of the “Ylfings maid.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Helgi escapes, goes to a fighting ship, kills King Hunding, and is thereafter called Helgi Hundingsbane.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Later, Helgi lies with his host at Brunavagar; It summarizes story-points implied by the poem (Helgi living with Hunding under an assumed name, being protected by a foster-father, pursuit by a capture-party, references to raids and battles, and councils of kings) and comments on scholarly/annotator explanations, including a claim that Sigrun is Svava reborn and the suggestion that Helgi could be the earlier Helgi born again.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that an annotator explained the child being named after Helgi Hjorvarthsson, and also accounts for Sigrun by saying she was Svava reborn; the notes add that one could instead say the new Helgi was the old one born again.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes state that Helgi appears to have stayed with Hunding under the name of Hamal, and later sends word of who he really is.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes identify Hagal as Helgi's foster-father and say he protects Helgi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes identify Blind as the leader of a band sent to capture content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l13064-l13143","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / FRA DAUTHA SINFJOTLA / OF SINFJOTLIS DEATH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 13064-13143","start":"13064","end":"13143","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note explains how the Helgi tradition became linked to the Volsung tradition, mainly through Helgi being identified as Sigmund’s son. It summarizes Sinfjotli’s backstory as told in the Volsungasaga: Siggeir betrays and kills Volsung and captures his sons; a wolf devours the brothers until Sigmund escapes with Signy’s help. Signy (Sigmund’s twin sister) disguises herself by changing forms with a witch and conceives Sinfjotli with Sigmund; Sigmund and Sinfjotli later take revenge, including killing Signy’s sons, escaping burial alive with the help of a smuggled sword, and burning Siggeir’s house. The note then discusses the organization of Eddic material and says the compiler inserted a short prose account ‘Of Sinfjotli’s Death’ to dispose of Sigmund and Sinfjotli before beginning the Sigurth poems.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The note states that the Helgi tradition (originally from Denmark) was early associated with the Volsung tradition (German/Frankish), with the main link being Helgi identified as Sigmund Volsungsson’s son.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Sinfjotli appears in the Helgi poems and is described as having a wordy dispute with Gothmund Granmarsson.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the Volsungasaga summary, Signy is identified as Sigmund Volsungsson’s twin sister and is married to Siggeir, who hates Sigmund for a sword that had belonged to Othin and was won by Sigmund.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Siggeir treacherously invites Volsung and his ten sons, kills Volsung, captures the sons, and has them set in the stocks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Each night a wolf (said by some to be Siggeir’s mother) comes from the woods and eats one of the brothers until only Sigmund remains; Signy helps Sigmund escape and the wolf is killed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Signy changes forms with a witch, visits Sigmund in that guise for three nights, and later gives birth to a boy named Sinfjotli, whom she sends to Sigmund.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Sigmund and Sinfjotli live in the woods and sometimes turn into wolves.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When grown, Sinfjotli and Sigmund go to Siggeir’s house, are betrayed by Signy and Siggeir’s two young sons, and Sinfjotli kills the two boys.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Siggeir has Sigmund and Sinfjotli buried alive; Signy smuggles Sigmund’s famous sword into the grave, and father and son dig themselves out with it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The next night Sigmund and Sinfjotli burn Siggeir’s house; Siggeir dies in the flames, and Signy perishes with him after refusing to leave.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The note states that the compiler of poems in the Codex Regius inserted the prose piece ‘Of Sinfjotli’s Death’ because he knew of no poem about the deaths of Sigmund and Sinfjotli and wanted to move on to the Sigurth poems.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sinfjotli","description":"A son of Sigmund; appears in Helgi poems (dispute with Gothmund) and in Volsungasaga narrative as the boy born to Signy and sent to Sigmund; later takes part in revenge against Siggeir.","role_refs":["role:4","role:8","role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sigmund Volsungsson","description":"A son of Volsung; survives the wolf’s predation; helped by Signy; fathers Sinfjotli (unknowing of her identity); later buried alive and escapes using a smuggled sword; takes revenge on Siggeir.","role_refs":["role:1","role:5","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5","ev:6","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Signy","description":"Sigmund’s twin sister; wife of Siggeir; helps Sigmund escape; changes forms with a witch and conceives Sinfjotli with Sigmund; later smuggles a sword into the grave; perishes with Siggeir in the burning house.","role_refs":["role:2","role:6","role:7","role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5","ev:6","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Siggeir","description":"Signy’s husband; kills Volsung and captures Volsung’s sons; has Sigmund and Sinfjotli buried alive; dies when his house is burned.","role_refs":["role:3","role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Volsung","description":"Killed by Siggeir after being treacherously invited to visit with his sons.","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Wolf (possibly Siggeir’s mother)","description":"Comes from the woods at night and eats Sigmund’s brothers until only Sigmund remains; is then killed (with Signy’s aid to Sigmund’s escape).","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Witch (form-exchange with Signy)","description":"A witch with whom Signy changes forms; in that guise Signy approaches Sigmund.","role_refs":["role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"Associated with a sword that had belonged to him and was won by Sigmund, which Siggeir desired.","role_refs":["role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Helgi","description":"Identified as a son of Sigmund; key link between Helgi and Volsung traditions per the lays.","role_refs":["role:18"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Two young sons of Signy and Siggeir","description":"They see and betray Sigmund and Sinfjotli; Sinfjotli kills Sinfjotli","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Signy gives birth to Sinfjotli and sends him to Sigmund.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"enemy and betrayer","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Siggeir treacherously invites and slays Volsung, captures the sons, and later buries Sigmund and Sinfjotli alive.","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:9"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"avenger","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Sinfjotli participates in the revenge, including killing the betraying boys and helping burn guise.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"participant in wolf-transformation","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Sinfjotli and Sigmund live in the woods, occasionally turning into The note discusses scholarly views about the origin and transmission of the Sigurth (Siegfried) story from the Rhine-Franks into Scandinavia (especially Norway) via early medieval contacts, emphasizing the mixing of fiction and history in saga tradition and the tendency of famous heroes to attract unrelated tales. It lists probable early features of the Sigurth legend: strength and valor, acquisition of a great treasure, wooing of a somewhat supernatural bride, and death at the hands of his kinsmen.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The note states that Gripisspo follows the prose Fra Dautha Sinfjotla in the Codex Regius and country, and that it was especially known in Norway and Norwegian settlements.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The note cites historical contact (commercial goods.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The note states that due to lack of contemporary material the early (7th-century) Rhine-country form of the Sigurth legend content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l13729-l13849","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY NOTE / GRIPISSPO / GRIPIRS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 13729-13849","start":"13729","end":"13849","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In a dialogue framed as prophecy, Sigurth questions Gripir about events involving Gunnar’s marriage and accusations of deceit. Gripir foretells that a marriage draught will be drunk for both Sigurth and Gunnar, that they will change forms while traveling home though each keeps his own mind, and that Sigurth will live in good wedlock with Guthrun. Brynhild, feeling badly mated, will seek revenge and tell Gunnar that Sigurth ill fulfilled his oath; despite this, Gripir says Sigurth gave her no shame though he deceived the monarch’s wife with wiles. Gripir further foretells that Gunnar and his kin (including Gotthorm and Hogni, the sons of Gjuki) will kill Sigurth, bringing lasting grief to Guthrun, and concludes by praising Sigurth’s renown and nobility.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Sigurth states that men will call him base for what he did, and he says he will not cheat with wiles the hero’s maiden whom he holds noblest.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gripir says Sigurth will dwell with a maid as if she were his mother, and that Sigurth’s name will remain as ruler of men as long as the world lives.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sigurth asks whether Gunnar will have a goodly wife, noting that she slept at Sigurth’s side for three nights though she is called the warriors’ bride.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Gripir says a marriage draught will be drunk for both Sigurth and Gunnar in Gjuki’s hall; when they fare home their forms will change, but the mind of each remains his own.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Gripir says Sigurth will be silent, remembering his oaths, and will dwell with Guthrun in good wedlock; Brynhild will deem herself badly mated and will seek wiles to avenge herself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Gripir says Brynhild will tell Gunnar that Sigurth ill fulfilled his oath when Gunnar trusted Sigurth with all his heart.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Gripir says the noble bride will do Sigurth little good; Sigurth gave her no shame, though he cheated the monarch’s wife with wiles.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sigurth asks whether Gunnar, Gotthorm, Hogni, and the sons of Gjuki will heed the woman’s words and redden their blades with their kinsman’s blood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Gripir says Guthrun will feel heavy grief when all her brothers bring Sigurth death, and that she will never again know happiness; Gripir attributes this to Grimhild’s work.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Sigurth content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l13852-l13962","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GRIPISSPO / GRIPIRS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 13852-13962","start":"13852","end":"13962","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes describe characters and plot traditions surrounding Gripir’s prophecy about Sigurth, including: the dragon Fafnir guarding treasure; Sigurth’s connections to Gjuki’s family; confusion from Brynhild’s dual identity across versions; a magic drink causing Sigurth to forget Brynhild; a wooing episode involving disguise/form-changing and a ring of fire; and an oath-bound killing carried out by a half-brother. The notes also compare northern and southern Germanic variants (e.g., the Nibelungenlied).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The manuscript gives the poem no title; Gripir (Sigurth’s uncle) and the serving-man Geitir are described as likely poetical inventions, and the Volsungasaga is said to mention Gripir presumably because of this poem.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The manuscript does not indicate speakers; editors differ on whether certain two-line speeches should be separated into distinct stanzas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Fafnir (brother of the dwarf Regin) is said to turn himself into a dragon to guard Andvari’s hoard; Gnitaheith is described as a relic of German tradition.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Notes describe conflicting story versions: Sigurth’s sequence of visiting Gjuki’s hall and encountering Brynhild/a Valkyrie differs among traditions, and an attempt is described to combine versions, producing confusion linked to Brynhild’s ‘dual identity.’","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Grani is identified as Sigurth’s horse; one account says Grani’s father was Sleipnir and that Othin gave Grani to Sigurth.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The poet is said to narrate Sigurth’s finding of a Valkyrie (not identified as Brynhild in the note), and there is discussion of whether the punished Valkyrie’s associated hero is Helgi or Hjalmgunnar.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Grimhild is said to give Sigurth a magic draught that makes him forget Brynhild.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In the northern version, Sigurth and Gunnar change forms; to win Brynhild one must ride through a ring of fire around her hall; Gunnar’s horse balks, Grani will not move for Gunnar, and Sigurth rides Grani through the flames after the form-change.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"An oath of blood-brotherhood among Sigurth, Gunnar, and Hogni is said to prevent the brothers from killing Sigurth directly, leading them to induce their half-brother Gotthorm to do it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A comparison is made: in the Nibelungenlied, Siegfried becomes invisible to lend Gunther strength for wooing feats, whereas in the northern version Sigurth and Gunnar change forms.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Gripir","description":"Sigurth’s uncle; described in the notes as probably a poetical invention.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"Hero figure discussed in multiple narrative variants (slaying Fafnir; relations with Gjuki’s family; forgetting Brynhild; form-changing episode).","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Geitir","description":"Serving-man; described as apparently an invention of the poets.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Grani","description":"Sigurth’s horse; one tradition makes him a descendant of Sleipnir and a gift from Othin.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"Said (in one account) to have given Grani to Sigurth; Sleipnir is identified as Othin’s eight-legged horse.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Fafnir","description":"Brother of the dwarf Regin; said to turn himself into a dragon to guard Andvari’s hoard.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Regin","description":"Dwarf and brother of Fafnir, mentioned in connection with the hoard guarded by the dragon.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Andvari","description":"Associated with the hoard guarded by Fafnir in dragon form (Andvari’s hoard).","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Gjuki","description":"Named as father of Gunnar, Hogni, and Guthrun; his hall is a destination in one of the described story sequences.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"Member of Gjuki’s family; participates in a wooing episode involving a form-change with Sigurth and attempting (then failing) to ride through flames; involved in oath constraints related to Sigurth’s death.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Hogni","description":"Associated with Gunnar and Sigurth in a blood-brotherhood oath that constrains the killing of Sigurth.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"Member of Gjuki’s family; mentioned in connection with a magic draught administered by her mother in one version.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Brynhild (Armed Warrior)","description":"Discussed as having a ‘dual identity’ across versions; her hall is said (in the Volsungasaga account) to be surrounded by a ring of fire; relationships and foster-family traditions are discussed.","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Unnamed Valkyrie (as described in the notes)","description":"Figure Sigurth is said to find in the poet’s use of Sigrdrifumol; note says she is not identified with Brynhild in that discussion.","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Grimhild","description":"Described as giving Sigurth a magic draught that makes him forget Brynhild; also associated with teaching how to change forms in the northern version described.","role_refs":["role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Gotthorm","description":"Half-brother induced to kill Sigurth due to constraints created by blood-brotherhood oaths.","role_refs":["role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Heimir","description":"Appears in the Volsungasaga account as someone Sigurth and Gunnar visit; he is said to tell them about the ring-of-fire requirement around Brynhild’s hall.","role_refs":["role:17"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Atli (Attila)","description":"Mentioned as Brynhild’s brother in older Norse poems (a relationship described as foreign to southern stories).","role_refs":["role:18"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:19","name_or_label":"Siegfried / Gunther (Nibelungenlied figures, as referenced)","description":"In the Nibelungenlied comparison, Siegfried becomes invisible to lend Gunther strength for wooing feats.","role_refs":["role:19"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"prophetic uncle figure (as framed by notes)","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Gripir is identified as Sigurth’s uncle in the notes and is the named prophecy figure for the poem; the note comments on his likely invention.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"hero / central actor in dragon-slaying and courtship cycle","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"Sigurth is discussed as slayer of Fafnir, visitor to Gjuki’s hall, recipient of a magic draught, participant in form-change and fire-riding, and eventual victim of a killing plot.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"serving-man","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Geitir is explicitly called a serving-man in the notes.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"exceptional horse / mount in ordeal","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Grani is Sigurth’s horse and is the horse that will carry Sigurth through the flames, but will not move for Gunnar.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"divine giver","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"Othin is said to have given Grani to Sigurth in one account mentioned by the notes.","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"treasure-guarding dragon (shapeshifted being)","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"Fafnir is said to turn himself into a dragon to guard Andvari’s hoard.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"dwarf kin of the dragon","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"Regin is identified as Fafnir’s brother and as a dwarf in the note.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"owner-associated figure of a named hoard","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"The treasure is explicitly called Andvari’s hoard in the notes.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"patriarch of the Gjuki family","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"Gjuki is stated to be father of Gunnar, Hogni, and Guthrun.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]

lines 14376-14492","start":"14376","end":"14492","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An editorial notes section summarizing identifications, variant traditions, and interpretive comments for Reginsmál: it explains characters (e.g., Regin, Hreithmar, Andvari, Loki, Óðinn), variant versions (Snorri, Völsunga saga, Þiðrekssaga, Helgi-cycle parallels), and glosses key items (gold as “waters’ flame,” Andvari’s ring that makes new gold, the curse on the treasure, ship-kennings, and other named objects like Gram and the fear-helm).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes identify Hjalprek as the father of Alf and the step-father of Sigurth, and refer to Grani in cross-reference to another poem.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Regin is glossed as “Counsel-Giver,” linked in the notes to a smith figure in a German story tradition; the notes also state that in a Þiðrekssaga version the figure is called Mimir, while “Regin” is there the name of the dragon.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes state that Völuspá names a Regin among the dwarfs, and suggest the name may have helped make Regin a dwarf in this poem’s presentation.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes state that Óðinn, Hœnir, and Loki appear together in company (also noted as appearing together in Völuspá).","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes discuss “Andvari’s fall” and state that in Snorri’s account its location differs (dark-elves world), while here the two falls/locations are treated as identical with the place where Loki killed the otter.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes explain that in Snorri’s account Otr ate with his eyes shut because of greed, and that Snorri says Loki caught the pike with his hands.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The notes define “waters’ flame” as a kenning for gold, explained as related to the sea-god Ægir lighting his hall with gold.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes state that Andvari’s ring had the power to create new gold, and explicitly compare this property to Baldr’s ring Draupnir.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The notes state that in the Völsunga saga Andvari lays a curse particularly on the ring, and identify “brothers twain” as Fafnir and Regin; they also discuss a set of “heroes” presumed to be slain in the story.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The notes gloss “Andvaranaut” as “Andvari’s Gem.”","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The notes state that “Gram” is a sword which, according to the Völsunga saga, Regin forged from fragments of the sword given by Óðinn to Sigmund; they also note Gnitaheith and the “fear-helm” term appearing here and in Fáfnismál.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The notes state that the fleet and subsequent storm are reminiscent of the Helgi cycle, and gloss ship-kennings such as “sail-horses/sea-steeds,” “sea-trees,” and “roller-steeds” as meaning ships.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The notes discuss Hreithmar’s daughters and report a suggestion that Hreithmar urges his daughter to bear a daughter who will have a son to avenge a great-grandfather.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:

/ THE BALLAD OF REGIN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 14494-14533","start":"14494","end":"14533","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes discuss: Othin’s use of multiple names and an episode (from the Volsungasaga) where his name is unknown when he visits Volsung’s house and leaves a sword for Sigmund; observations that some stanzas resemble or derive from Hovamol materials; explanatory notes on a stanza mentioning the sun as the moon’s sister and a wedge-like battle formation attributed to Othin; a note on numerous minor goddesses classed among lesser Norns; prose background on Lyngvi and related saga inconsistencies; and a description of Lyngvi’s death by the ‘bloody eagle’ method, advised by Regin and carried out with a sword.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that Othin gives himself the names Hnikar and Fjolnir, and that Feng does not appear elsewhere.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"According to the Volsungasaga, no one knew Othin’s name when he came to Volsung’s house and left a sword there for Sigmund.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes claim that certain stanzas are strongly suggestive of Hovamol and likely came from a similar collection; another stanza may have been taken from a longer version of Hovamol.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes identify “Moon’s sister” as the sun and link this phrasing to Vafthruthnismol.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes report that a wedge-like battle formation was said to have been invented by Othin and taught only to the most favored warriors.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes state that Norse mythology included many minor deities and that female minor deities were generally classed among the lesser Norns.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The prose note identifies Lyngvi as the son of Hunding who killed Sigmund out of jealousy over Sigmund’s marriage to Hjordis; it also mentions a brother Hjorvarth with Lyngvi and says Sigurth kills Hjorvarth, noting saga inconsistencies about repeated deaths.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes describe the ‘bloody eagle’ execution: Regin advises carving it on captured Lyngvi’s back; Regin uses a sword to cleave Lyngvi’s back, severing back from ribs, and draws out the lungs; Lyngvi dies with courage.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The notes state that in the Regius manuscript there is no break between a prose passage and the prose introduction to Fafnismol.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"A god associated here with multiple names; visits Volsung’s house with his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l14536-l14693","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / FAFNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF FAFNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 14536-14693","start":"14536","end":"14693","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An editor’s introductory note describes the manuscript and intertextual context of the poem Fáfnismál. A dialogue begins in which Fafnir questions Sigurth’s parentage and identity; Sigurth initially hides his name because a dying man’s curse is believed powerful, then reveals it. Fafnir warns that gold and rings will be Sigurth’s bane.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states that Fafnismol is in the Codex Regius and is quoted by Snorri in Gylfaginning and Skaldskaparmal; Fafnir writhes and strikes out with head and tail, and then they look at each other.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A prose note states that Sigurth initially conceals his name because it was believed a dying man’s spoken curse could have great power if it used the foe’s name.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the dialogue, Fafnir asks the youth who he is and whose son he is, referring to Sigurth reddening his blade in Fafnir’s blood and striking to the heart.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Sigurth answers first with an alias (“The Noble Hart”), claiming to be motherless and to have had no father, and to live lonely.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Fafnir challenges Sigurth’s claim to have had no father and calls the statement a lie.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sigurth then reveals his name as Sigurth, son of Sigmund, and says he struck Fafnir with the sword.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Fafnir predicts that the sounding gold, glow-red wealth, and rings will be Sigurth’s bane.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"A warrior who travels with Regin to Gnitaheith, hides in a trench, and kills Fafnir by thrusting a sword into his heart; After the slaying, Regin cuts out Fafnir’s heart and drinks blood, then asks Sigurth to cook the heart on a fire. Sigurth burns his finger testing it, tastes the heart-blood, and gains the ability to understand birds, which then warn him that Regin intends betrayal and suggest killing him to take the hoard.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Fafnir states that someone will always hold the hoard until a destined day, and that there is a time when every man will journey to hell.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Sigurth asks who the Norns are that help in need and bring the babe from the mother; Fafnir answers that the Norns are of many births and have differing kinships (to gods, to elves, and some as Dvalin’s daughters).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sigurth asks the name of an isle where all the gods and Surt will mingle in sword-fighting; Fafnir names it Oskopnir and says Bilrost will break when they cross, and the steeds will swim in the flood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Fafnir says he wore a fear-helm to frighten mankind while guarding his gold, and that he breathed venom while lying by the hoard his father had.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Fafnir counsels Sigurth to ride home, warning that sounding gold, glow-red wealth, and rings will be Sigurth’s bane; he also says Regin betrayed him and will betray Sigurth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After the fight, Regin returns, hails Sigurth for victory, calls Fafnir his brother, and disputes with Sigurth about Regin’s role versus Sigurth’s courage and effort in the slaying.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Regin cuts out Fafnir’s heart with a sword named Rithil and drinks blood from the wounds; he then asks Sigurth to sit while he holds the heart to the fire for cooking.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sigurth cooks Fafnir’s heart on a spit; when he tests it with his finger, he burns it, puts the finger in his mouth, and when the heart-blood touches his tongue he understands the speech of birds.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Nut-hatches speak in the thickets: one comments on Sigurth cooking the heart; fire is described as playing about her; Ygg has smitten her with a thorn because she felled a fighter whom Ygg wished to save.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The maiden is described as helmed and as having ridden forth on Vingskornir from the fight; her sleep will not break because the Norns have set it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Sigurth rides along Fafnir’s trail to his lair and finds it open; the gate-posts, gates, and all the beams are iron; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15126-l15171","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FAFNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF FAFNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 15126-15171","start":"15126","end":"15171","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An editorial note discusses a textual problem about whether one or two birds speak in certain stanzas and how the speeches align with two different story versions (one pointing Sigurth to Guthrun and Gunnar’s hall; the other pointing him to Brynhild on Hindarfjoll). It cites the Volsungasaga’s condensed version (one bird advising Sigurth to ride up to Hindarfjoll where Brynhild sleeps to gain wisdom). Additional notes identify figures and kennings (Hindarfjoll; ‘light of the flood’ = gold; ‘bane of the wood’ = fire), define Brynhild as a Valkyrie, gloss Ygg as Othin, identify the ‘thorn’ as a sleep-thorn, and explain that ‘sigrdrifa’ is an epithet misread as a proper name, which influenced later editorial tradition. A brief prose note remarks on manuscript continuity and lists names (Hrotti; Thruster).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The note argues that the relevant stanzas can be read as involving either one bird or two birds speaking, and that they reflect two distinct story versions.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"One set of stanzas is said to apply to Guthrun and suggests Sigurth will go straight to Gunnar’s hall; another set is said to apply to Brynhild and indicates Sigurth will find her before visiting the Gjukungs.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note states that in the Volsungasaga the passage is condensed so that one bird advises Sigurth to ride up on Hindarfjoll, where Brynhild sleeps, and there gain much wisdom; the Guthrun-bird does not appear there.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Gjuki is identified as the father of Gunnar and Guthrun.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Hindarfjoll is glossed as “Mountain of the Hind,” and “Light of the flood” is glossed as gold.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Brynhild is described as a “battle-maid” and is explicitly defined here as a Valkyrie; “bane of the wood” is glossed as fire; “Ygg” is glossed as Othin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The “thorn” is identified (by reference to a prose note in Sigrdrifumol) as a sleep-thorn; the note says the story of the reason for Brynhild’s punishment is told elsewhere (in prose following stanza 4 of Sigrdrifumol).","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Vingskornir is identified as Brynhild’s horse, noted as not elsewhere mentioned.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The note explains that the word translated “victory-bringer” (sigrdrifa) was assumed by the compiler to be a proper name and later editors followed this, though it is described as an epithet for Brynhild.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A prose note states there is no break in the manuscript between adjacent prose passages in the compilation and lists the names “Hrotti; Thruster.”","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"A figure whose movements are discussed; in the cited saga summary he is advised by a bird to ride up to Hindarfjoll to where Brynhild sleeps and gain wisdom.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"A figure to whom one set of stanzas is said to apply; daughter of Gjuki.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"Associated with ‘Gunnar’s hall’; identified as son of Gjuki.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Brynhild","description":"A ‘battle-maid’ explicitly defined as a Valkyrie;     "summary": "Sigurth rides up the mountain Hindarfjoll, sees a great fire-like light reaching heaven, and enters a tower of shields where an armored sleeper lies. She recounts how she killed Hjalmgunnar in battle against Othin’s promise and was punished by Othin with a sleep-thorn and a decree of marriage, which she counters with a vow never to marry a fearful man. Sigurth asks for wisdom; Sigrdrifa teaches various runes (winning-, ale-, birth-, wave-, branch-, speech-, thought-runes) and describes their divine origin and wide distribution among gods, elves, Vanir, and humans. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15442-l15532","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / SIGRDRIFUMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE VICTORY-BRINGER / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 15442-15532","start":"15442","end":"15532","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A speaker addresses an unnamed “thou” and delivers a sequence of admonitions (“I rede thee”) about honorable and prudent conduct: avoid wrongdoing toward kin, do not swear uncertain oaths, avoid verbal quarrels (especially at the Thing) and drunken brawls, beware witches and sexual entanglements, choose fighting over being burned alive, shun lying and lust, perform burial and washing rites for corpses, distrust the “race of wolves,” and avoid wrath and treachery among friends.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker declares they will not flee even if fate is near and will strive to win the addressee’s loving word in return as long as they live.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker gives the first counsel: the addressee should be free of guilt toward kinsmen and not take vengeance even if harmed, promising reward after death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The second counsel is not to swear an oath if one does not know it to be true; oath-breaking is said to bring bitter fate.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The third counsel is not to fight in words with fools at the Thing; an unwise man often utters worse words than he thinks.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker notes that being silent can be judged cowardice and that fame is seldom safe unless wide renown is won; a liar is to be sent to death to pay the price of lies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The fourth counsel is to avoid being the guest of a wily witch encountered on the road, even if night comes quickly.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker says evil witches often sit by the way and blunt blade and courage of fighting men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The fifth counsel warns that seeing fair maidens sitting on benches, one should not lose sleep through kinship ties and should beware kissing women.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The sixth counsel is to avoid words with a drunken warrior when men wrangle and ale-talk rises to wrath; wine is said to steal many men’s wits.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker states brawls and ale often bring ill: death for some and sorrow for some.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The seventh counsel says that if battle is sought with a mighty foe, it is better to fight than to burn alive in the hall of a rich hero.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The eighth counsel is to shun evil and beware lying words; the addressee is told not to take a maid or another man’s wife nor lure them to lust.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The ninth counsel is to render burial if a fallen corpse is found, whether dead of sickness, in the sea, or by weapon-wounds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The tenth counsel prescribes bathing and washing corpses (hands and head), wiping and combing them before placing them in a coffin, and praying they sleep in peace.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The eleventh counsel is never to trust the word of the “race of wolves,” especially if one has killed their brother or father; a “wolf in a son” may exist even if he takes gold.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The speaker remarks that battle, hate, and harm seldom fall asleep; a warrior needs wits and weapons to be boldest.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The speaker counsels shunning wrath and false treachery with friends; leaders’ lives will not be long because foes are great.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Speaker (“I”)","description":"A first-person speaker who declares steadfastness and delivers a numbered series of counsels (“I rede thee”).","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Addressee (“thou”)","description":"An unnamed second-person addressee instructed on conduct regarding kin, oaths, speech, travel, women, drinking, battle, burial rites, and trust.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Kinsmen","description":"Kinsmen toward whom one should be free of guilt and from whom one may suffer harm without taking vengeance.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Wily witch / evil witches by the way","description":"Witches encountered on the road, described as evil and able to blunt blade and courage.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Maidens / women (including another man’s wife)","description":"Women described as fair maidens sitting on benches; the addressee is warned about kissing and lust and told not to take a maid or another man’s wife.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Drunken warrior","description":"A drunken warrior with whom one should not exchange words during wrangling and ale-talk.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Mighty foe","description":"A foe “full of might” with whom one may seek battle.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Rich hero (hall-owner)","description":"A “hero rich” whose hall is mentioned as a place where one might be burned alive.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Fallen corpse / the dead","description":"A corpse found dead of sickness, in the sea, or by weapon-wounds, to be buried, washed, combed, and placed in a coffin with prayers for peace.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"“Race of wolves” / wolf-kin (including a son)","description":"People characterized as the “race of wolves,” whose word should not be trusted; a “wolf” may be in a son even if he takes gold.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Friends / leaders","description":"Friends among whom wrath and treachery should be avoided; leaders face great foes and are said not to live long.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Advisor / giver of counsels","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The speaker repeatedly states “Then [nth] I rede thee,” giving numbered admonitions.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Recipient of counsel","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"The addressee is repeatedly addressed as “thou” and instructed what to do or avoid.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Dangerous roadside supernatural adversary","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"A “wily witch” is to be avoided; “witches evil” are said to blunt blade and courage.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"Recipient of funerary care","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"The addressee is told to render burial and wash, comb, and coffin the corpse, praying for peace.","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"Untrustworthy antagonist (wolf-like kin)","assigned_to":["fig:10"],"basis":"The addressee is warned never to trust the “race of wolves,” especially under blood-feud conditions.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"Potentially harmed party (kinship relationship)","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Counsel concerns guilt toward kinsmen and refraining from vengeance even if they do harm.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"Potential object of sexual temptation","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"Warnings about kissing women and prohibitions against taking a maid or another man’s wife or luring them to lust.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"Impaired instigator of conflict","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"The drunken warrior is linked to wrangling and ale-talk rising to wrath; wine steals wits.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"Battle opponent","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"A “foe that is full of might” is the object of sought battle.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:10","label":"Hall-owner associated with lethal burning","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"Mention of being burned alive “in the hall of the hero rich.”","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:11","label":"Social allies and political leaders at risk","assigned_to":["fig:11"],"basis":"Counsel forbids treachery with friends and comments on leaders’ short lives due to great foes.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Oath / troth","literal_form":"Swearing an oath; troth; oath-breaking","associated_figures":["fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"Thing (assembly)","literal_form":"The Thing (public assembly)","associated_figures":["fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"Ale-talk / wine (intoxicants)","literal_form":"Ale; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15840-l15965","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / BROT AF SIGURTHARKVITHU / FRAGMENT OF A SIGURTH LAY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 15840-15965","start":"15840","end":"15965","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Hogni and Gunnar speak about killing Sigurth: Gunnar accuses Sigurth of broken oaths, while Hogni attributes Gunnar’s hostility to Brynhild’s incitement and jealousy. Gotthorm is fed cooked wolf and cut snake before the men set their hands to murder. Sigurth is slain; a raven foretells blood on Atli’s blade and binding oaths. Guthrun asks where Sigurth is; Hogni admits Sigurth was slain with swords, and Sigurth’s gray horse mourns. Brynhild speaks and laughs, asserting Sigurth would have ruled if he had lived, and she foretells wider death for the oath-breaking Niflung race. After drinking, Gunnar lies awake thinking about what the raven and eagle told him from a tree. Brynhild recounts a grim dream of corpses and Gunnar bound, and recalls an earlier scene where Sigurth placed a gold-wound sword between them; the blade is described as forged in fire and damp with venom. A prose note states variant traditions about whether Sigurth was killed outdoors, in a forest, at a council-place, or in bed, but agrees he was deceived and attacked while lying down and unprepared.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Gunnar says Sigurth swore oaths to him and broke them, betraying him where he most should have kept them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Hogni says Brynhild has whetted Gunnar’s heart to hate and grudges Guthrun’s honor and Gunnar’s continued joy.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"They cook a wolf and cut up a snake, and give Gotthorm the flesh before the men lay hands on the hero to murder him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sigurth is slain; a raven calls from a limb that their blood will redden Atli’s blade and their oaths will bind them in chains.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Guthrun asks where Sigurth is; Hogni answers that they have slain Sigurth with swords, and the gray horse mourns by its dead master.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Brynhild laughs once so that the building echoed and says they will joy in lands and men now that they have slain the noble hero.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After evening drinking and talk, all sleep but Gunnar lies awake, tossing and thinking about what the raven and eagle told him from a tree as they rode home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Brynhild tells Gunnar a grim dream: corpses in the hall, her bed cold, and Gunnar riding joylessly bound in fetters among foemen; she says the Niflung race shall die and their oaths are broken.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Brynhild recalls that Sigurth let a gold-wound sword lie between them; the blade’s edge was forged with fire and damp with drops of venom.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A prose note reports differing accounts of where Sigurth was killed (out of doors, in a house/bed, in a forest, or at a council-place) but says all agree he was deceived in trust and attacked while lying down and unprepared.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"A hero/noble king who is accused of broken oaths and is slain by swords; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l16057-l16186","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / GUTHRUNARKVITHA I / THE FIRST LAY OF GUTHRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 16057-16186","start":"16057","end":"16186","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note frames \"Guthrunarkvitha I\" as a self-contained poem of intense lament, situating it within the Sigurth cycle and noting parallels/attestations in other Germanic sources. The prose preface states Guthrun sits by Sigurth’s corpse, unable to weep; a tradition says she ate Fafnir’s heart and therefore understands birds’ speech. In the opening stanzas, warriors and then women attempt to console Guthrun by recounting their own losses. Herborg, queen of the Huns, tells of the deaths of her husband and sons, a ship disaster that killed her kin, and her subsequent war-captivity and abuse while forced to serve a monarch’s wife. Finally, Gollrond orders Sigurth’s corpse uncovered and placed so Guthrun must look upon his bloodied head, blinded eyes, and pierced breast.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note describes the poem as a clear unit, emotionally intense, not quoted elsewhere, and possibly unknown to the Volsungasaga compilers; it mentions figures appearing in this poem (including a sister and daughter of Gjuki and Herborg, queen of the Huns).","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The note states Guthrun’s lament is among the oldest parts of the story, with traces in the seventeenth Aventiure of the Nibelungenlied, and identifies Guthrun with Kriemhild in parentheses.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the prose preface, Guthrun sits by the dead Sigurth; she does not weep though her heart is near to bursting, and people come to console her but find it difficult.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The prose preface says it is told that Guthrun ate of Fafnir’s heart and that she understood the speech of birds.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Guthrun thinks to die while sitting in sorrow by Sigurth; she has no tears, does not wring her hands, and does not wail like other women.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Wise warriors come to Guthrun to lighten her heavy woe, but she cannot weep and her heart seems as if it will break.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Wives of warriors, gold-adorned, come and each speaks of the bitterest pain she has borne as an attempt to comfort Guthrun.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Gjaflaug, identified as Gjuki’s sister, says husbands, daughters, sisters, and brothers have been taken from her, yet she has lived.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Herborg, queen of the Huns, says her seven sons and her husband fell in fight; she also recounts that her father, mother, and four brothers died amid waves when wind smote and seas crashed through a ship’s sides.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Herborg says she prepared the bodies for the grave and buried the dead with her own hands; no one came to comfort her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Herborg says she was bound and taken in war and then forced to deck and bind the shoes of a monarch’s wife every morning; the monarch’s wife beat her often.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Gollrond, identified as Gjuki’s daughter, says the foster-mother’s wisdom does not find the way to comfort the young wife, and she orders the warriors’ corpse uncovered.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The shroud is lifted from Sigurth; his head is laid on Guthrun’s knees and she is urged to look on him and lay her lips to his as if he lived.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Guthrun looks once and sees Sigurth’s hair clotted with blood, his blinded eyes, and his breast pierced by a blade.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Guthrun (Kriemhild)","description":"A wife mourning by the dead Sigurth; she cannot weep and is the central figure of the poem; a tradition says she ate Fafnir’s heart and understands birds’ speech.","role_refs":["role:1","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"Guthrun’s husband; he is dead, lies as a corpse under a shroud, bloodied, with eyes blinded and breast pierced by a blade.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Warriors (men)","description":"Wise warriors come to Guthrun attempting to lighten her heavy woe; later they are told to uncover the warrior’s corpse.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Wives of the warriors (women)","description":"Gold-adorned women come to Guthrun and each speaks of her own grief.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Gjaflaug","description":"Gjuki’s sister; she recounts multiple family losses (husbands, daughters, sisters, brothers) yet says she has lived.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Gjuki","description":"Named as the brother of Gjaflaug and father of Gollrond (via identifications in the stanzas).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Herborg","description":"Queen of the Huns; recounts deaths of husband and sons, a ship disaster killing her kin, burial of the dead, then war-captivity and abuse while serving a monarch’s wife.","role_refs":["role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Herborg’s husband","description":"Said by Herborg to have fallen in fight.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Herborg’s seven sons","description":"Said by Herborg to have fallen in fight in the southern land.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Herborg’s father, mother, and four brothers","description":"Said by Herborg to have died amid waves when wind smote and seas crashed through a ship.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Monarch’s wife (unnamed)","description":"The woman Herborg is forced to serve; she orders the corpse uncovered and orchestrates presenting Sigurth’s head to Guthrun.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Fafnir","description":"Named in the prose preface as the being whose heart Guthrun is said to have eaten.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Birds","description":"Their speech is said to be understood by Guthrun after eating Fafnir’s heart.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Brynhild","description":"Mentioned in the introductory note as Guthrun’s enemy and the cause of Sigurth’s death (within the narrative context discussion).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"mourning wife / lamenter","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Guthrun sits sorrowing by Sigurth’s corpse and cannot weep; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l16266-l16376","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GUTHRUNARKVITHA I / THE FIRST LAY OF GUTHRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 16266-16376","start":"16266","end":"16376","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes discuss variants and interpretations around Guthrunarkvitha I and related poems/saga material: Guthrun allegedly eats Fafnir’s heart and gains grimness/wisdom (and possibly bird-speech); obscure relatives (Gjaflaug, Herborg, Gollrond); identification of Herjan as Othin and his maids as Valkyries; and story-variants in which Sigurth’s murder is motivated partly by desire for cursed gold (Andvari/Loki), with parallels noted in German tradition (including the Nibelungenlied). The notes also explain a kenning for gold as the ‘flame of the snake’s bed,’ reflecting serpents/dragons as treasure-guardians, and summarize a variant involving Atli, Brynhild, Gunnar, and deception about identity.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that in the Volsungasaga Sigurth gave Guthrun some of Fafnir’s heart to eat, after which she became grimmer and wiser, and they remark that it is not elsewhere stated that Guthrun understood the speech of birds.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes identify Herjan as Othin and say his maids are the Valkyries.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes say that desire for Sigurth’s treasure (gold cursed by Andvari and Loki) was one motive for Sigurth’s murder, and that this motive appears in the Nibelungenlied as part of the German tradition.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes gloss the phrase “Flame of the snakes bed” as meaning gold, explaining that serpents and dragons were traditional guardians of treasure on which they lay.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes describe a story-variant in which Atli induced Brynhild to marry Gunnar by falsely telling her that Gunnar was Sigurth, and they connect Atli’s action (in the present stanza) to desire for Sigurth’s treasure.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes state that Gjaflaug, Herborg, and Gollrond are not otherwise known/mentioned (or are of unclear status), and discuss possible interpolations or manuscript issues in multiple stanzas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"A figure discussed in notes; said (in Volsungasaga) to have eaten some of Fafnir’s heart and become grimmer and wiser; possibly associated with understanding birds’ speech (not otherwise attested).","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"A figure discussed in notes; said (in Volsungasaga) to have given Guthrun some of Fafnir’s heart; his murder is discussed as motivated partly by desire for his treasure.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Fafnir","description":"Associated with “Fafnir’s heart” and with treasure-guardian traditions involving serpents/dragons.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Othin (Herjan)","description":"Identified as Herjan; said to have maids who are Valkyries.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Valkyries","description":"Called Othin’s maids in the notes.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Andvari","description":"Named in connection with gold described as cursed by Andvari and Loki.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Loki","description":"Named in connection with gold described as cursed by Andvari and
