content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l16509-l16665","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / SIGURTHARKVITHA EN SKAMMA / THE SHORT LAY OF SIGURTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 16509-16665","start":"16509","end":"16665","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Speakers debate devotion to Brynhild versus the appeal of wealth (including the gold of the Rhine) and affirm that it is not fitting to break sworn oaths. Gunnar proposes rousing their younger brother Gotthorm—who did not share in the oaths—to attack Sigurth; Sigurth is stabbed, then rises and hurls his sword, killing Gotthorm. Guthrun wakes beside Sigurth in blood and is told not to weep; Sigurth speaks of their son and blames Brynhild for the harm. Brynhild reacts strongly (swoons, then laughs once at Guthrun’s wailing) and argues about responsibility, her prior independence, her troth to Sigurth, pressures associated with Atli, and her longing for Sigurth’s rings/hoard; she anticipates further vengeance. Gunnar and others try to restrain Brynhild, and Gunnar calls on Hogni for counsel.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker declares Brynhild (daughter/child of Buthli) the best of women and says he would rather lose his life than yield her love.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A question is raised about betraying a hero for wealth, mentioning the gold of the Rhine and holding the hoard in peace to win fortune.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Hogni says it does not befit them to cleave with swords the oaths and vows they swore.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"It is stated that while “we four” hold sway and while a “Hunnish hero” lives, they know no mightier men or higher kinship on earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A speaker anticipates that if five sons are soon begotten their race will grow, but notes Brynhild’s hate is very bitter.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Gunnar says they must rouse Gotthorm, their younger brother, because he did not enter into the oaths and vows they swore.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Gotthorm is easily roused, and the sword comes to stand in Sigurth’s heart.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In vengeance, Sigurth rises in the hall and hurls his sword at the slayer; the glittering steel of Gram flies from the king’s hand at Gotthorm.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Gotthorm falls cleft asunder, with hands and head sinking forward and legs and feet falling backward.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Guthrun wakes from sleep beside Sigurth and finds her joy fled; she lies in blood beside the “friend of Freyr.”","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Guthrun smites her hands together; Sigurth rises up and tells her not to weep, saying her brothers live.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sigurth says their son is too young to flee from the home of his foes and speaks of a fearful, deadly plan and new counsel that has been heeded.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Sigurth says no son, even if she has seven, will ride to the Thing like the son of their sister, and he says the blame lies on Brynhild alone.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Sigurth says Brynhild loved him above all men, but he was never false to Gunnar; he kept the oaths and kinship he swore, and none may call him the lover of Gunnar’s queen.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Brynhild sinks in a swoon when Sigurth dies; she smites her hands so hard that cups ring in the cupboard and geese cry in the courtyard.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Brynhild laughs once with all her heart when she hears the grievous wail of Gjuki’s daughter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Gunnar rebukes Brynhild, calling her a lover of hate and “mother of ill,” and says she is foredoomed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Gunnar says Brynhild would have been worthier if before her eyes they had slain Atli and if she had seen her brothers’ bleeding bodies and wounds to bind.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Brynhild tells Gunnar that his hatred little heeds Atli; she thinks Atli will live longer and remain greater in might.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Brynhild says Gunnar shaped these ills early; she previously knew no bonds or sorrow and had wealth in her brothers’ home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Brynhild says she sought no husband before the Gjukungs came to their land; three kings came on steeds and had no need of their journey.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Brynhild says she gave her troth to a great hero who sat gold-decked on Grani’s back; she contrasts his eyes and appearance with Gunnar’s though both seemed kingly.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Brynhild says Atli told her she should not share their wealth of gold or lands unless she gave her hand; she mentions gold he gave her in childhood and wealth in youth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Brynhild says she pondered fighting in her byrnie, letting warriors fall and defying her brother, which would become widely known and bring sorrow to many.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Brynhild says she let the bond be made because she longed for the hoard and for the rings that Sigmund’s son won; she says she sought no other treasure.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Brynhild says she loved only one and never changed heart; she says Atli will know in the end when he hears she has gone on the death-road.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"A statement follows that a wife of fickle will should not yield to another man and that vengeance for Brynhild’s ills shall come.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"Gunnar rises and flings his arms around Brynhild’s neck; many seek to hold her, but she casts them back and will not let them hold her from the long road.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"Gunnar calls Hogni in counsel, saying their need of wisdom is full great.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Brynhild (daughter/child of Buthli)","description":"A woman whose love is desired; she reacts to Sigurth’s death (swoon, laughter) and speaks at length about her past, wealth, troth, and vengeance.","role_refs":["role:4","role:9","role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"A hero killed by a sword wound; he rises in vengeance and hurls the sword Gram to kill his slayer, then speaks to Guthrun about their son, the plot, and blame.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"A monarch/king who proposes rousing Gotthorm, rebukes Brynhild, and tries to restrain her; he calls Hogni for counsel.","role_refs":["role:2","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Hogni","description":"A man of few words who says it is not fitting to break oaths; later is called to counsel for wisdom.","role_refs":["role:3","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Gotthorm","description":"The younger brother who did not enter the oaths; he is roused to wrath and is the slayer struck down by Sigurth’s sword.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Guthrun (Gjuki’s daughter)","description":"Sleeps beside Sigurth, wakes in blood, smites her hands, and wails; addressed by Sigurth.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"A named figure discussed as powerful; said to have demanded Brynhild’s hand for wealth-sharing, and is addressed in Gunnar and Brynhild’s speeches.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Buthli","description":"Named as Brynhild’s father/parent (Buthli’s child/daughter).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Gjuki","description":"Named as Guthrun’s father (Gjuk(i)’s daughter).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Sigmund","description":"Named as Sigurth’s father via the phrase “the son of Sigmund.”","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Freyr","description":"A divine figure referenced in the kenning “friend of Freyr” for Sigurth.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Grani","description":"A horse on whose back the great hero sat, described as “gold-decked.”","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Hunnish hero (unnamed)","description":"An unnamed “Hunnish hero” whose continued life is referenced in a statement about might and kinship.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"target of treacherous killing","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"Sigurth is stabbed (a sword stands in his heart).","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"instigator of rousing a killer","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Gunnar proposes rousing Gotthorm to wrath to act outside the shared oaths.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"oath-defender / opponent of oath-breaking","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Hogni states it does

{"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l16921-l17039","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SIGURTHARKVITHA EN SKAMMA / THE SHORT LAY OF SIGURTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 16921-17039","start":"16921","end":"17039","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes discuss variant readings and narrative variants in the Sigurth/Brynhild cycle: Sigurth’s killing (in bed in this account, as in the Volsungasaga), the sword Gram, traditions about Freyr as ancestor, kinship references (Sigmund), competing versions of Sigurth and Brynhild’s relationship (including an alternative with a daughter, Aslaug), a version where Gunnar and Sigurth besiege Atli and are bought off by giving Brynhild to Gunnar under deception, Brynhild as valkyrie, a ‘bond’ based on mistaken identity, omissions implying Brynhild’s resolve to die, and a note that “born again” may reflect Christian influence regarding suicide and rebirth.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that in the Volsungasaga (and as implied here) Sigurth is killed in his bed rather than in the forest.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes identify “Gram” as Sigurth’s sword, while also noting the word may not be a proper name and could mean “the hero.”","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes state that “friend of Freyr” likely means “king,” and mention a late tradition that Freyr (not Othin) was ancestor of the Volsungs.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes gloss “My son” as Sigmund.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes summarize that Sigurth says that even if Guthrun later has seven sons, none will equal Sigmund, son of Gunnar’s and Hogni’s sister.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes state Sigurth’s claim of guiltlessness fits the poem’s version of his relations with Brynhild, but not an alternative version where he meets Brynhild earlier and they have a daughter, Aslaug.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The notes describe the poet’s accepted version: Gunnar and Sigurth besiege Atli and are bought off by giving Atli’s sister Brynhild to Gunnar as wife, with her consent won by a deception that Gunnar is Sigurth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes explain that in this version Atli points out Sigurth as Gunnar; Brynhild falls in love with the hero, recognizing him as the dragon-slayer riding Grani and adorned with spoils from Fafnir; an oath to marry Gunnar must still be carried out after the deception is discovered.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The notes state that Brynhild here appears again as a Valkyrie.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The notes describe “the bond” as Brynhild thinking she was marrying Sigurth (owner of the treasure) but being tricked into marrying Gunnar.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The notes infer omissions: Sigurth attempts to repair the wrong by giving up Guthrun in Brynhild’s favor; Brynhild refuses, and a gap likely contained Brynhild’s determination to die.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The notes suggest the phrase “Born again” may show Christian influence, implying that if Brynhild killed herself she could not be born again.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"Hero associated with the sword Gram; identified as the dragon-slayer who rode content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l17349-l17443","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / DRAP NIFLUNGA / THE SLAYING OF THE NIFLUNGS / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 17349-17443","start":"17349","end":"17443","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note explains that the Eddic compiler used short prose links to create a continuous Sigurth-cycle narrative. The prose bridge “Drap Niflunga” summarizes events after Sigurth and Brynhild are dead: Atli (Guthrun’s second husband) invites Gunnar and Hogni; Guthrun foresees treachery and warns them via runes and a ring token; nevertheless they come, and Atli’s side kills them—Hogni’s heart is cut out and Gunnar is thrown into a serpent-den, lulls the serpents by harp-playing, but is finally killed by an adder’s sting. The note section discusses variant sources, including that some details are the annotator’s attempted harmonizations and that one tradition has Atli’s mother take the form of the adder.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states that the Eddic compiler aimed to create a coherent Sigurth-cycle narrative by piecing poems together with prose links, largely using material drawn from the poems.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The note describes “Drap Niflunga” as a short prose narrative link following Helreith Brynhildar, used as a transitional bridge in the collection.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"With Sigurth and Brynhild dead, the narrative focus turns to Atli’s slaying of the sons of Gjuki and to later incidents involving Svanhild and Hamther.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage says “Drap Niflunga” summarizes material belonging to the Burgundian tradition and notes that it is in many respects parallel to the Nibelungenlied.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Gunnar and Hogni take all the gold that Fafnir had had, and there is strife between Atli and the Gjukungs, with Atli holding them guilty of Brynhild’s death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"It is agreed that Guthrun will be given to Atli as wife, and she is given a draught of forgetfulness to drink before she consents to the marriage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Atli invites Gunnar and Hogni to come to him and sends a messenger named Vingi or Knefrth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Guthrun is aware of treachery and sends a warning message in runes; as a token she sends Hogni the ring Andvaranaut with a wolf’s hair tied in it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Gunnar had sought Oddrun (Atli’s sister) for his wife but did not have her; he marries Glaumvor. Hogni’s wife is Kostbera; their sons are named Solar and Snvar and Gjuki.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When the Gjukungs arrive, Guthrun asks her sons to plead for the lives of Gunnar and Hogni, but they refuse.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Hogni’s heart is cut out; Gunnar is cast into a serpent-den, plays the harp and puts the serpents to sleep, but an adder stings him in the liver.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The note section discusses variant accounts: the annotator is said to be combining different poem traditions about the runic warning and the ring token, and it states that in one source the adder is Atli’s mother in that form.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Eddic compiler / annotator (as described in the note)","description":"Described as having undertaken to piece together a coherent narrative by using prose links and (in the notes) as attempting to combine variant accounts.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"Said to be dead (with Brynhild), and named as father of Svanhild.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Brynhild","description":"Said to be dead; Atli holds the Gjukungs guilty of her death.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Atli (King Atli)","description":"Guthrun’s second husband; invites Gunnar and Hogni; conflict with the Gjukungs; his side kills Gunnar and Hogni.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"Given to Atli as wife after drinking a draught of forgetfulness; sends a runic warning and ring token; asks her sons to intercede for Gunnar and Hogni.","role_refs":["role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Gunnar (son of Gjuki)","description":"Takes Fafnir’s gold; is invited to Atli; later cast into a serpent-den; plays harp to lull serpents; killed by an adder sting.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Hogni (son of Gjuki)","description":"Takes Fafnir’s gold; is invited to Atli; receives warning token ring; later has his heart cut out.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Fafnir","description":"Associated with the gold that Gunnar and Hogni take.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Vingi / Knefrth (messenger)","description":"Sent by Atli as messenger to invite Gunnar and Hogni; in the notes, variant traditions about the name(s) are discussed.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Oddrun (Atli’s sister)","description":"Said to have been sought by Gunnar for wife, but he did not obtain her.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Glaumvor","description":"Named as Gunnar’s wife (after he did not obtain Oddrun).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Kostbera (Hogni’s wife)","description":"Named as Hogni’s wife; in the notes she is described as skilled in runes and attempting to decipher obscured runes.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Erp and Eitil (sons of Atli)","description":"Named as Atli’s sons; the notes discuss their role in later revenge traditions.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Svanhild","description":"Named as daughter of Sigurth and Guthrun (and mentioned in connection with later incidents).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Hamther","description":"Named as son of Guthrun and her third husband Jonak (mentioned as part of later incidents).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Jonak","description":"Named as Guthrun’s third husband and father of Hamther.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Jormunrek (Ermanarich)","description":"Named as husband of Svanhild (in the note’s summary of subsequent incidents).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Atli’s mother (as adder, per the note)","description":"In the note, said (per Oddrunargratr) to have assumed the form of the adder that stings Gunnar.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:19","name_or_label":"Serpents (in the serpent-den)","description":"Serpents in the den are put to sleep by Gunnar’s harp-playing.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:20","name_or_label":"Adder (in the serpent-den)","description":"Stings Gunnar in the liver; in a note this adder is linked to Atli’s mother taking that form in one tradition.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:9"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Compiler/annotator creating prose narrative links","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The note describes a compiler piecing poems together with prose links and later notes discuss an annotator combining variant accounts.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Deceased figures whose deaths precede the summarized events","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:3"],"basis":"The passage states Sigurth and Brynhild are both dead before the story turns to Atli and the Gjukungs.","e

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l17446-l17573","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY NOTE / GUTHRUNARKVITHA II, EN FORNA / THE SECOND, OR OLD, LAY OF GUTHRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 17446-17573","start":"17446","end":"17573","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory note describes the poem’s age, transmission, and relation to German tradition. The lay then opens with Guthrun speaking with Thjothrek and recounting her marriage to Sigurth, his superiority, and how her brothers arranged his killing. Sigurth’s horse Grani returns riderless; Gunnar and Hogni confirm Sigurth’s death and indicate that ravens, eagles, and wolves are around his body. Guthrun searches in the woods for what remains, expresses deep grief and suicidal/despairing thoughts, then narrates traveling from a mountain for five days to Hoalf’s hall and staying with Thora in Denmark for seven half-years.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states that Guthrun’s lament tradition was widely known wherever the Sigurth story existed and likely early in verse form, and that multiple Norse poems (10th–11th centuries) centered on the lament.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The introductory note states the poem is preserved with omissions/interpolations, was available to the Volsungasaga compilers (who paraphrased it and quoted five stanzas), and has continuity from Sigurth’s death through later events (including Atli’s dreams).","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The introductory note claims the poem’s origin may trace to a lament reaching the North from Germany in verse form, and notes the absence of many characteristic Norse additions; it also states that Sigurth is slain in the forest 'as German men say' and that several plot elements belong directly to German tradition.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"King Thjothrek is said to be with Atli and to have lost most of his men; Thjothrek and Guthrun lament together, and Guthrun speaks.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Guthrun says her mother bore her; she loved her brothers; Gjuki 'dowered' her with gold and gave her to Sigurth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Guthrun compares Sigurth’s eminence over Gjukis sons to a leek over grass, a stag over beasts, and glow-red gold over silver-gray.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Guthrun states her brothers would not let her have Sigurth as husband and that they ultimately slew Sigurth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Grani runs from the Thing with thundering feet; Sigurth does not return; the saddle-bearer is covered with sweat.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Guthrun seeks to speak with Grani; the steed bows its head to the grass and is said to know its master is slain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Gunnar bows his head; Hogni tells the news of Sigurth slain, saying Sigurth lies hewed to death 'at our hands' and is given to wolves.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Hogni tells Guthrun she will see Sigurth on the southern road where ravens cry, eagles cry for food, and wolves howl about her husband.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Guthrun replies to Hogni with a curse-like statement that ravens will rend Hogni’s heart in an unknown land; Hogni responds that her grief would be greater if ravens should rend his heart.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Guthrun turns away from the speaker and goes into the woods to find what wolves left; she says she did not weep, wring her hands, or wail as other women do when she sat by Sigurth slain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Guthrun says the night never seemed so black as when she sat in sorrow by Sigurth; the stanza text is partially missing/elliptical.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Guthrun says it seemed best if she could lose her life or be burned like birch-wood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Guthrun says she traveled from the mountain for five days until she saw Hoalf’s hall, and that she stayed seven half-years with Thora, Hokon’s daughter, in Denmark.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"A woman who speaks a lament recounting her marriage to Sigurth, his death at her brothers’ hands, and her subsequent grief and travels.","role_refs":["role:1","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:7","ev:13","ev:16"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Thjothrek (King Thjothrek)","description":"Said to be with Atli, having lost most of his men; laments his griefs together with Guthrun.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"Mentioned as being with King Thjothrek; the introductory note also references Atli’s dreams foretelling the death of sons (as part of the poem’s scope).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Guthrun’s mother","description":"Said to have borne Guthrun.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Guthrun’s brothers (including Gunnar and Hogni)","description":"Guthrun says her brothers slew Sigurth; contextualize a described ordeal by boiling water (with consecrated kettle) and a punishment of drowning a culprit in a bog, especially for women.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The annotator states that the note’s material is derived from the poem itself, except for identifying Herkja as Atli’s former concubine.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Herkja is identified with the historical Kreka and with Helche of the Nibelungenlied, where she appears as Etzel’s (Attila’s) first wife.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The manuscript omits the names of the speakers throughout.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The reference to a “holy stone” is described as uncertain and is suggested as possibly identical with an “ice-cold stone of Uth” mentioned in an oath in Helgakvitha Hundingsbana II.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Editorial uncertainty is noted regarding whether the manuscript’s “Thjothmar” should be changed to “Thjothmar’s son,” or whether Thjothmar is another name/error for Thjothrek; an editor (Finnur Jonsson) is said to retain Thjothmar and adjust Thjothrek elsewhere for consistency.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A note references the death of Thjothrek’s men and states the manuscript repeats “thirty” in defiance of metrical requirements.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"It is noted that stanza order differs in the manuscript (one stanza follows another) and that many editions transpose them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Saxi’s identity is said to be unclear; the stanza is said to point to a time when the ordeal by boiling water was regarded as a foreign institution and required a southern (Christian) king to consecrate the kettle used in the test.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The ordeal by boiling water is said to have followed closely the introduction of Christianity (around the year 1000).","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A punishment is described in which a culprit is cast into a bog to be drowned; this punishment is said to be particularly reserved for women and is mentioned in sagas.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Herkja","description":"Named figure identified by the annotator as Atli’s former concubine and linked to Kreka/Helche traditions.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"Named figure; Herkja is described as his former Helche is described as his first wife.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Thjothrek","description":"Named figure referenced in notes (including mention of his men).","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Thjothmar","description":"Named figure/reading in the manuscript; editorial discussion suggests possible {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l18383-l18502","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ODDRUNARGRATR / THE LAMENT OF ODDRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 18383-18502","start":"18383","end":"18502","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial introductory note and stanza notes for “Oddrunargratr” identifying characters and relationships, discussing textual issues, referencing other Eddic poems and related traditions, and summarizing elements such as Oddrun’s knowledge of birth-runes/charms, a love affair, obscure geography, variant story-versions around Brynhild’s marriage, and references to Sigurth’s treasure from Fafnir.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that nothing further is known of Heithrek, Borgny, or Vilmund beyond what is in the poem; an annotator has added the name of Borgny’s father.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Oddrun is described as sister of Atli and Brynhild, and as proficient in “birth-runes”; the notes cross-reference Sigrdrifumol for this.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes describe Oddrun’s love for Gunnar (Guthrun’s brother) and say Gunnar is the husband of Oddrun’s sister Brynhild; the notes cross-reference other poems for this story context.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes state that “Morningland” is obscure geographically, possibly identical with “Hunland,” and describe increasing confusion in the poem’s geography later.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes mention manuscript/editorial uncertainties about stanza divisions, missing lines, and unidentified speakers in multiple places.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes gloss “Charms” with a cross-reference to Sigrdrifumol.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The notes identify “Hogni’s slayer” as Vilmund and mention a tradition where Hogni’s heart is cut out (referenced to Drap Niflunga).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes mention Frigg as a goddess of healing and Freyja as the friend of lovers (with cross-references).","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The notes infer that Borgny was present at Atli’s court during Oddrun and Gunnar’s love affair and criticized Oddrun; a “draught” is mentioned in reference to a secret meeting of the lovers.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The notes identify Buthli as the father of Oddrun, Atli, and Brynhild.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The notes describe Brynhild as possibly referred to as a Valkyrie (“wish-maid”) and explain the {
  "record_id": "batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l18504-l18555",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "ODDRUNARGRATR / THE LAMENT OF ODDRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 18504-18555",
    "start": "18504",
    "end": "18555",
    "translation": "The Poetic Edda",
    "notes": "Notes discussing geography, manuscript variants, possible lost stanzas, and parallels in Volsungasaga and Nibelungenlied."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Editorial notes on Oddrunargratr discuss: a boundary forest called Murky Wood between Atli's realm and the Gjukungar; manuscript line-order issues and possible losses; Atli's likely treacherous invitation to the Gjukungs and the killing of Högni and Gunnar; an episode in which Gunnar uses a harp to put serpents to sleep (with related versions in the Volsungasaga and an analog in the Nibelungenlied); confused heroic-epic geography involving Hlesey and a sound; a variant in which 'Atli's mother' is connected with Gunnar's death by serpent; and a kenning-like explanation that 'serpents-bed' can mean gold, making 'serpents-bed goddess' a term for a woman (Borgny).",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "A forest called Murky Wood is described as dividing Atli's realm from that of the Gjukungs, with a cross-reference to Atlakvitha and other journey descriptions.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The notes report a manuscript issue where two lines stand in reversed order.",
      "category": "other",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Editors suspect missing lines or a missing stanza; the notes state that Gudrun has evidently already become Atli's wife at the relevant point.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "A possibly lost stanza is proposed to have told of Atli's treacherous invitation to the Gjukungs; a related tradition (Drap Niflunga) is cited for the slaying of Hogni and Gunnar.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "The notes describe an episode (in Volsungasaga) where Gudrun gives her brother a harp, and he uses it to put serpents to sleep.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "The harp-and-sleeping episode is stated to be related to a Nibelungenlied episode in which Volker plays Gunther's followers to sleep before a final battle.",
      "category": "other",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Geirmund is noted as otherwise unknown and described as likely an ally/retainer of Atli or possibly his brother; Hlesey is identified as possibly the Danish island Læsø, and the notes remark on inconsistent geography, including a sound separating Geirmund's home from Hlesey/Atli's dwelling.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7", "ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "A note discusses a version involving 'Atli's mother' and contrasts it with Volsungasaga, where Gunnar puts all but one serpent to sleep with harp-playing and is killed by a mighty adder biting to his heart; it is suggested 'Atli' may be a scribal error for a word meaning 'of serpents'.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "A term glossed as 'Serpents-bed goddess' is explained as meaning 'woman' (identified as Borgny), with 'goddess of gold' as a frequent term for woman and 'gold' often called 'the serpents' bed'.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "The notes mention an editorial choice about whether a line should be read as the poet's statement or as part of Oddrun's speech.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:11"]
    }
  ],
  "figures": [
    {
      "id": "fig:1",
      "name_or_label": "Atli",
      "description": "Ruler with a realm separated from the Gjukungs by Murky Wood; described in conjecture as sending a treacherous invitation; has a mother mentioned in a variant.",
      "role_refs": ["role:1", "role:2"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:4", "ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:2",
      "name_or_label": "Gjukungs (Gjukungr clan)",
      "description": "People/kin with a realm separated from Atli's by Murky Wood; associated with the visit leading to killings.",
      "role_refs": ["role:3"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:3",
      "name_or_label": "Gudrun",
      "description": "Stated to have already become Atli's wife; in Volsungasaga gives her brother a harp.",
      "role_refs": ["role:4", "role:5"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:4",
      "name_or_label": "Hogni",
      "description": "Named as one of those slain in related accounts of Atli's invitation.",
      "role_refs": ["role:6"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:5",
      "name_or_label": "Gunnar",
      "description": "Named as slain; in Volsungasaga plays a harp to put serpents to sleep; is ultimately killed by an adder biting to his heart.",
      "role_refs": ["role:6", "role:7"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4", "ev:5", "ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:6",
      "name_or_label": "Geirmund",
      "description": "Otherwise unknown; suggested to be an ally/retainer of Atli or possibly his brother.",
      "role_refs": ["role:8"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:7",
      "name_or_label": "Oddrun",
      "description": "Mentioned in connection with going to Geirmund's home; also mentioned regarding whether a line is part of her speech.",
      "role_refs": ["role:9"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7", "ev:11"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:8",
      "name_or_label": "Borgny",
      "description": "Identified as the woman meant by the phrase glossed 'serpents-bed goddess'.",
      "role_refs": ["role:10"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:9",
      "name_or_label": "Volker",
      "description": "In the Nibelungenlied parallel, plays to put Gunther's followers to sleep.",
      "role_refs": ["role:7"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:10",
      "name_or_label": "Gunther",
      "description": "In the Nibelungenlied parallel, his followers are played to sleep by Volker.",
      "role_refs": ["role:11"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:11",
      "name_or_label": "Serpents / adder",
      "description": "Serpents are put to sleep by harp-playing in Volsungasaga; a mighty evil adder bites Gunnar to death.",
      "role_refs": ["role:12"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5", "ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:12",
      "name_or_label": "Atli's mother",
      "description": "Mentioned in a note as part of a version; contrasted with the Volsungasaga account.",
      "role_refs": ["role:13"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    }
  ],
  "roles": [
    {
      "id": "role:1",
      "label": "ruler/host in the narrative tradition",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:1"],
      "basis": "Atli is treated as having a realm and dwelling, and as the one who may invite the Gjukungs.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:4", "ev:8"]
    },
    {

      "label": "treacherous inviter (conjectured)",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:1"],
      "basis": "Editors suggest a lost stanza may have told of Atli's treacherous invitation.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {

      "label": "visiting kin/guests (Gjukungs)",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:2"],
      "basis": "The Gjukungs are the group invited/visiting in the conjectured episode leading to killings.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {

      "label": "wife of Atli",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:3"],

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:5",
      "label": "giver of a harp (in Volsungasaga parallel)",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:3"],
      "basis": "Gudrun gives her brother the harp in the Volsungasaga version described.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:6",
      "label": "slain victim",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:4", "fig:5"],
      "basis": "Drap Niflunga is cited as telling of the slaying of Hogni and Gunnar.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:7",
      "label": "musician whose playing induces sleep (serpents or warriors)",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:5", "fig:9"],
      "basis": "Gunnar uses a harp to put serpents to sleep; Volker plays Gunther's followers to sleep.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5", "ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:8",
      "label": "ally/retainer (suggested)",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:6"],
      "basis": "Geirmund is described as seeming to be an ally/retainer of Atli or possibly his brother.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:9",
      "label": "speaker (possible)",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:7"],
      "basis": "A note concerns whether a line is part of Oddrun's speech.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:11"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:10",
      "label": "woman referenced by a gold/serpent-bed kenning",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:8"],
      "basis": "The note equates 'serpents-bed goddess' with 'woman' and identifies her as Borgny.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:11",
      "label": "leader whose followers are lulled (in Nibelungenlied parallel)",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:10"],
      "basis": "Volker plays the followers of Gunther to sleep.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:12",
      "label": "enchanted animals and lethal attacker",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:11"],
      "basis": "Serpents are put to sleep by harp-playing; an adder bites Gunnar to death.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5", "ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:13",
      "label": "maternal figure in a variant tradition",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:12"],
      "basis": "A note labels 'Atli's mother' as part of a version contrasted with Volsungasaga.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    }
  ],

The notes mention: a dream interpretation about rivers and grain; references to guardian spirits or lesser Norns; identifications of named characters (e.g., Gunnar, Hogni, Kostbera/Bera, Glaumvor, Vingi, Atli) and others; a river crossing where an oar/keel is broken and the boat is left to drift away to prevent retreat (paralleled with the Nibelungenlied); a demand for Sigurth’s gold now belonging to Guthrun; and a scene where a thrall shouts of fighting and Hogni laughs over the slain Vingi.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A prose paraphrase says that dreaming of rivers signifies that grain shall flow, and that chaff often rises above the feet when going to the fields.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A line is interpreted as referring to guardian spirits or lesser Norns.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Gunnar, Hogni, and three others (Snevar/Snævar, Solar, Orkning) are discussed; after landing the boat is splintered or allowed to drift away, preventing retreat.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A paraphrased dialogue includes a request to be welcomed and to hand over a store of gold (Sigurth’s gold), said now to belong to Guthrun, and a refusal implying readiness to fight; the feast is described as prepared \"with little grudging toward eagle and wolf.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hogni is said (editorially) to laugh loudly where the slain Vingi lay; Hogni is described as unarmed and not seeing Atli’s armed followers elsewhere in the courtyard.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A manuscript reading is summarized as \"word of the warring without\" coming into the house, and a thrall shouting loudly in front of the hall.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"Named character; {
  "record_id": "batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l20229-l20335",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "ATLAMOL EN GRNLENZKU / THE GREENLAND BALLAD OF ATLI / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 20229-20335",
    "start": "20229",
    "end": "20335",
    "translation": "The Poetic Edda",
    "notes": "Passage consists of Bellows' editorial notes on stanzas 69–89 of Atlamól."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Editorial notes describe plot elements and textual issues in Atlamól: Guðrún feigns submission to Atli to gain time for revenge; hostility is symbolized as concealed by friendliness using red and white shields; a paraphrase reports Guðrún taking Atli’s sons (Erp and Eitil) from their play; Atli is identified as the angry speaker in a disputed exchange; a horrific detail about skulls is discussed as possibly influenced by Vǫlund tradition; a phrase ‘another light’ is taken as a sign of Christian influence; and later-tradition material is summarized in which a son of Hǫgni (called Hniflung/Aldrian in later sources) ultimately shuts Attila/Atli in a cave to starve.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Guðrún is described as suddenly changing her tone to make Atli believe she is submissive, in order to gain time for her vengeance.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "A note explains that Guðrún concealed hostility (symbolized by a red shield) with a show of friendliness (a white shield).",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "A paraphrase reports that in the evening Guðrún took the sons of King Atli (Erp and Eitil) from where they were playing with a block of wood.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "The notes state that ‘the angry one’ is Atli in a passage where the manuscript does not name the speakers.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "A note states that Guðrún’s reference to ‘morning’ points back to Atli’s taunt in an earlier stanza (64).",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "The notes discuss a line about ‘skulls’ as an added touch of horror and suggest it may be borrowed or influenced by material from the Vǫlund tradition; the Vǫlsunga saga is said to include the incident.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l20834-l20904","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HAMTHESMOL / THE BALLAD OF HAMTHER / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 20834-20904","start":"20834","end":"20904","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Hamther and Sorli travel an ill road and see their sister’s son hanging on a tree. They reach a hall where men are drinking; a horn is sounded and Jormunrek is warned that helmeted warriors have come—men whose sister he murdered. Jormunrek boasts and threatens to bind and hang them, but fighting breaks out with bloodshed. Hamther addresses Jormunrek and speaks of burning him; Jormunrek orders that the attackers be stoned because steel cannot harm them. Sorli criticizes Hamther for opening a bag that brought harmful counsel; Hamther laments that if their slain brother Erp were alive the king’s head would be off, and says the Norns drove him to kill Erp. The brothers speak of wolves/hounds of the Norns and of fate spoken by the Norns; they stand over Goths they have cut down. Finally Sorli and Hamther fall and die.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"While traveling, Hamther and Sorli see their sister’s son on a tree; the scene is described as wind-cold and gruesome (with “cranes-bait” crawling).","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In a hall there is din and deep drinking; horses’ hoofs are not heard until a hardy warrior sounds a horn.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Men report to Jormunrek that helmeted warriors are outside and warn him to take wise counsel because he murdered their sister.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Jormunrek laughs, calls for his arms, looks on a white shield, and raises a golden cup; he says he would bind Hamther and Sorli with bow-strings and hang Gjuk’s heirs on the gallows.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"There is clamor in the hall; cups are shattered; men stand in blood from the breasts of the Goths.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hamther tells Jormunrek he will see his hands and feet flung in hot fire.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Jormunrek orders his men to stone Hamther and Sorli because sword and spear cannot bite them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sorli rebukes Hamther for opening a bag from which baleful counsel often came, and remarks on the lack of wisdom.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hamther says Jormunrek’s head would be off if Erp were living; he states they killed Erp on the road and that the Norns drove him to slay the brother who should have been holy in fight.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Hamther says it does not befit them to strive among themselves like wolves; the brothers reference “hounds of the Norns” and state that none outlives the night when the Norns have spoken.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The brothers say they have fought greatly and stand over Goths laid low by their blades; lines 392-462","start":"392","end":"462","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An English literary introduction describing Persian lyric poetry and presenting Hafiz as its greatest representative, contrasting him with other poets, explaining his Sufi use of symbolic/veiled language (wine, love, etc.), quoting a vivid image of fire/smoke from his grave, and closing with remarks on later attempts to revive Persian letters and subsequent political decline.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage distinguishes Persian lyric poetry (love, wine, youth, nature) from heroic and didactic forms and notes its presence from early times.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Rudagi and the Samanid princes are mentioned (tenth century) in connection with early poets of sentiment.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Firdusi is said to show a joyful lyric outlook in some minor poems.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Shams al-Din Mohammed Hafiz is presented as the greatest Persian lyric poet; war and strife in his country are said not to appear in his poems.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Hafiz is said to have been born and died in Shiraz and to have left his native place only once (to visit in Yazd) before returning; travel is described as having no inducement for him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hafiz is said to have put on the garb of a dervish but to be free of the dervish’s conceit; a saying is attributed to him calling the ascetic a serpent.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hafiz is compared to Omar Khayyam in some respects but is described as not being a philosopher; his Divan is said to be popular and his songs widely sung.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A saying attributed to Hafiz values earthly shade and fields alongside the “Garden of Paradise,” mentioning a willow-tree and the margin of a fruitful field.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hafiz is described as a thorough Sufi; a remark by Shah Shuja notes Hafiz writes in one song of wine, Sufism, and the beloved; the text says readers are often unsure where reality ends and Sufi “vacuity” begins.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Sufism is described as using veiled language and taking everyday things as symbols of transcendentalism, enabling outward Islamic observance while the mind wanders in fantasy/speculation.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A self-referential image attributed to Hafiz describes opening his grave after death and seeing smoke rising, showing that fire still burns in his dead heart and has set his winding-sheet alight.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The passage lists major poets (Firdusi, Omar, Sa’di, Hafiz; with Jami as an exception later) and states later revival attempts at the courts of Shah Abbas and Akbar did not match the earlier “heyday,” attributing this to Persia’s political downfall.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Shams al-Din Mohammed Hafiz","description":"Presented as the greatest Persian lyric poet; associated with Shiraz; described as a Sufi using symbolic/veiled language; several sayings/images are attributed to him.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Rudagi","description":"Named as an early figure in the tradition of poets of sentiment in the tenth century context.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Samanid princes","description":"Mentioned in connection with tenth-century poetic milieu in which poets of sentiment sang and charmed hearers.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Firdusi","description":"Named among great Persian poets; said to show a joyful lyric outlook in some minor poems.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Omar Khayyam","description":"Used as a comparison point for Hafiz; smoke from the grave; winding-sheet alight","literal_form":"Opening the grave reveals smoke; fire still burns in the dead heart and sets the winding-sheet alight.","associated_figures":["fig:1"],"taxonomy_refs":["fire"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"sym:5","label":"Veiled language / everyday things as symbols","literal_form":"Sufism is described as using veiled language and treating everyday things as symbols of transcendentalism.","associated_figures":["fig:1"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"scenes":[{"id":"scene:1","label":"Literary introduction and positioning of Hafiz in Persian lyric tradition","summary":"The narrator surveys Persian poetic forms and introduces Hafiz as the greatest lyric poet, giving brief biographical notes (Shiraz, limited travel) and emphasizing his melodic imagery and ethical humanity.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:3","fig:4","fig:5"],"symbol_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"scene:2","label":"Sufi symbolism and ambiguity of literal vs mystical meaning","summary":"Hafiz is described as a thorough Sufi; The introduction notes the poem’s supernatural elements (demons, peris, necromancers) and gives examples (serpents growing from King Zohak’s shoulders; Zerdusht ascending a ladder from earth to heaven). Persian invasion that might have altered Europe’s literary development.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introduction states that in shoulders of King Zohak.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Another example is given: a ladder of Zerdusht on which he mounted from earth to {
  "record_id": "batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l660-l735",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "FIRDUSI / INTRODUCTION / THE SHH NMEH / KAIMERS; lines 660-735",
    "start": "660",
    "end": "735",
    "translation": "Persian Literature, Volume 1",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "The passage presents Kaimers (Kayumars) as Persia’s first lawgiver-king who dwells in the mountains and wears beast skins. His son Saimuk is killed in battle by a demonic adversary’s son. Kaimers mourns until a mysterious voice urges patience and renewed war. Saimuk’s son Hsheng (Hushang) is appointed leader, commands obedience from wild and tame animals, kills the Demon and his offspring, and after Kaimers’s death ascends the Persian throne.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Kaimers is described as the first person in Persia to establish laws and act as a monarch.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Kaimers dwells among the mountains and wears garments made from the skins of beasts.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "During Kaimers’s reign, wild animals assemble around his throne and do him homage.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Kaimers has a son, Saimuk, who raises a martial force to punish a Demon who seeks to overthrow Kaimers and Saimuk.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Saimuk is proudly garbed in leopard’s skin when he goes to war.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Saimuk is killed in combat, falling lifeless from an enemy’s \"dragon-grasp.\"",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Kaimers weeps bitterly and remains inconsolable for a long time after Saimuk’s death; after a year a mysterious voice tells him to be patient and to send another army against the Demons to gain victory.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "Saimuk leaves a son named Hsheng, who is described as having combined knowledge and goodness and is given his father’s dignity and station.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Kaimers appoints Hsheng as leader of the army; at that time every species of animal, wild and tame, is said to be obedient to his command and to do him homage.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "Hsheng, by the blessing of God, kills the Demon and the Demon’s offspring with his own hand; the army and accompanying animals then defeat and tear to pieces the enemy forces; after Kaimers’s death Hsheng ascends the throne of Persia.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    }
  ],

{
  "record_id": "batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l902-l1028",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK; lines 902-1028",
    "start": "902",
    "end": "1028",
    "translation": "Persian Literature, Volume 1",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "A charitable king, Mirts, distributes milk to the poor and is favored by God. His son Zohk is deceived by Iblis (the Evil Spirit) disguised as a virtuous man into swearing secrecy and then killing his father by means of a concealed pit on the path to the house of prayer, after which Zohk usurps the throne. Iblis continues to influence Zohk, invents rich cooking for him, and requests to kiss Zohk’s bare shoulder; from the kiss two black serpents spring forth and cannot be removed by sages or magicians. Iblis later returns disguised as a physician, claims it is Zohk’s destiny, and advises feeding the serpents daily with human brains, aiming at widespread human destruction, though the passage notes Iblis has no influence in the house of God and humanity continues to increase.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Mirts is described as a king of the Arabs who owns many milk-giving animals and distributes their milk in charity to the poor; God increases favor upon him.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Zohk, Mirts’s son, is said to possess ten thousand Arab horses and is surnamed Bwurasp; Iblis appears to him disguised as a good and virtuous man and speaks pleasantly with him.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Iblis demands a solemn compact and oath of secrecy before speaking further; Zohk agrees and swears not to divulge the secret.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "After the oath, Iblis urges Zohk to kill his father and take sovereignty; Zohk is frightened by threats and asks for a method.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "A pit/well is dug and covered with grass on the path to Mirts-Tzi’s house of prayer; Mirts falls in at night, breaks limbs, and dies; Zohk takes the throne.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Iblis becomes highly influential with Zohk, including in the royal kitchen; in earlier days bread and fruit were usual foods, and Iblis is called the original inventor of cooking art, preparing meats and eggs and varied dishes.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "In gratitude, Zohk offers Iblis a reward; Iblis asks only to kiss the monarch’s naked shoulder; after the kiss Iblis vanishes and two black serpents spring from the touch.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "People search for Iblis in the palace but cannot find him; learned men and sage magicians try to charm away the serpents but find no cure.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Iblis returns disguised as a physician, says the affliction accords with Zohk’s horoscope and destiny, and advises feeding the serpents daily with human brains to prolong Zohk’s life and ease his misery.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "Iblis is pleased, believing this plan will destroy many humans, but the passage states his craft has no influence in the house of God and Adam’s descendants continue increasing.",
      "category": "other",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    }
  ],
  "figures": [
    {
      "id": "fig:1",
      "name_or_label": "Mirts (Mirts-Tzi)",
      "description": "A king of the Arabs who gives charitable distributions of milk and later dies after falling into a concealed pit on the way to his house of prayer.",
      "role_refs": ["role:1", "role:5"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:2",
      "name_or_label": "Zohk (Bwurasp)",

Softened, Greng promises support, but Jemshd distrusts him and flees. An envoy traveling with troops recognizes Jemshd asleep near a tower, chains him, and sends him to Zohk. Zohk humiliates the captive king, offers him a choice of death, then has him fastened between planks and sawn in two. News reaches Zbulistn; Jemshd’s wife dies by taking poison. The passage adds that Jemshd’s sisters were seized and confined in Zohk’s harem and later released by Feridn, and that Zohk’s tyranny includes feeding serpents on human brains and killing two young victims daily.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A princess weeps and pleads with her father not to be accessory to the murder of King Jemshd, warning that a bad name endures until the day of doom and invoking the day of judgment.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"King Greng is softened by his garden.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Jemshd distrusts Greng’s professions and seeks escape after hearing that vizirs are consulting about securing his person for fear Zohk will invade if Jemshd’s retreat is discovered.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Jemshd flees toward Chn and into Ind, comes to a tower, laments his Feridn then takes Zohk’s empty throne and appropriates the throne and treasury after learning Zohk has marched toward Ind with an immense army. Arnawz explains Zohk chose that route expecting to meet Feridn there or to subdue a land associated with sorcery and obtain a renowned magician to charm Feridn, since Zohk is oppressed by fear of Feridn’s name.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kavah directs Feridn’s route over mountains and plains near the river Dijleh (Tigris) tower.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Feridn overthrows the talisman and destroys or vanquishes enchanted monsters and hideous shapes that appear before him, using his mace.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Feridn captures the building and releases secluded “black-eyed damsels,” including Shahrnz and Arnawz, identified as the two sisters of Jemshd; the freed inmates express gratitude to Heaven.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Feridn ascends Zohk’s empty throne, which had been for himself.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Feridn asks Arnawz why Zohk chose the route toward Ind; Arnawz says Zohk expects to encounter Feridn there, or else {
  "record_id": "batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l2121-l2241",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "KAVAH, THE BLACKSMITH / FERIDN / FERIDN AND HIS THREE SONS / MINCHIHR; lines 2121-2241",
    "start": "2121",
    "end": "2241",
    "translation": "Persian Literature, Volume 1",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Feridn mourns his murdered son Irij and hopes for an avenger. Irij’s wife Mahafrid bears a daughter; Feridn marries her to Pishung, and their son Minchihr is born and celebrated as resembling Irij and Feridn. Minchihr is raised and trained as a warrior and publicly treated as king. As Feridn distributes gold and gathers an army, the guilty brothers Slim and Tur fear invasion and send a messenger with lavish gifts and repentance, blaming Iblis and offering fealty. Feridn seats Minchihr beside him, interprets the gifts as fear, then rejects the attempt to buy peace, demands to know where Irij’s body lies, and declares that Minchihr will meet them in arms and that only blood can repay blood. Feridn displays his champions (including Kavah and others) to the messenger and sends the gifts away, invoking an oracle about oppressors reaping bitter fruit and using a tree-and-branch image to describe the surviving line.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Feridn cherishes the memory of his murdered son Irij and hopes a son will be born to take vengeance for the death.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Mahafrid (wife of Irij) gives birth to a daughter; Feridn later marries this daughter to Pishung, and from that union Minchihr is born.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Minchihr is described as resembling Irij and Feridn, and his birth is celebrated with rejoicing.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Minchihr is nurtured in infancy, then instructed in arts to form a warrior; Feridn places him on the throne and crowns him, and soldiers acknowledge him as king and urge vengeance for the murder of his grandfather.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Feridn opens his treasury and distributes gold among the people, enabling Minchihr to gather an immense army devoted to him.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Slim and Tur learn of Minchihr’s preparations and valor and are terrified; they decide to pursue peace by sending splendid presents and conciliatory language to regain Feridn’s goodwill.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Elephants are loaded with treasure including a crown of gold, and a messenger is sent with acknowledgment of guilt, repentance, and an offer of obedience and fealty; the message blames Iblis for leading them astray.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "At Feridn’s court, Minchihr is seated on a golden chair beside Feridn; Feridn tells Minchihr the gifts are an omen showing the enemy’s fear, then hears the messenger’s plea that the brothers will pay with gems and even resign their kingdoms for peace.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Feridn scorns the attempt to disguise the crime, asks where Irij’s body lies, calls the brothers unnatural, and declares Minchihr will be seen surrounded by soldiers, clad in steel, and wielding life-destroying swords.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "Feridn shows the messenger his warriors one by one (including Kavah and Kavah’s two sons) and rejects barter: gold cannot redeem blood; he cites an oracle about oppressors reaping bitter fruit, promises punishment, and uses an image of a rooted-up favorite tree with one branch remaining; he insists on blood-for-blood vengeance and dismisses the gifts.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    }
  ],
  "figures": [
    {
      "id": "fig:1",
      "name_or_label": "Feridn",
      "description": "An aged monarch who mourns Irij, raises Minchihr, gathers support, and refuses to accept gifts in place of vengeance.",
      "role_refs": ["role:1", "role:7"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:2", "ev:4", "ev:5", "ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:2",
      "name_or_label": "Irij",
      "description": "Feridn’s son who was murdered; his memory motivates planned retribution.",
      "role_refs": ["role:2"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:3",
      "name_or_label": "Mahafrid",
      "description": "The wife of Irij who gives birth to a daughter.",
      "role_refs": ["role:3"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:4",
      "name_or_label": "Pishung",
      "description": "Husband of Irij’s daughter and father of Minchihr.",
      "role_refs": ["role:4"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:5",
      "name_or_label": "Minchihr",
      "description": "Heir born from the marriage of Irij’s daughter to Pishung; resembles Irij and Feridn; raised and trained, acknowledged as king, and positioned as avenger.",
      "role_refs": ["role:5", "role:6"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:2", "ev:4", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:6",
      "name_or_label": "Slim",
      "description": "One of two brothers who fear Minchihr’s coming vengeance; sends gifts and repentance through a messenger.",
      "role_refs": ["role:8"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
