    "end": "13550",
    "translation": "Persian Literature, Volume 1",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Queen Hmai secretly has a son (Drb) and publicly announces his death. Months later she has the infant wrapped in rich garments, sealed in a box, and cast into the Euphrates at night to prevent him from being found and becoming king. A washerman finds the floating box in the morning, discovers the baby with valuables, and he and his wife adopt and nurse him. Drb grows up talented and proud, receives education and martial training, learns the circumstances of his discovery, and takes remaining rubies for travel. When a war with the king of Rum arises, Drb joins the general Rishnawd’s call for recruits; Hmai notices his royal appearance and feels a fleeting maternal instinct.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Hmai gives birth to a son, has him raised secretly by a nurse, and publicly declares that the child died the same day he was born.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "When the child is seven months old, Hmai wraps him in rich garments, places him in a box, fastens the cover, and orders two confidential servants at night to throw it into the Euphrates.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Hmai reasons that if the boy is found in the city, her authority will end and the crown will be placed upon his head; she casts him into the river while allowing for the possibility that God may preserve him elsewhere.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "The box floats down the Euphrates and is noticed in the morning by a washerman, who draws it to shore, opens it, and finds rich clothing and a sleeping infant.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "The washerman brings the infant to his wife; she feeds the child with her own milk, and the couple also finds jewels and rubies in the box.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "The washerman and his wife name the child Drb, and later leave their home to avoid discovery of the boy and the wealth.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "As Drb grows, he is described as unusually skilled (including wrestling) and resists assisting in washing clothes, running away from the work.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "Drb is sent to school and is said to excel his master; he seeks further instruction and a fine horse to learn warrior skills, and is trained with bow, javelin, and sword.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Drb learns from his foster-mother how he was found; she says two valuable rubies remain, and Drb binds one on his arm and sells the other to fund travel.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "The king of Rum sends an army into Iran; Hmai orders her general Rishnawd to raise a corresponding force and issues a proclamation inviting young men seeking military glory.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:11",
      "text": "Drb answers the proclamation and is presented to Hmai; she notices his royal-looking form and feels an instinctive, motherlike agitation that soon passes.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    }
  ],

      "role_refs": ["role:3", "role:4"],

      "name_or_label": "Washerman’s wife (foster-mother)",

      "role_refs": ["role:6"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4", "ev:6", "ev:7"]
    },

  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "During a stormy march, the youth Drb sleeps under a damaged archway. A supernatural voice repeatedly warns the arch not to collapse because the sleeper is Bahman’s son destined for the Persian throne. Drb is found sleeping; when he is moved, the arch collapses. Rishnawd recognizes a ruby token on Drb’s arm and confirms he is the child Hma had cast into the Euphrates. Drb is honored and given command; he displays exceptional valor in battle against the forces of Rm, leading to Persian victory and a peace settlement with tribute. Rishnawd sends Hma the ruby; she recognizes Drb as her son, makes offerings at a fire-altar and gives charity, meets and embraces him, and then relinquishes crown and throne to him.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "A tremendous wind and heavy rain occur after the first march; soldiers shelter under tents except Drb, who has none and sleeps under an archway.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "A supernatural voice is heard, repeating warnings that the arch must stand firm because the sleeper beneath is destined for a royal throne and is identified as Bahman’s son.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "When a person looks under the archway, Drb is discovered in deep sleep and the arch above him is rent and broken; after Drb is removed, the arch collapses with a crash.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Rishnawd recognizes a ruby on Drb’s arm and, with corroboration from a washerman and his wife, concludes Drb is Bahman’s son whom Hma had caused to be thrown into the Euphrates.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Rishnawd treats Drb with honor, seats him at his right hand, and appoints him to a high command in the army.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "In battle against the Rms, Drb in the advanced guard performs prodigies of valor; later he proposes attacking with a chosen band while the leader remains quiet, and he presses the enemy to flight.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "After further fighting, the Persians are triumphant; Kasar sends a messenger acknowledging aggressions and offering tribute, and peace terms are settled and he is permitted to return home.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "Rishnawd sends Hma news of victory and Drb’s valor and transmits the ruby as evidence of his birth; Hma becomes convinced Drb is her son.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Hma proceeds to an Atish-gadeh (fire-altar), makes an offering, orders a great fire to be lighted, and gives large sums in charity to the poor.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "Hma meets Drb with a retinue, embraces and kisses him as a mother, and then relinquishes the crown and throne in his favor after reigning thirty-two years.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    }
  ],

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l14382-l14506","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"DRB AND DR / SIKANDER / FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD; lines 14382-14506","start":"14382","end":"14506","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A sequence of editorial footnotes explains customs and metaphors in the Shahnameh tradition and related Persian/Eastern court life: women’s seclusion as a sign of innocence; poetic comparisons (stars vs moon; heart like the new moon); instruments of royal camps; wartime plunder and burning; a love metaphor involving the liver; perfumed and embellished royal letters; feasting before undertakings; the meaning of a punishment term involving a tree/stake; heroic boasting compared to Achilles; counsel that kings should have judgment; idioms of regret involving ashes; palace garden-pavilions with waterworks; coronation/festival practices of scattering gems or gold/pearls; details like golden slippers, amber/juniper gum, and banners bearing an elephant to denote royal descent.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Tahmneh is said to declare her innocence to Rustem by stating that no one has seen her outside her private chamber or heard her voice.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes state that seclusion of women of rank in Persia and other parts of the East is described as customary and not viewed by them as intolerable; zenanas are described as well supplied, and Eastern women are said to have influence and power.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A footnote claims an old song in Percy’s Collection contains a similar idea and quotes Sir Henry Wotton about common stars versus the moon rising.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"“Kus” is defined as a tymbal or large brass drum beaten in the palaces or camps of Eastern princes.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes state that in the Shahnameh, when an army is put in motion, inhabitants and country (hostile or friendly) are given up to plunder and devastation, and things in their progress are burnt and destroyed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A note says Hmn was not at first aware that Sohrab was wounded in the liver, and it adds that Oriental and Greek/Roman poets place the residence of love in the liver.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A note describes that royal/distinguished letters are written on perfumed paper, covered with gold devices, and the degree of embellishment is regulated by rank; this example is scented with amber.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Four days of uninterrupted feasting are described as an ancient practice before important undertakings or setting out on a journey.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Zra is identified as Rustem’s brother and as having immediate superintendence of the Zabul troops.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A punishment term “dar” is explained as a tree on which felons are hanged, or more generally as breaking/tearing the body upon a stake.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A note says Rustem recounts his services to Ks, including conquests in multiple lands, and compares this boasting to Achilles’ claims (quoted via Pope’s Iliad).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A note states that kings ought to have judgment and discretion and that no advantage comes from impetuosity and rage; Gudarz is described as a venerable general whose opinion had weight with Ks.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ks is said to use the phrase “ashes fell into my mouth” to express repentance/regret; a similar metaphor is noted in Hindustan (“ashes have fallen into my meat”).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A simile is given: “My heart became as slender as the new moon.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Palace arbors/garden-pavilions are described as within palace walls, fitted with reservoirs, fountains, and flower-trees; Turkish “kiosks” are said to be on an eminence near a running stream.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"A note describes an eastern ceremony (at coronations) of powdering kings with gold-dust and seed-pearl / “scattering gems,” and mentions related practices of throwing money to people; it cites Milton, Warburton, Hafiz (“nisar”), and Clarke’s account of sultanas powdered with diamonds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A note says that in battle-array descriptions Firdusi often includes “golden slippers.”","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"“Sandurūs” (sandaraca) is identified as gum juniper; the editor substituted “amber.”","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Banners are said to be adorned with the figure of an elephant to denote royal descent.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"A note states that “he” (an unnamed referent in these footnotes) was also the son-in-law of Rustem.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Tahmneh","description":"A woman who declares her innocence by asserting strict seclusion and silence.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Rustem","description":"The person to whom Tahmneh makes her declaration; also referenced as a hero whose services and relatives are noted.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:8","ev:10","ev:19"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Women of rank in Persia / women of the East (group)","description":"Described as living in seclusion (zenanas) that is customary and comfortable, with influence and power.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Sir Henry Wotton","description":"Attributed author of quoted lines comparing lesser night ‘beauties’ (stars) to the moon’s rise.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Eastern princes (group)","description":"Associated with palaces/camps where the kus drum is beaten.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Armies in motion (group)","description":"Described (in Shahnameh commentary) as plundering and burning in their progress.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Hmn","description":"Said not to be initially aware that Sohrab was wounded in the liver.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Sohrab","description":"Said to be wounded in the liver (a locus of love in poetic tradition).","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Royal and distinguished letter-writers/recipients (group)","description":"Associated with perfumed, gold-decorated paper regulated by rank.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Zra","description":"Identified as Rustem’s brother and supervisor of the Zabul troops.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Ks (king)","description":"Referenced as the recipient of Rustem’s services/boasts and as a king influenced by Gudarz; uses an idiom of regret involving ashes.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Gudarz","description":"Described as a venerable and distinguished Persian general whose opinion had influence with Ks.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Achilles","description":"Cited as a comparand for boasting of unrequited achievements (via Pope’s Iliad quotation).","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Milton","description":"Cited as alluding to an eastern custom of showering kings with pearl and gold.","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Hafiz","description":"Cited for using the term “nisar” for throwing/scattering money or gifts.","role_refs":["role:15"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Clarke (traveler)","description":"Cited for a description of Constantinople sultanas powdered with diamonds.","role_refs":["role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Sultanas of the Seraglio at Constantinople (group)","description":"Described (via Clarke) as having hair powdered with diamonds.","role_refs":["role:17"],"evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l14812-l14977","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD / THE RUBIYT OF OMAR KHAYYM / THE RUBIYT; lines 14812-14977","start":"14812","end":"14977","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A sequence of quatrains (Rubáiyát) that moves from dawn imagery and tavern exhortations to reflections on spring, wine, roses, worldly power, mortality, and the unknowable “whence/whither” of human fate, including an imagined ascent through the “Seventh Gate” to Saturn’s throne that still fails to resolve the master-knot of destiny.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Dawn is described as the Sun scattering the Stars, driving away Night, and striking a sultan’s turret with light.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A voice in a tavern questions why a worshipper is drowsing outside when the temple is prepared within.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At the cock’s crow, people at the tavern call to open the door, noting that their time is short and that after departure they may not return.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"With the New Year and spring, the soul retires to solitude; Moses’ “White Hand” is said to appear on a bough and Jesus to breathe/sigh from the ground.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Iram and Jamshid’s seven-ringed cup are said to be gone, yet a ruby kindles in the vine and gardens bloom by the water.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The speaker urges filling the cup, casting off repentance, and notes the “Bird of Time” has little way to flutter and is on the wing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Life is likened to wine oozing drop by drop and leaves falling one by one; the rose of yesterday is gone; summer that brings the rose will take away named kings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker dismisses concern for kings and heroes, and describes a place on a strip of herbage between desert and sown where slave and sultan are forgotten; “Peace to Mahmud on his golden throne” is spoken.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"An idyllic scene is described: a book of verses, jug of wine, loaf of bread, and “thou” beside the speaker singing in the wilderness, which would be paradise enough.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The poem contrasts seeking worldly glories or a prophet’s paradise and advises taking “cash” rather than “credit.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Worldly hopes are said to turn to ashes or vanish like snow on the desert after a brief time.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The world is likened to a battered caravanserai with alternating night and day portals where sultans stay for their destined hour and depart.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Animals (lion, lizard, wild ass) are said to inhabit or pass over former royal courts and a hunter’s resting place.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Roses, hyacinths, and reviving herbs by a river-lip are imagined as arising from buried bodies (blood, heads, lips).","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The speaker urges filling the cup to clear regrets and fears; tomorrow may bring dissolution into vast past time; loved ones have already drunk and gone to rest.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14","ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The speaker says the living will descend beneath the couch of earth, become dust, and lie without wine, song, or singer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A muezzin from a “Tower of Darkness” calls people fools and claims their reward is neither here nor there.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Saints, sages, and prophets are said to be thrust aside; their words are scattered and their mouths stopped with dust.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The speaker reports frequenting doctors and saints and hearing arguments, but leaving by the same door without answers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The speaker states: “I came like Water, and like Wind I go,” and describes not knowing why, whence, or whither.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19","ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The speaker imagines rising from earth’s center through the seventh gate to sit on Saturn’s throne and unravelling many knots, but not the master-knot of human fate.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"A door without a key and a veil that cannot be seen through are described; talk of “Me and Thee” ends in silence.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:22"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Earth, seas, and heaven are said not to answer questions; seas mourn in purple and heaven rolls with signs revealed and hidden by night and morning.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:23"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Speaker (“I”)","description":"A first-person voice that urges drinking, reflects on mortality and ignorance of whence/whither, and narrates an ascent through the seventh gate.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:14","ev:18","ev:21"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Beloved/companion (“Thou”, “my Belov’d”)","description":"Addressed as a companion beside the speaker in the wilderness; urged to fill the cup.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Sun","description":"Drives away night and strikes a turret with a shaft of light.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Stars","description":"Scattered into flight before the Sun from the field of night.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Night","description":"Driven away by the Sun; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l15144-l15307","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD / THE RUBIYT OF OMAR KHAYYM / THE RUBIYT; lines 15144-15307","start":"15144","end":"15307","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A sequence of stanzas attributed to Omar Khayyam’s Rubaiyat imagery: heaven and hell as states, humans as shadows in a cosmic show and game, destiny as an irreversible writing, the sky as an inverted bowl, creation and final reckoning, exhortations to drink, debates about predestination and punishment, the serpent in paradise, a visit to a potter’s house where clay vessels speak about the potter and their making/breaking, requests for burial with grape and leaf so that wine may rise from ashes, reflections on repentance and spring, longing for a revealing fountain, and a wish for an angel to alter the roll of fate or to remould the scheme of things nearer to desire.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Heaven is described as the vision of fulfilled desire, and hell as a shadow cast from a soul on fire.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Humans are compared to moving shadow-shapes that come and go around a sun-illumined lantern held at midnight by a master of the show.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Humans are described as pieces of a game played on a checkerboard of nights and days; the player moves, checks, slays, and stores pieces away.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A ball goes where the player strikes it; the one who tossed a person into the field is said to know all about it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The moving finger writes and then moves on; piety, wit, or tears cannot cancel or wash out what is written.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The sky is described as an inverted bowl under which people live and die; it is said to move impotently like humans.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Earth’s clay is said to be used to knead the last man; the first morning of creation is said to write what the last dawn of reckoning will read.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker urges drinking because people do not know whence they came, why they go, or where.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The speaker says the vine has struck a fiber that clings to his being; he imagines a key filed from base metal that can unlock a door outside which a dervish howls.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"One flash of a “one True Light” caught in a tavern is said to be better than being lost in a temple.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The speaker protests being provoked from nothing to consciousness under a yoke of unpermitted pleasure and everlasting penalties.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The speaker addresses a maker who beset the road with pitfalls and then imputes the fall to sin; he also says the maker devised the snake with paradise and asks for forgiveness given and taken.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Under cover of departing day, Ramazan departs; the speaker stands alone in a potter’s house surrounded by shapes of clay.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Clay vessels of many sorts stand along the floor and wall; some are described as loquacious and others silent.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Several vessels speak about being taken from common earth, moulded to a figure, and possibly being broken or returned to shapeless earth; another questions whether the potter’s hand shook; another asks who is the potter and who the pot.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15","ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"One vessel reports that some say a maker threatens to toss to hell the pots he marred; another says to fill it with familiar juice so it may recover.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A little moon looks in while the vessels speak; the vessels nudge each other, calling “Brother! Brother!” and mentioning the potter’s shoulder-knot creaking.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The speaker asks to be provided with grape, washed after death, and laid shrouded in a living leaf by a garden-side.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The speaker says buried ashes may fling up a snare of vintage into the air that overtakes a passing true-believer unaware.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The speaker says idols he loved have harmed his credit, drowning glory in a shallow cup and selling reputation for a song; he describes repentance sworn often, then spring with rose-in-hand tearing penitence to pieces.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The speaker laments that spring vanishes with the rose and youth’s manuscript closes; he asks where the nightingale that sang in branches has flown.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:22"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The speaker wishes the desert of the fountain would yield a glimpse to reveal something for a fainting traveler; he wishes an angel would arrest the yet unfolded roll of fate and alter or obliterate it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:23","ev:24"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The speaker addresses Love and imagines conspiring with “Him” to shatter the scheme of things and remould it nearer to the heart’s desire.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:25"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Speaker (“I”)","description":"A first-person voice who reflects on fate, creation, drinking, and death, visits the potter’s house, and addresses other figures in direct speech.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:13","ev:19","ev:25"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Controller figure (“Master of the Show” / “Player” / “He” / “Potter” / “Recorder”)","description":"A figure described as holding a lantern at midnight, playing a game with human pieces, tossing people into the field, writing fate, making vessels, and (in reported speech) threatening hell for marred pots.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:17"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Dervish","description":"A dervish is mentioned as one who might flout the speaker, and as howling outside a door that a key could unlock.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Clay vessels / pots","description":"Multiple vessels made of common earth, standing in the potter’s house, some speaking and questioning their maker and their fate.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14","ev:15","ev:17"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Little Moon","description":"The moon is described as looking into the potter’s house while the vessels speak.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"True-believer (passing by)","description":"A true-believer is mentioned as a passerby who may be overtaken by the snare of vintage rising from buried ashes.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Vintners","description":"Vintners are mentioned as buyers of wine; the speaker wonders what they buy as precious as what they sell.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Man / humans","description":"Humans are described as shadow-shapes, game pieces, and creatures living under the sky; man is said to be made of baser earth.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Snake (in Paradise)","description":"A snake is said to be devised along with paradise.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Angel (winged)","description":"A winged angel is wished for who could arrest the yet unfolded roll of fate and change the record.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:24"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Love (addressed)","description":"Love is addressed as a partner in a hypothetical conspiracy to remake the scheme of things.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:25"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Narrator / reflective speaker","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The first-person voice makes assertions, issues exhortations to drink, recounts standing in the potter’s house, and requests burial arrangements.","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:13","ev:19"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Cosmic controller (showmaster/player/potter/recorder)","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"A master holds the lantern; a player moves and slays pieces; “He” tosses people into the field; the moving finger writes; the potter makes vessels; a stern recorder is invoked for fate.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:24"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Speaking created objects (pots)","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Vessels in the potter’s house speak, reason about their making/breaking, and question the potter-pot relation.","evidence_refs":["ev:15","ev:16","ev:17"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"Mortal creatures under fate","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"Humans are depicted as shadow-shapes and game pieces, living and dying under the sky-bowl; man is described as made of earth.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:6","ev:12"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"Passerby susceptible to vintage ‘snare’","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"A true-believer passing by is said to be overtaken unaware by vintage flung up from ashes.","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"Observer looking in","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"The little moon is described as looking in while the vessels speak.","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"Religious ascetic / critic outside the ‘door’","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"The dervish is invoked as flouting the speaker and as howling outside a door that could be unlocked.","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"Wine-traders","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"Vintners are mentioned in connection with buying and selling wine.","evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"Serpent of paradise (devised with paradise)","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"The snake is named as something devised with paradise in the address to the maker.","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"role:10","label":"Potential intervener in fate’s record","assigned_to":["fig:10"],"basis":"A winged angel is imagined who could arrest the roll of fate and alter the record.","evidence_refs":["ev:24"]},{"id":"role:11","label":"Co-conspirator in remaking reality (hypothetical)","assigned_to":["fig:11"],"basis":"Love is addressed as someone who could conspire with the speaker to shatter and remould the scheme of things.","evidence_refs":["ev:25"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Fire (soul on fire; flaming)","literal_form":"A soul on fire; flaming shoulders of a foal of heaven","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:8"],"taxonomy_refs":["fire"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:9"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"Serpent / snake in paradise","literal_form":"The snake devised with paradise","associated_figures":["fig:9"],"taxonomy_refs":["serpent"],"evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"Water / fountain","literal_form":"A fountain in a desert desired to yield a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l15309-l15336","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RUBIYT OF OMAR KHAYYM / THE RUBIYT / THE DIVAN / BY HFIZ; lines 15309-15336","start":"15309","end":"15336","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two stanzas address the cyclical rising of the moon and imagine a future time when the moon will look for the speakers in the same garden, but one will be absent. The speaker addresses a cupbearer and asks that, when passing among guests, the cupbearer reach the spot where the speaker once made someone/something and turn down an empty glass. An editorial note explains that many odes (ghazals) appear disunified; each couplet is likened to a pearl, and the whole ode to a string of pearls, with rhyme linking couplets more than sense, allowing couplets to be rearranged in manuscripts.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The moon is described as rising again and again and waxing and waning repeatedly in the future.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The moon is said to rise and look for the speakers through the same garden, and to look for one person in vain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A figure addressed as \"Sáki\" (cupbearer) is imagined passing among guests described as 'star-scattered on the grass'.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker instructs the Sáki to reach a particular spot 'where I made One' and to turn down an empty glass.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"An editorial note states that many odes have an apparent lack of unity; each couplet is compared to a single pearl and the ghazal to a string of pearls.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The note states that rhyme, not necessarily sense, links couplets; couplets may be reordered without harming effect, and manuscripts vary in number and order of odes/couplets.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Speaker (\"I\")","description":"A first-person speaker who reflects on future absence and gives an instruction about an empty glass at a particular spot.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Addressee: Sáki (cupbearer)","description":"Addressed directly and asked to carry out a 'joyous errand' and turn down an empty glass at a certain spot.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"The Moon","description":"A rising moon that repeatedly waxes and wanes and is imagined to look for the speakers again in the garden.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Guests","description":"Guests among whom the Sáki passes; they are described in relation to being 'star-scatter'd on the grass'.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Orientals (as referenced in note)","description":"Referenced as making a comparison between couplets and pearls, and the ghazal and a string of pearls.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"speaker/poetic voice","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"First-person statements and instructions are given by \"I\".","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"cupbearer/addressee","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"The speaker addresses \"Sáki\" and instructs him to act with an empty glass.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"celestial marker of recurring time","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"The moon is described as repeatedly waxing/waning and rising again to look for the speakers.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"gathering participants (guests)","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Guests are present in the imagined scene through which the Sáki passes.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"commentators on poetic form","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"They are said to compare couplets to pearls and ghazals to strings of pearls.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Waxing and waning moon","literal_form":"Rising moon; waxing and waning","associated_figures":["fig:3"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"Garden (revisited place)","literal_form":"\"this same Garden\"","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:3"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"Empty glass","literal_form":"An empty glass that is turned down","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"sym:4","label":"Pearls and string (ghazal structure)","literal_form":"Each couplet as a pearl; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l15339-l15408","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RUBIYT / THE DIVAN / BY HFIZ / INTRODUCTION; lines 15339-15408","start":"15339","end":"15408","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introduction recounts a story (treated as spiritually true though historically doubtful) in which Tamerlane confronts the poet-saint Hafiz about a bold verse, but is disarmed by Hafiz’s calm wit and rewards him. The narrator then characterizes Hafiz’s poetry as joyful and hedonically appreciative yet grounded in Sufi theology: the human soul comes from the One God, life is a staged journey toward God, and worldly beauties and pleasures (wine, song, love, sensory delights) are regarded as divine gifts and intermediaries that unite the soul more closely with God, culminating in return/re-absorption into a divine source.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Tamerlane reaches Shiraz, halts at the city gates, and sends two followers into the bazar to find the dervish Muhammad Shams-ad-din (Hafiz).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Hafiz, wearing a simple woollen Sufi garment, is brought before Tamerlane in a pavilion decorated with silks and jewelry and remains un-abashed.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Tamerlane angrily asks whether Hafiz is the poet who offered Samarkand and Bokhara for the black mole on his lady’s cheek; Hafiz admits it and replies that his munificence has left him destitute and dependent on Tamerlane’s generosity.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Tamerlane is pleased by Hafiz’s reply and self-possession and dismisses him with a liberal present.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The narrator states the story cannot be factually true because Tamerlane reached Shiraz after Hafiz’s death, but claims it is true “in spirit” and reveals Hafiz’s character.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hafiz is described as uttering an unbroken strain of joy and contentment; his poverty is described as a fountain of satisfaction, and he accepts life’s joys supported by belief in the One God’s goodness manifested in sweet, genial, and beautiful things.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The narrator contrasts Hafiz with Epicurus and with classic Latin poets (Horace, Martial), and mentions Dante placing Epicurus among those who denied immortality in the Inferno.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sufi theology is described: the One God is exuberantly benign; from God’s creative essence proceeds the human soul; earthly experience fits it for re-entrance into a “circle of light” and re-absorption into a “primeval fountain of being.”","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Life is described as a journey of many stages; each manifestation encountered on the road is described as a manifestation and gift of God; each stage toward God is compared to a wayside inn where one rests before continuing.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Pleasures and sensory The passage ends with an idyllic description of his resting place in Shiraz.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hafiz is characterized as consistently joyful, described as passing through life \"like a happy pilgrim\" and being sure of a welcome at his goal.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The text says Hafiz considers every manifestation of life he is conscious of to be stirrings within him of a divinity of which he is a portion.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Hafiz's tomb is described as being visited as the \"Mecca\" of literary pilgrims, and his verses are widely memorized and recited.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Biographical details are given: born at Shiraz in the early fourteenth century and died in 1388.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The name \"Hafiz\" is glossed as meaning \"the man who remembers\" and is linked to his memorization of the Koran for his work teaching Mohammedan scriptures.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Dervishes in the monastic college disapproved of his manner of life, and he satirized his colleagues in response.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Rulers and kings offered Hafiz honors and hospitality.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hafiz started for India by invitation of a Southern Prince; a vessel was sent to meet him, but sea hardships led him to return to Shiraz without finishing the journey.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Because of his pantheism and manner of life, Hafiz was initially denied burial in consecrated ground; {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l16371-l16460","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LXXXV / LXXXVI / LXXXVII / LXXXVIII; lines 16371-16460","start":"16371","end":"16460","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Angels I saw at night knock at the wine-house gate\"; \"Lost Joseph shall return to Kanaan's land\"; \"Noah shall steer the ark o'er billows dark\"","summary":"A sequence of lyric stanzas attributed to Hafiz: (1) critique of religious hypocrisy and praise of wine/drinking paired with gracious deeds and purity; (2) a visionary scene in which angels and spirits visit a wine-house, shape Adam from clay, and pour wine; (3) a refrain of consolation (“Despair not”) invoking the return of Joseph, the changefulness of fate, pilgrimage hardship, and the flood of death countered by Noah steering the ark, ending with prayer and reading the Koran as solace.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker says the town preacher may find his language hard, and declares that someone bent on deceit and fraud is not a true Muslim.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker urges learning drinking and doing gracious deeds, and says mere abstention from wine is not a great merit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker states that the Divine Name is efficient and that a “dev” does not become Solomon through guile and cunning.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker says Heaven’s benisons are won by purity alone, illustrated by a comparison to pearl and coral not springing from every clod and stone.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker reports seeing angels at night knocking at the wine-house gate; they shape Adam’s clay and cast it into molds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Spirits of an unseen world pour “wildering wine” with the speaker, described as earth-bound.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker says that a duty was allotted to him, “mad as I am,” as Heaven aspires to be free from a heavy trust.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker says he and his friend have regained sweet peace; houris are described as dancing and draining thanksgiving cups.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The speaker remarks that with Fancy’s many “wisps” it is no wonder he has strayed, and notes that Adam was “by a grain bewrayed.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker asks to excuse the “wrangling sects” numbering seventy-two, saying they knock at Fable’s portal because Truth eludes their view.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A contrast is made between a lesser flame and “true fire” that consumes to ashes what the moth has stored.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The poem repeatedly urges “Despair not,” asserting that “Lost Joseph shall return to Kanaan’s land” and that gloom will bloom with flowers.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The poem says that even if the “flood of death” sweeps away life’s fabric, “Noah shall steer the ark o’er billows dark.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The poem states that if one is bent on the Ka‘bah, one may brave desert sand and be torn by acacia thorns, yet his suffering.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker says endurance, intellect, and peace have flown from his bosom, lured by an idol’s silver ear-lobes and heart of stone.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker describes an ‘image’ with piercing looks and ‘peris’ beauty, slender shape, In CLVII, the speaker urges a companion to cast off deceptive religious garb, drink wine, behave like drunken men who lift the veil from fate’s mystery, and even threaten to seize paradise’s delights; the poem ends with a self-check that such boasting exceeds the limits of their “rug.” In CLIX, the speaker declares himself Love’s slave yet free of both worlds, recalls an angelic origin and a fall into an earthly cloister via Adam, says paradise images fade beside the beloved’s street, and ends by asking that his tears be dried lest he perish in their rushing tide.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker calls on a companion to remove a worn “dress” associated with cheating and to draw a line through an emblem of deceit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker proposes sacrificing convent revenues and alms for wine and passing a dervish-robe through a “vintry’s fragrant flood.”","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker says they will dash forth intoxicated, take wine from a feasting foe’s stores, and by force bring the foe’s “charmer” out of doors.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Fate is described as concealing her mystery behind a veil; the speaker claims that
